videos.blurb: The official Service reference — types, selectors, Endpoints, and virtual-IP behavior that this module's debugging drills are built on.

modules.title: Helm: Charts, Values & Templating
modules.summary: Package Kubernetes manifests the way professionals do: chart anatomy, values and templating, releases and revisions, install/upgrade/rollback — and the panel's 'why Helm instead of plain YAML' answered properly.
objectives: Describe chart anatomy (Chart.yaml, values.yaml, templates) and what a release and revision are
Render and debug templates with helm template, predicting output from values
Perform installs, upgrades, and rollbacks and read revision history
Argue 'why Helm instead of plain YAML' as a structured panel answer
Author an original chart for a multi-resource app following chart best practices

notes.title: Chart Anatomy: Chart.yaml, values.yaml, templates/
notes.body: A Helm chart is a directory: Chart.yaml (metadata: name, version, appVersion, dependencies), values.yaml (default configuration values), templates/ (Go-templated Kubernetes manifests), and optionally charts/ (bundled subcharts) and _helpers.tpl (named template definitions). Worked example: a chart named payments, version 1.3.0. values.yaml sets replicaCount: 2, image: {repository: payments, tag: v9}. templates/deployment.yaml contains replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }} and image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}". Installing renders those placeholders into a real Deployment with replicas: 2 and image payments:v9. The key insight: the chart is the PACKAGE (versioned, shareable, pinned by version), values.yaml is the DEFAULT CONFIGURATION, and the release is the chart installed with specific values — one chart, many releases (dev, staging, prod) differing only in values. This separation is what lets a single reviewed artifact deploy safely to every environment without copying manifests.

notes.title: Values and Templating: Predicting Rendered Output
Releases, Revisions, and Rollback
notes.body: Installing a chart creates a RELEASE (a named instance: helm install payments ./payments-chart -n shop); every helm upgrade creates a new REVISION of that release, and Helm keeps the history. Worked example: release payments is at revision 3. You upgrade with a bad image tag — pods CrashLoopBackOff. helm history payments shows revisions 1-4 with statuses; helm rollback payments 3 reverts to revision 3's values and manifests, and the Deployment rolls back. Solution notes: rollback is fast because Helm stored every prior rendered manifest — but it rolls back VALUES too, so a config change bundled with the bad image also reverts (usually what you want). Guardrails: helm upgrade --atomic auto-rolls-back on failure, and --wait makes the command block until pods are ready instead of declaring victory at manifest-apply time. Revisions are your time machine — but only if you upgrade through Helm, never by hand-editing the live objects.

notes.title: Panel: Why Helm Instead of Plain YAML?
notes.body: Panel question: 'Why Helm instead of plain YAML?' Model answer, structured: 'Parameterization — one chart deploys to dev, staging, and prod with different values files instead of three copied YAML trees that drift. Versioning — charts are versioned packages, so I know exactly what 1.3.0 contains and can pin it. Lifecycle — install, upgrade, rollback, and uninstall are first-class operations with revision history; plain YAML has no rollback story. Reuse — one maintained chart (or a public one) serves every team instead of everyone hand-rolling Deployments. And hooks and tests — pre-install hooks for migrations, chart tests for smoke checks.' Worked contrast: the plain-YAML team keeps dev.yaml, staging.yaml, prod.yaml; a securityContext added to prod.yaml never reaches dev.yaml, and nobody can say which version is deployed where. Helm's values files make environment differences EXPLICIT and diffable — that's the operational win the panel wants named.

notes.title: Writing a Chart: Structure and Helpers
notes.body: Author charts like maintainers do. Worked example — chart for a two-tier app (api + postgres): Chart.yaml declares name: shop, version: 0.1.0, and a dependency on the bitnami/postgresql chart (helm dependency update fetches it into charts/). templates/ holds deployment.yaml, service.yaml, configmap.yaml for the api; _helpers.tpl defines named templates like shop.fullname and shop.labels used across every resource for consistent naming and labeling. values.yaml exposes ONLY what operators should change (replicaCount, image.tag, resources, ingress.host) — everything else stays in templates. The discipline: values.yaml is your chart's API — every value documented with a comment, sane defaults, required values validated with the required function ('required "db password needed" .Values.db.password') so misconfiguration fails at template time with a clear message, not as a CrashLoopBackOff at 2 AM.

notes.title: Safety: lint, template, dry-run, diff
notes.body: The chart safety pipeline catches errors before they reach the cluster. Worked example: you add a new value resources: {limits: {memory: 1Gi}} but indent it one space wrong in values.yaml — helm lint ./chart reports the schema issue; helm template --values prod.yaml ./chart renders and you spot replicas: <no value> where a typo'd .Values.replicacount returned nil (Go templates render missing values as '<no value>', not errors). helm install --dry-run=server goes further, validating against the real api-server without creating anything. Solution habit: lint → template → diff (helm diff upgrade, via plugin) → upgrade --atomic --wait. The panel-relevant story: 'I caught a nil image tag in helm template output during review — the pipeline would have deployed image :<no value> to prod.' Template-time verification is the cheapest verification there is.

cards.front: What are the three core parts of a chart, and what is a release?
cards.back: Chart.yaml (metadata), values.yaml (defaults), templates/ (templated manifests). A release is a chart installed with specific values — one chart, many releases.

cards.front: values.yaml sets replicaCount: 3; template has 'replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}'. Rendered output?
cards.back: replicas: 3

cards.front: What does the dash in {{- if }} do?
cards.back: Trims preceding whitespace/newline — controls blank lines in rendered YAML.

cards.front: Template references .Values.image.tag but values.yaml has no image key. What renders?
cards.back: <no value> — Go templates render missing values as '<no value>', not an error. Caught by helm template review.

cards.front: How do you preview rendered manifests without installing?
cards.back: helm template ./chart --values prod-values.yaml — renders locally; add --dry-run=server to validate against the api-server.

cards.front: Release payments is at revision 4 (broken). Command to revert to revision 3?
cards.back: helm rollback payments 3

cards.front: What does helm upgrade --atomic do?
cards.back: Automatically rolls back to the previous revision if the upgrade fails.

cards.front: Name three arguments for Helm over plain YAML.
cards.back: Parameterization across environments, versioned packages, and first-class install/upgrade/rollback with revision history (plus reuse, hooks, tests).

cards.front: What is _helpers.tpl for?
cards.back: Named template definitions (fullname, labels, selectors) reused across all resources for consistent naming/labeling.

cards.front: How do you force a clear error when a required value is missing?
cards.back: The required function: required "message" .Values.x — fails template rendering with your message.

cards.front: What does helm lint check?
cards.back: Chart structure and values/schema issues — the first static gate before template/install.

cards.front: Why should environment differences live in values files, not copied YAML trees?
cards.back: Differences become explicit, diffable, and reviewable — copied trees drift silently (the prod-only securityContext problem).

quiz.q: values.yaml: {replicaCount: 2, image: {repo: api, tag: v5}}. Template: 'replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}\nimage: {{ .Values.image.repo }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}'. Rendered?
choices: An error — nested values aren't allowed
quiz.explain: Straightforward value insertion: 2, api, v5. Nested maps are normal in values.yaml — the template path mirrors the structure.

quiz.q: values.yaml: {ports: [80, 443]}. Template: '{{- range .Values.ports }}\n- containerPort: {{ . }}\n{{- end }}'. Rendered?
choices: - containerPort: 80 only — range takes the first
quiz.explain: range iterates the list; '.' is each element in turn. Two iterations produce two list items.

quiz.q: values.yaml: {ingress: {enabled: false, host: x.example.com}}. Template: '{{- if .Values.ingress.enabled }}\nhost: {{ .Values.ingress.host }}\n{{- end }}'. Rendered?
choices: Empty — the if block is skipped
quiz.explain: enabled is false so the entire if block (including the host line) is skipped. Conditionals cleanly include/exclude whole manifest sections.

quiz.q: An upgrade deployed a bad image tag; pods are crash-looping. Fastest recovery?
choices: helm rollback <release> <last-good-revision> — restores prior manifests and values
Delete the chart and reinstall from scratch
Edit the live Deployment by hand
Wait for the image to be fixed upstream
quiz.explain: Rollback is the first-class recovery: Helm stored every revision's rendered manifests. helm history identifies the last good revision.

quiz.q: Panel: 'Why Helm instead of plain YAML?' Best answer?
choices: Parameterization per environment, versioned packages, and install/upgrade/rollback with revision history — environment differences become explicit values files instead of drifting YAML copies
quiz.explain: The three pillars — parameterization, versioning, lifecycle — plus the drift argument (copied trees diverge silently). That's the full-credit structure.

quiz.q: helm template output shows 'image: "payments:<no value>"'. What happened and what's the fix?
choices: The template references a value missing from values.yaml — add the value or use required/default to fail loudly or fall back
quiz.explain: <no value> means the values path doesn't exist. Fix by defining it, defaulting it (default "v1" .Values.image.tag), or required-gating it.

quiz.q: You want dev, staging, prod from one chart. How?
choices: One chart + three values files (values-dev.yaml, values-staging.yaml, values-prod.yaml) selected with -f at install/upgrade
Three clusters can't share a chart
quiz.explain: One chart, many value sets — the core Helm workflow. -f/--values overlays environment specifics onto shared defaults.

quiz.q: What does helm upgrade --wait change about the command?
choices: It blocks until the workloads report ready instead of returning at manifest-apply time
quiz.explain: --wait makes the command honest: success means pods actually became ready, not just that manifests were accepted.

quiz.q: A chart needs postgres. Best practice for including it?
choices: Declare it as a dependency in Chart.yaml and run helm dependency update — versioned, maintained upstream
Tell operators to install postgres manually first
quiz.explain: Dependencies keep charts composable and versioned; vendored copies rot. Subchart values are configurable via the parent's values.yaml.

items.prompt: values: {name: web, replicas: 4}. Template: 'name: {{ .Values.name }}-svc\nreplicas: {{ .Values.replicas }}'. Render?
items.answer:
name: web-svc
replicas: 4
items.explain: Literal text concatenates with the inserted value: 'web' + '-svc'. Trace character by character.

items.answer: replicas: 5
items.explain: eq compares the strings; env is prod so the if-branch renders, else is skipped.

items.prompt: values: {hosts: [a.example.com, b.example.com]}. Template: '{{- range .Values.hosts }}\n- host: {{ . }}\n{{- end }}'. Render?
items.answer:
- host: a.example.com
- host: b.example.com
items.explain: range over the two-element list; '.' is each hostname in order.

items.prompt: values: {}. Template: 'tag: {{ .Values.image.tag | default "stable" }}'. Render?
items.answer: tag: stable
items.explain: Missing value is nil; the default pipeline substitutes 'stable'. Pipelines read left to right.

items.prompt: values: {tls: true}. Template: 'port: {{ if .Values.tls }}443{{ else }}80{{ end }}'. Render?
items.answer: port: 443
items.explain: Inline if/else without dashes; tls is true so 443 renders. (Dashes only affect whitespace.)

items.prompt: templates/service.yaml uses {{ include "shop.fullname" . }} and _helpers.tpl defines shop.fullname as '{{ .Release.Name }}-{{ .Chart.Name }}'. Release 'pay', chart 'shop'. Render?
items.answer: pay-shop
items.explain: include renders the named template with the current scope ('.' passed along); .Release.Name=pay, .Chart.Name=shop.

items.prompt: values: {resources: null}. Template: 'memory: {{ .Values.resources.limits.memory }}'. Render?
items.answer: Renders '<no value>' (or errors on strict nil dereference in some Helm versions) — never rely on it; guard with if/default/required.
items.explain: Chained access into null is the classic template crash. Defensive templates check existence first.

items.prompt: Install chart ./api as release 'orders' into namespace shop with prod values. Full command?
items.answer: helm install orders ./api -n shop -f values-prod.yaml (--create-namespace if needed).
items.explain: install RELEASE CHART; -n scopes the namespace; -f overlays values. Order of args matters: release name before chart path.

items.prompt: Upgrade release 'orders' to a new chart version with staging values, auto-rollback on failure, waiting for readiness.
items.answer: helm upgrade orders ./api -n shop -f values-staging.yaml --atomic --wait
items.explain: --atomic = rollback on failure; --wait = block until ready. The safe-upgrade incantation.

items.prompt: List releases in namespace shop and show revision history of 'orders'.
items.answer: helm list -n shop; helm history orders -n shop
items.explain: list shows releases; history shows revisions with status — the two commands that answer 'what is deployed where'.

items.prompt: Uninstall release 'orders' but keep its history. Then really remove everything.
items.answer: helm uninstall keeps history by default now (use --keep-history explicitly on older); full removal is helm uninstall orders -n shop (history purged per retention).
items.explain: Modern Helm retains release history on uninstall; know your version's behavior before promising auditability.

items.prompt: Your values-prod.yaml sets image.tag: v10 but the deploy shows v9. Two possible causes?
items.answer: Another -f file later in the command overrode it (--set or a later -f wins), or the release was upgraded without -f values-prod.yaml (fell back to chart defaults).
items.explain: Value precedence: --set > later -f > earlier -f > chart defaults. Always re-pass -f on upgrade.

items.prompt: helm upgrade fails with 'cannot re-use a name that is still in use'. Meaning?
items.answer: You're running install for an existing release name — use upgrade, not install.
items.explain: Release names are unique per namespace; install vs upgrade is the oldest Helm gotcha.

items.prompt: You hand-edited the live Deployment; next helm upgrade reverts your edit. Why, and what's the rule?
items.answer: Helm owns the rendered manifests — upgrade re-applies chart state, wiping manual edits. Rule: all changes go through values/chart + upgrade.
items.explain: Helm is the source of truth once adopted; out-of-band edits are silently reverted. Drift detection (helm diff) catches this.

handsOnLab.title: Author and Operate an Original Chart
handsOnLab.brief: Write a Helm chart from scratch for a two-tier sample app (API + database dependency), parameterize it per environment, and operate it through install, upgrade, failed upgrade, and rollback.
steps: Scaffold with helm create demo, then strip it to only what your app needs; study each generated file before deleting.
Write Chart.yaml (name, version, appVersion) and add a database subchart dependency; run helm dependency update.
Define _helpers.tpl with fullname and labels named templates; use them in every resource.
Write templates for Deployment, Service, and ConfigMap using values for replicas, image tag, and resources; document each value in values.yaml.
Add a required-gated DB password value; verify helm template fails clearly when it's unset.
Create values-dev.yaml and values-prod.yaml differing in replicas, resources, and ingress host.
helm lint, then helm template with each values file; diff the two renders and confirm only intended differences.
helm install demo-dev ./demo -n dev -f values-dev.yaml --create-namespace; verify the app runs.
helm upgrade with a deliberately bad image tag and --atomic; observe the automatic rollback.
Break it on purpose (helm upgrade without --atomic), then helm rollback to the good revision; show helm history.
handsOnLab.deliverable: Original chart source, both values files, template renders, and a history transcript showing the failed upgrade and rollback.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: helm history shows the rollback revision as deployed, the app is healthy, and you can explain every line of your _helpers.tpl.

mockTask.q: Panel: 'Your team manages 40 microservices with plain YAML — one folder per environment per service. Deployments are scary and nobody knows what's in prod. Pitch Helm.'
choices: 'Helm is the industry standard, so we should adopt it.'

'One versioned chart per service replaces 120 drifting YAML trees; values files make env differences explicit and diffable; upgrades get revision history and one-command rollback; and shared chart patterns (helpers, required values) stop every team hand-rolling Deployment boilerplate.'
'Plain YAML can't do namespaces; Helm can.'
mockTask.explain: Pitch the concrete pains: drift (copied trees diverge), unknown prod state (no versioning/history), scary deploys (no rollback story), boilerplate sprawl. Then name Helm's answers to each. Panels promote the candidate who argues from operational pain, not fashion.

videos.title: Helm Quickstart
videos.blurb: The official Helm quickstart — install a first chart and grasp releases and values before this module's authoring and lifecycle drills.

modules.title: Terraform Fundamentals: Declarative IaC
modules.summary: Infrastructure as Code the Terraform way: declarative vs imperative, providers and resources, the init/plan/apply loop, state as the source of truth, removing resources safely — and the panel's Terraform-vs-Ansible opener.
objectives: Contrast declarative and imperative infrastructure management and explain why idempotency matters
Read and write basic HCL: providers, resources, variables, and outputs
Run the init/plan/apply workflow and interpret a plan's create/update/destroy actions
Explain what state is, how drift happens, and how to reconcile it
Remove infrastructure via config removal vs the removed block, and argue Terraform vs Ansible as a panel answer

notes.title: Declarative vs Imperative: Say What, Not How
notes.body: Imperative says HOW: 'run these commands in order' (a shell script creating a VM: az vm create, then configure, then tag — run it twice and you get two VMs). Declarative says WHAT: 'a VM with these properties should exist' — Terraform compares desired state to actual state and only acts on the difference. Worked example: an HCL block declares azurerm_resource_group.main with name 'rg-shop-prod' and location 'East US'. First terraform apply creates it. Second terraform apply — with zero changes — reports 'No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration.' Solution to 'why does this matter?': idempotency. The script is dangerous to re-run; the Terraform config is safe to re-run forever, which is what makes it reviewable in pull requests and runnable in pipelines. The panel one-liner: 'declarative describes the end state and converges; imperative describes steps and repeats them.'

notes.title: Providers, Resources, and HCL Blocks
notes.body: HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language) organizes config into blocks. terraform { required_providers } pins provider versions; provider 'azurerm' { features {} } configures authentication; resource 'azurerm_resource_group' 'main' { name, location } declares one real object — the block TYPE plus two LABELS (resource type, local name). Worked example: you need a storage account for the dev team. You write resource 'azurerm_storage_account' 'dev' with name 'stdevshop001', resource_group_name referencing azurerm_resource_group.main.name (a reference, not a copy — Terraform builds the dependency graph from it), account_tier 'Standard', account_replication_type 'LRS'. terraform init downloads the azurerm provider; terraform validate checks syntax. Solution insight: references create implicit dependencies — Terraform knows to create the resource group first because the storage account points at it. No ordering scripts needed; the graph does it.

notes.title: init / plan / apply: The Loop
notes.body: The workflow is always the same three steps. terraform init: downloads providers and configures the backend (one-time per working directory, re-run when providers change). terraform plan: refreshes state, diffs desired vs actual, and prints the action plan — '+' create, '~' update in place, '-' destroy, '-/+' replace. terraform apply: executes the plan after your confirmation. Worked example: you add the storage account block and run plan. Output shows: azurerm_storage_account.dev will be created (+), 1 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy. You review the name, tier, replication — then apply. Solution discipline: plan is the code review for infrastructure — in pipelines, plan runs on every PR and apply only on merge to main, with the plan artifact attached. Never apply without reading the plan: a '-' you didn't expect is someone's production database.

notes.title: State: The Source of Truth (and Drift)
notes.body: terraform.tfstate maps your config to real-world IDs — it's how Terraform knows that azurerm_resource_group.main corresponds to the actual Azure resource. Worked example (real panel scenario): a teammate manually adds a data disk to the VM in the Azure portal. Next terraform plan shows NO changes — because the disk isn't in config OR state, Terraform is blind to it. Then someone runs apply after an unrelated change and... still no changes to the disk, but now your documented infrastructure lies. Solution: reconcile deliberately — either terraform import the disk into state (adopting it: terraform import 'azurerm_managed_disk.example["disk1"]' <resource-id>, noting the for_each address escaping with quotes) and add the matching config, or delete it manually to restore truth. The rule: state + config = documented reality; anything outside both is shadow infrastructure. Backends (azurerm, s3) with state locking exist so two applies never corrupt this file.

notes.title: Removing Resources: Destroy vs the removed Block
notes.body: Panel question: 'What exactly do you do in the Terraform file to remove a resource?' Two mechanisms, different meanings. Worked example: the dev storage account is no longer needed. Option A — delete the resource block from config, run plan: Terraform shows '- destroy' for the storage account; apply deletes the REAL Azure resource. Option B — replace the block with a removed { from = azurerm_storage_account.dev, lifecycle { destroy = false } } block: plan shows the resource dropped from state but NOT destroyed — the real storage account keeps running, unmanaged. Solution guidance: use plain removal when you want the infrastructure GONE (decommissioning); use the removed block when the resource must keep running but leave Terraform management (handing ownership to another team/tool). The panel wants the distinction named precisely: 'deleting the block destroys on apply; the removed block forgets without destroying.'

notes.title: Panel: The Biggest Difference — Terraform vs Ansible
notes.body: Panel question: 'What's the biggest difference between Terraform and Ansible? If Ansible can create VMs, why not just use Ansible?' Model answer: 'State. Terraform keeps a state file mapping config to real resources, so it knows what exists, detects drift, and plans minimal changes — create, update, or destroy exactly what's needed. Ansible is procedural and stateless: a playbook runs tasks in order with no memory of what it did before, so removing a VM means writing explicit removal tasks, and drift between runs is invisible. That's why you don't manage VM lifecycles in Ansible: no plan/apply safety net, no drift detection, painful ordering for dependencies.' Worked contrast: decommissioning 20 VMs in Terraform = delete the blocks, review the plan's 20 destroys, apply. In Ansible = write a teardown playbook and hope it matches what the build playbook created. Each tool's strength: Terraform for PROVISIONING lifecycle, Ansible for CONFIGURATION of what's already there.

cards.front: Declarative vs imperative in one sentence each.
cards.back: Declarative: describe the desired end state; the tool converges to it. Imperative: describe the steps; the tool repeats them.

cards.front: Why is Terraform's apply idempotent while a shell script isn't?
cards.back: Terraform diffs desired vs actual state and acts only on differences; re-running with no changes does nothing. A script re-executes every command.

cards.front: What are the two labels in resource 'azurerm_resource_group' 'main'?
cards.back: Resource TYPE (azurerm_resource_group) and local NAME (main) — the name used for references like azurerm_resource_group.main.name.

cards.front: What does terraform init do? terraform plan? terraform apply?
cards.back: init: downloads providers, configures backend. plan: diffs desired vs actual, prints + create / ~ update / - destroy. apply: executes the plan.

cards.front: In a plan, what do '+', '~', '-', '-/+' mean?
cards.back: Create, update in-place, destroy, destroy-then-recreate (replace).

cards.front: What is terraform.tfstate and why must it be locked?
cards.back: The map from config to real resource IDs — Terraform's memory. Locking (via backend) prevents concurrent applies corrupting it.

cards.front: A disk was added manually in the portal. Plan shows no changes. Why?
cards.back: It's in neither config nor state — Terraform is blind to it. That's drift; reconcile via import (+config) or manual deletion.

cards.front: Import address for a for_each managed disk instance 'disk1'?
cards.back: terraform import 'azurerm_managed_disk.example["disk1"]' <resource-id> — quote the address so the shell doesn't eat the brackets.

cards.front: You delete a resource block from config and apply. What happens to the real resource?
cards.back: Terraform plans '- destroy' and DELETES the real infrastructure on apply.

cards.front: What does the removed block do differently?
cards.back: Drops the resource from state WITHOUT destroying it — the real infrastructure keeps running, unmanaged by Terraform.

cards.front: Biggest Terraform vs Ansible difference, in one breath?
cards.back: State: Terraform tracks real resources, plans minimal changes, and detects drift; Ansible is stateless/procedural — no memory, no plan, drift invisible.

cards.front: If Ansible can create VMs, why not manage VM lifecycles with it?
cards.back: No state/drift detection, no plan/apply safety review, and teardown requires hand-written removal tasks that can diverge from build tasks.

quiz.q: You run terraform apply twice in a row with no config changes. What does the second run do?
choices: Reports no changes — the diff of desired vs actual is empty
quiz.explain: Idempotency via state: the second apply diffs config against state+reality, finds no differences, and changes nothing. That's the declarative contract.

quiz.q: Plan output shows '-/+ azurerm_virtual_machine.web'. What will apply do?
choices: Update it in place with no downtime
Destroy and recreate it — expect replacement (and plan for the downtime/data implications)
quiz.explain: -/+ is replace: some arguments force replacement. Treat it as a new resource — data disks, IPs, and downtime need explicit handling.

quiz.q: A teammate added a data disk to the VM in the Azure portal. The team must KEEP it. Correct reconciliation?
choices: Delete it — manual changes are forbidden
terraform import the disk into state (with the for_each-escaped address) and add the matching config, so plan goes clean
Ignore it — plan shows no changes anyway
Delete the state file and re-apply
quiz.explain: The panel's drift scenario: import adopts the real resource into state, then config codifies it — desired, actual, and documented all agree again.

quiz.q: Panel: 'What exactly do you do in the Terraform file to remove a resource?'
choices: Run terraform destroy -target on the command line only
Delete the resource block → plan shows destroy → apply deletes the real resource; OR use a removed block to drop it from state without destroying
Comment it out — Terraform ignores comments
quiz.explain: Two precise mechanisms: block deletion destroys on apply; the removed block forgets without destroying. Name both and when each applies.

quiz.q: When would you use the removed block instead of deleting the block?
choices: When you want the infrastructure destroyed faster
When the real resource must keep running but leave Terraform management (e.g. handing ownership to another team)
When the resource is already destroyed
quiz.explain: removed { from=..., lifecycle { destroy=false } } = forget, don't destroy. The decommissioning path is plain block deletion.

quiz.q: Panel: 'Biggest difference Terraform vs Ansible?'
choices: State: Terraform tracks real resources and plans/detects drift; Ansible is stateless and procedural
quiz.explain: State is the structural difference — it gives you plan/apply review, drift detection, and lifecycle management. Everything else follows from it.

quiz.q: Why shouldn't VM provisioning live in Ansible playbooks?
choices: No state means no drift detection, no plan safety net, and teardown playbooks diverge from build playbooks
Ansible can't create VMs at all
quiz.explain: Ansible CAN create VMs (modules exist) — the argument is lifecycle: stateless tooling can't manage lifecycles safely. Provision with Terraform, configure with Ansible.

quiz.q: Two engineers run apply simultaneously without a locked backend. Risk?
choices: State corruption: both write terraform.tfstate, one overwrites the other, and reality diverges from state
quiz.explain: State is a single file both processes read-modify-write; without locking (azurerm/s3 backends provide it), concurrent applies corrupt it.

quiz.q: Where do provider credentials/secrets belong in a Terraform workflow?
choices: Hardcoded in provider blocks committed to git
Environment variables or a secret manager (e.g. Vault), injected at runtime — never in tfvars committed to git
In the state file — it's encrypted by default
quiz.explain: The session's real-world pattern: code on GitHub, secrets via env vars, tfvars excluded from git, Jenkins credential injection / Vault. State files can contain secrets — protect the backend too.

items.prompt: resource 'azurerm_resource_group' 'main' { name = 'rg-x' location = 'East US' } — what real object does this declare, and what is 'main'?
items.answer: One Azure resource group named rg-x in East US. 'main' is the local name for references (azurerm_resource_group.main.id).
items.explain: Type + local name + arguments. The local name never appears in Azure — only in your config's references.

items.prompt: resource 'azurerm_storage_account' 'dev' { resource_group_name = azurerm_resource_group.main.name } — what does the reference do?
items.answer: Pulls the RG's actual name AND creates an implicit dependency — Terraform creates the RG before the storage account.
items.explain: References are both data flow and ordering. No depends_on needed when the graph is inferable.

items.prompt: variable 'location' { default = 'East US' } and the resource uses location = var.location. How do you override at apply time?
items.answer: terraform apply -var 'location=West US' (or a .tfvars file / TF_VAR_location env var).
items.explain: Variables are the parameterization seam; -var, tfvars, and TF_VAR_* env vars are the three override paths.

items.prompt: output 'rg_id' { value = azurerm_resource_group.main.id } — when is this useful?
items.answer: After apply it prints the real ID; other configs/modules consume outputs as inputs (composition).
items.explain: Outputs are a module's return values — the composition mechanism for multi-config setups.

items.prompt: terraform { required_providers { azurerm = { source = 'hashicorp/azurerm' version = '~> 3.0' } } } — what does this pin and why?
items.answer: The provider source and version constraint (~> 3.0 = >=3.0, <4.0). Pinning prevents a provider upgrade from silently changing behavior.
items.explain: Unpinned providers are a supply-chain risk: init could fetch a new major version with breaking changes.

items.prompt: Plan shows '+ azurerm_storage_account.dev' and '~ azurerm_resource_group.main'. In one sentence, what happens on apply?
items.answer: The storage account is created; the resource group is updated in place (e.g. tags changed).
items.explain: Read plans as sentences: + create, ~ modify, - destroy. Every apply should be narratable before confirmation.

items.prompt: You see count = 3 on a resource. What does Terraform create, and how are instances addressed?
items.answer: Three instances: azurerm_x.name[0], [1], [2]. (for_each uses string keys instead.)
items.explain: count = indexed instances; for_each = keyed instances. for_each is preferred when instances have identity (removing one doesn't shift the others).

drills.title: Panel Q&A: Terraform vs Ansible & Lifecycle

items.prompt: Panel: 'Biggest difference between Terraform and Ansible?' 30-second answer.
items.answer: 'State. Terraform records every real resource in state, so it plans minimal changes and detects drift. Ansible is procedural and stateless — it runs tasks with no memory, so removal and drift are manual.'
items.explain: Lead with the one word (state), then the two consequences (planning, drift). That's the full-credit shape.

items.prompt: Panel: 'If Ansible can create VMs, why not just use Ansible?'
items.answer: 'Because lifecycle needs state: decommissioning in Terraform is deleting blocks and reviewing a destroy plan; in Ansible it's a separate teardown playbook that rots. And drift — manual portal changes — is invisible to Ansible but shows in Terraform plan.'
items.explain: Two concrete costs: teardown divergence and invisible drift. Concrete beats abstract in panels.

items.prompt: Panel: 'Walk me through a resource's full lifecycle, testing to prod.'
items.answer: 'Write config in a branch, plan on PR, apply to dev, promote the same config through stage/QA with per-env tfvars, plan against prod, apply with approval — state per environment, same code.'
items.explain: The session's real workflow: GitHub code, env-separated state, plan-as-review, gated apply. Same config, different tfvars.

items.prompt: Panel: 'The dev team needs a storage account; here are the container names. Codify it.' What do you write?
items.answer: A resource group + azurerm_storage_account + azurerm_storage_container with for_each over the container names (later a map of name→access type when requirements change to per-container access).
items.explain: This is the session's for_each scenario: start with a set of names, evolve to a map when per-item config appears.

items.prompt: Panel: 'Requirements changed — each container needs its own access type (private/blob/container). Modify the code.'
items.answer: Change for_each from a set of names to a map of name→access_type, and set container_access_type = each.value.
items.explain: The canonical for_each evolution: set → map when per-instance attributes appear. each.key/each.value carry the data.

items.prompt: Panel: 'How was Terraform run at your previous job — where were secrets?'
items.answer: 'Code on GitHub, secrets via environment variables — tfvars never committed. Jenkins injected credentials at runtime, with Vault for secrets and Consul for config/service discovery.'
items.explain: The session's actual answer: code in git, secrets out of git, injected at runtime. Memorize this shape — panels ask it verbatim.

items.prompt: When is Ansible the RIGHT tool alongside Terraform?
items.answer: Configuration management on already-provisioned machines — installing packages, templating app configs, rolling service restarts. Terraform provisions; Ansible configures.
items.explain: The complementary framing: it's not Terraform-vs-Ansible as rivals, it's lifecycle vs configuration — each doing what it's designed for.

handsOnLab.title: Your First Terraform Lifecycle
handsOnLab.brief: Write HCL for a resource group and storage account, run the full init/plan/apply loop, evolve the config with for_each, simulate drift, and practice both resource-removal mechanisms.
steps: Install Terraform; write main.tf with terraform/provider blocks (azurerm, pinned version) and one resource group.
Run terraform init and terraform validate; explain what init downloaded and where.
Add azurerm_storage_account with a reference to the resource group's name; run plan and narrate every line.
Apply; confirm in the portal/CLI, then run apply again and confirm idempotent no-changes.
Add azurerm_storage_container with for_each over a set of three container names; plan and apply.
Evolve: change for_each to a map of name→access_type (private/blob/container); plan shows in-place updates; apply.
Simulate drift: manually change a tag in the portal; run plan and observe Terraform detect it; revert via apply.
Simulate unmanaged drift: manually add a second storage account in the portal; confirm plan is blind to it; import it with terraform import and codify it.
Remove one container from the for_each map; plan shows destroy for that instance only; apply.
Delete the storage account block; review the destroy plan; apply. Then practice the removed block on the resource group (forget, don't destroy).
handsOnLab.deliverable: main.tf evolution (git commits per step), plan transcripts for the drift and removal scenarios, and a one-page lifecycle cheat sheet.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: You can narrate any plan line-by-line, explain what state contains, and choose correctly between block deletion and the removed block.

mockTask.q: Panel: 'Your Ansible playbooks already create VMs. Convince me we need Terraform too.'
choices: 'Terraform's state gives us plan/apply review, drift detection, and declarative lifecycle: decommissioning is deleting blocks and reviewing destroys, while Ansible teardown playbooks diverge from build playbooks and manual portal changes stay invisible. Keep Ansible for configuring the machines Terraform provisions.'
'Ansible can't create VMs, so we have no choice.'
mockTask.explain: Concede Ansible's strength (configuration), then land the lifecycle argument: state → plan review → drift detection → safe teardown. The winning frame is complementary, not replacement — 'Terraform provisions, Ansible configures' shows senior judgment, not tool tribalism.

videos.title: Terraform Tutorials
videos.blurb: HashiCorp's official tutorial library — start with the configuration-language and workflow tracks to ground this module's HCL and init/plan/apply notes.

cards.back: Configuration (.tf files), the state file (terraform.tfstate), and the real cloud infrastructure.
cards.front: What three things does terraform plan compare?

cards.back: The resource's provider ID, its attributes as last known, and dependency mappings — a JSON snapshot written by the last apply.
cards.front: What does terraform.tfstate store for each resource?

cards.back: Local state cannot be shared, is lost with the machine, and allows concurrent applies that corrupt state. Remote backends add shared storage plus locking.
cards.front: Why must a team use a remote backend instead of local state?

cards.back: It takes a lease on the state blob in Azure Storage; any second state-writing operation fails fast with a lock error.
cards.front: How does the azurerm backend implement state locking?

cards.back: It refreshes state against reality and reports drift without proposing any configuration changes — safe for CI drift alerts.
cards.front: What does terraform plan -refresh-only do?

cards.back: 0 = no changes, 1 = error, 2 = changes (drift or pending) detected. Pipelines alert on 2.
cards.front: What do exit codes 0, 1, 2 mean for terraform plan -detailed-exitcode?

cards.back: terraform state list
cards.front: Command to list every resource address tracked in state?

cards.back: terraform import <resource-address> <provider-id> — e.g. terraform import azurerm_storage_account.legacy <full Azure resource ID>.
cards.front: What is the exact syntax of terraform import?

cards.back: It does not create, modify, or delete cloud resources, and (classic CLI flow) it does not generate configuration — you write the resource block first.
cards.front: What does terraform import NOT do?

cards.back: A non-empty plan may propose replacing the disk, which would destroy the data on it. Fix the config until the plan is clean before committing.
cards.front: Why must terraform plan be empty after importing a data disk?

cards.back: Quote the full keyed address: terraform import 'azurerm_managed_disk.data["logs"]' <id> — single quotes stop the shell from interpreting the brackets.
cards.front: How do you import one instance of a for_each resource?

cards.back: Only after a human confirms no apply is actually running (check CI logs, ask the team). Never script it; a stale lock means a crashed run, not a free pass.
cards.front: When is terraform force-unlock acceptable?

items.answer: That Terraform has a label-to-ID mapping for that resource in state — it believes the object exists and will manage it. It proves nothing about whether the object still exists in Azure; refresh determines that.
items.explain: State list shows the map, not reality. A deleted-in-portal object still appears until refresh prunes it.
items.prompt: You run terraform state list and see azurerm_resource_group.main. What does that entry prove?

items.answer: Alert the team (Slack/email/ticket) that drift or pending changes were detected, and stop — it must not apply. Exit 2 is the drift signal.
items.explain: 0 = clean, 1 = error, 2 = differences found. The pipeline's job is detection, not remediation.
items.prompt: terraform plan -detailed-exitcode exits 2 in your drift-check pipeline. What does the pipeline do next?

items.answer: terraform state mv azurerm_resource_group.main azurerm_resource_group.primary
items.explain: state mv rewrites the label-to-ID mapping in the state file only; no provider API calls are made.
items.prompt: Name the exact command that renames a tracked resource without touching the cloud.

items.answer: Wait for their run to finish, then re-run. Do not force-unlock — the lock is doing its job.
items.explain: The lock error is the safe outcome. Force-unlock while an apply runs causes state corruption.
items.prompt: Your teammate's apply is running. You run terraform apply and get a lock error naming their run. What do you do?

items.answer: In a Blob container in the configured storage account (the key field names the blob); the lock is a lease on that blob.
items.explain: Backend block fields: resource_group_name, storage_account_name, container_name, key. Lease = lock.
items.prompt: Where does the azurerm backend store state, and what serves as the lock?

items.answer: To the configured remote backend (the Azure blob), not the local terraform.tfstate. The local file is no longer the source of truth.
items.explain: init -migrate-state copies existing state into the backend and rewrites the backend pointer.
items.prompt: After terraform init -migrate-state, where does terraform write state on the next apply?

items.answer: State must live in access-restricted storage (private container, RBAC/locked-down keys), never in git, and ideally with versioning so a bad write can be rolled back.
items.explain: State is a secrets-bearing artifact; treat its storage with the same care as a vault.
items.prompt: terraform show -json outputs secrets in plain text from your state pull. What does this imply for state storage?

items.answer: 1) Write the azurerm_managed_disk (and attachment) block matching reality. 2) terraform import each address with its Azure ID. 3) terraform plan until the plan is empty. 4) Commit the config.
items.explain: Import is zero-downtime adoption. The empty plan is the proof the block matches reality; anything else risks replacing the disk.
items.prompt: Panel: a VM data disk was added manually in Azure and must be kept. Give the four-step sequence.

items.answer: Change the block to disk_size_gb = 256 to match reality, then re-run plan. Never apply a replacing plan to a disk holding data.
items.explain: The block must describe what exists, not what you wish existed. Reconcile config to reality first.
items.prompt: You import the disk but plan shows it will be replaced because disk_size_gb differs (you wrote 128, reality is 256). Fix?

items.answer: terraform import 'azurerm_managed_disk.data["uploads"]' /subscriptions/S/resourceGroups/rg/providers/Microsoft.Compute/disks/d-uploads
items.explain: Single-quote the whole address; double quotes around the key are Terraform for_each syntax that must survive the shell.
items.prompt: Write the import command for the second instance of resource azurerm_managed_disk.data with for_each key "uploads" and disk ID /subscriptions/S/resourceGroups/rg/providers/Microsoft.Compute/disks/d-uploads.

items.answer: Bash treats ["uploads"] as a glob pattern — 'no matches found' error or a mangled address. The shell must never interpret the brackets.
items.explain: This is the exact failure the panel question probes: shell escaping, not Terraform syntax.
items.prompt: What happens if you run the for_each import without any quotes in bash?

items.answer: Yes, drift on a managed resource. Apply will revert the SKU to the config value (update in place), which may fight the autoscaler — the real fix is modeling the SKU properly or managing it outside Terraform.
items.explain: Terraform converges reality to config. Fighting automation with apply is a design smell.
items.prompt: An autoscaler changed a VMSS SKU outside Terraform. Next plan shows ~ sku. Is this drift, and what will apply do?

items.answer: Config-driven import with import blocks (Terraform 1.5+): declare import { to = ...; id = ... } blocks, review them in plan, and apply — bulk, reviewable, repeatable.
items.explain: Import blocks bring imports into the plan/apply workflow instead of one-off CLI commands.
items.prompt: You need to adopt 40 existing VNets. Doing 40 CLI imports by hand is error-prone. What modern Terraform feature helps?

items.answer: No. Import only writes the state file (the label-to-ID mapping). Zero cloud API changes were made — that is why it is safe for the data disk.
items.explain: Import is a bookkeeping operation: config address + provider ID -> state entry. Creation/modification only happens via apply.
items.prompt: After a successful import, terraform plan is clean. A teammate asks 'did import change anything in Azure?' Answer?

handsOnLab.brief: You will create a Docker container outside Terraform, adopt it with terraform import, reconcile the plan to empty, then simulate drift and observe detection. All work is local and safe; nothing leaves your machine.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: terraform plan returns 'No changes' with the container running, exit code 2 was observed after docker stop, and docker ps is empty after cleanup.
handsOnLab.deliverable: A lab directory containing main.tf, generated.tf (reconciled to an empty plan), and a DRIFT-LOG.md recording the exit code 2 observation and the state rm/re-import recovery.
steps: Verify prerequisites: run terraform version (>= 1.5) and docker info. If Docker is unavailable, install Docker Desktop first — the lab needs a real provider target.
Create ~/workspace/il28-m33-lab and write main.tf with the kreuzwerker/docker provider (~> 3.0) and an empty stub: resource "docker_container" "web" { }.
Outside Terraform, create the object to adopt: run docker run --name importlab --detach --publish 8080:80 nginx:latest, then confirm with docker ps.

Run terraform init, then adopt it: terraform import docker_container.web $(docker inspect -f '{{.ID}}' importlab). Read the output — note it says 'Import successful' and mentions state, not the cloud.
Run terraform plan. It errors on missing required arguments (image, name). This is expected: classic import does not generate configuration.

Run terraform show -nocolor > generated.tf to dump the imported state as config, then edit generated.tf: remove read-only attributes (ip_address, network_data, gateway, ip_prefix_length, id) and the deprecated links block.
Re-run terraform plan until it reports no changes. This empty plan is your proof the block matches reality — the same gate you would demand for the panel's data disk.
Inspect state: run terraform state list and terraform state show docker_container.web. Identify the container ID recorded in state.
Simulate drift: run docker stop importlab (a change made outside Terraform). Run terraform plan -detailed-exitcode; echo $? and confirm exit code 2 with a plan to restart the container.

Practice safe state surgery: run terraform state rm docker_container.web, then terraform plan — observe it now wants to CREATE (the object became invisible). Re-import it with the same import command to restore tracking.
Write a backend "local" block with a custom path, run terraform init -migrate-state, and confirm the state file moved to your chosen path.
Clean up: run terraform destroy -auto-approve, then docker rm -f importlab, and verify docker ps shows nothing left.

Write the azurerm_managed_disk and attachment blocks to match the real disk, terraform import both addresses, run terraform plan until it is empty, then commit
Leave it unmanaged and document it in the runbook — importing production disks is too risky
Run terraform apply with -target on the VM so Terraform discovers the disk automatically
mockTask.explain: Import is zero-downtime adoption: it only writes state, touching nothing in Azure. The empty plan is the safety gate — a non-empty plan could propose replacing the disk and destroying data. Deleting/recreating loses data; leaving it unmanaged keeps it invisible to drift detection forever; -target does not discover unmanaged objects.
mockTask.q: Panel: 'A data disk was added to a production VM directly in the Azure portal. It holds live application data, it is not in our Terraform repo, and leadership wants it under Terraform management with zero downtime. Walk me through exactly what you do.'

notes.body: Terraform reasons about three things: your configuration (.tf files, what you want), the state file (terraform.tfstate, what Terraform last believed existed), and the real cloud (what actually exists). Every plan is a three-way comparison. When you run terraform apply, Terraform saves a JSON snapshot of every resource it created — its provider ID, attributes, and dependencies — into terraform.tfstate. On the next run, it refreshes: it re-reads each real object and compares it against both the state and the config. Worked example: you create azurerm_resource_group.main in config, apply, and the state records its Azure ID. You then rename the resource block label from main to primary in the .tf file without changing anything else. terraform plan proposes to destroy the old object and create a new one — because the state maps labels to IDs, and the new label has no mapping. The fix is terraform state mv azurerm_resource_group.main azurerm_resource_group.primary, which renames the mapping with zero cloud changes. Key interview line: the state file is the map; the config is the destination; never confuse the two.
notes.title: State is Terraform's memory: config, state, reality
Remote backends: shared, locked, durable state

notes.body: State-writing operations — apply, import, state mv — acquire the backend lock first. If engineer A is mid-apply and engineer B runs terraform apply, B's run stops immediately with an error naming the lock holder, and makes zero changes. The lock releases when A's run finishes, even if it fails partway. Worked example of the failure mode locking prevents: without locking, A and B both read state at version 10. A creates a VM and writes version 11. B, still holding the version-10 snapshot, creates a disk and writes version 11 too — overwriting A's VM record. The VM now exists in Azure but in no state file: orphaned, untracked, billed forever. If a run crashes and leaves a stale lock, you confirm no apply is running (check CI logs, ask the team), then run terraform force-unlock <lock-id> — a deliberate manual step, never scripted. Interview line: locking turns a silent corruption into a loud, safe error; force-unlock is a human decision, not an automation step.
notes.title: State locking: what happens when two applies collide

notes.body:
Drift is any change made outside Terraform — a teammate resizing a VM in the portal, an autoscaler swapping a SKU, a disk added by hand. During refresh (the default first phase of plan and apply), Terraform re-reads each managed object; anything that differs from state is drift. Worked example: your config sets azurerm_virtual_machine.app vm_size = "Standard_D2s_v3". Someone changes it to Standard_D4s_v3 in the Azure portal. Next terraform plan shows:

  ~ vm_size = "Standard_D2s_v3" -> "Standard_D4s_v3"

The ~ means update in place: plan will revert the change to match config. Use terraform plan -refresh-only -detailed-exitcode for drift reporting in CI: exit code 0 means no drift, 1 means error, 2 means drift detected — your pipeline can alert on 2 without proposing changes. Critical nuance for the panel: objects Terraform never managed (like a hand-created data disk with no resource block) are invisible to drift detection — plan cannot see what it does not track. Drift only covers managed resources; unmanaged objects must be imported first, which is exactly the data-disk scenario.
notes.title: Drift: when reality diverges from state

notes.body:
terraform import maps an existing real object to a resource block in your configuration and writes it into state — it never creates, modifies, or deletes cloud resources. The workflow is: write the resource block (it can start nearly empty), run terraform import <address> <provider-id>, run terraform plan, and reconcile any diff by filling in attributes until the plan is clean. Worked example: a storage account stlegacydata was created in the portal. You write:

resource "azurerm_storage_account" "legacy" {
  name                     = "stlegacydata"
  resource_group_name      = "rg-data"
  location                 = "eastus"
  account_tier             = "Standard"
  account_replication_type = "LRS"
}

Then run terraform import azurerm_storage_account.legacy /subscriptions/<sub-id>/resourceGroups/rg-data/providers/Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/stlegacydata. Import succeeds; terraform plan then shows which attributes your block got wrong (for example, it may propose changing access_tier because the real account differs). You adjust the block until plan is empty. Only then is the object truly under management. Classic import does not generate configuration — you write the block. Terraform 1.5+ also offers import blocks for config-driven bulk import, but the CLI flow above is the panel answer.
notes.title: terraform import: adopt, don't rebuild

notes.body:
The panel question: a data disk was added to a VM manually in Azure. It is not in the repo, it must be kept (data on it), and the team wants Terraform to manage it. The trap answers are 'delete it and let Terraform recreate it' (data loss) or 'leave it unmanaged' (drift blindness forever). The correct sequence, worked end to end. Step 1: write the resource block matching the real disk:

resource "azurerm_managed_disk" "app_data" {
  name                 = "vm-app-data-disk-01"
  location             = "eastus"
  resource_group_name  = "rg-app"
  storage_account_type = "Premium_LRS"
  create_option        = "Empty"
  disk_size_gb         = 128
}

Step 2: import it — terraform import azurerm_managed_disk.app_data /subscriptions/<sub-id>/resourceGroups/rg-app/providers/Microsoft.Compute/disks/vm-app-data-disk-01. Step 3: also model the attachment with azurerm_virtual_machine_data_disk_attachment, importing it too (its ID is a composite of VM and disk IDs). Step 4: run terraform plan until it shows no changes, then commit. If plan still wants to replace the disk, your block does not match reality — fix the block, never apply a replacing plan onto a disk holding data. Say this sentence in the panel: 'Import is zero-downtime adoption; the plan must be empty before I commit, because a non-empty plan against a data disk is a data-loss risk.'
notes.title: Panel scenario: the manually added VM data disk

notes.body:
When a resource uses for_each, each instance's address includes its key in brackets: azurerm_managed_disk.data["logs"]. Your shell interprets brackets and quotes, so the address must be quoted as a single argument. The panel's exact command is: terraform import 'azurerm_managed_disk.example["disk1"]' <id> — single quotes around the whole address so the shell passes the double quotes through to Terraform untouched. Worked example: disks declared as

resource "azurerm_managed_disk" "data" {
  for_each = toset(["logs", "uploads"])
  name     = "vm-disk-${each.key}"
  ...
}

To import the logs disk: terraform import 'azurerm_managed_disk.data["logs"]' /subscriptions/<sub-id>/resourceGroups/rg-app/providers/Microsoft.Compute/disks/vm-disk-logs. Without the quotes, bash treats ["logs"] as a glob pattern and the command fails with 'no matches found' or mangles the address. On Windows PowerShell the same single-quote wrapping works. Verify with terraform state list afterward — you should see azurerm_managed_disk.data["logs"] listed. Interview one-liner: 'Single-quote the full address; the shell must never see the brackets.'
notes.title: Importing for_each resources: address escaping

handsOnLab.brief: You will build the panel's storage scenario as a reusable module, rehearse the list-to-map refactor against local_file resources (so plan/apply actually run with no cloud credentials), then author the real azurerm HCL and validate it.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: terraform plan after the phase-2 edit showed exactly one update + one addition; removing 'reports' destroyed only that file; terraform validate passes on the Azure HCL.
handsOnLab.deliverable: A lab directory with the working local_file module rehearsal (applied), the validated azurerm HCL, and PANEL-WALKTHROUGH.md narrating the list-to-map refactor.
steps: Create the layout: ~/workspace/il28-m34-lab with modules/files/{main.tf,variables.tf,outputs.tf}, plus root main.tf, variables.tf, environments/dev.tfvars.
In modules/files/variables.tf declare variable "files" of type map(string) with a description (filename -> file content).
In modules/files/main.tf write resource "local_file" "item" with for_each = var.files, filename = "${path.module}/${each.key}.txt", content = each.value.
In modules/files/outputs.tf expose output "file_names" as a name-to-path map using a for expression over local_file.item.
In root main.tf call the module with source = "./modules/files" and pass files = { logs = "private", reports = "blob" } (content simulates access type). Run terraform init.
Run terraform fmt -recursive and terraform validate. Fix any errors before continuing.
Run terraform apply -auto-approve. Verify two files exist and run terraform output file_names.

Phase-2 refactor: change the map to { logs = "private", reports = "container", uploads = "blob" } — one value changed, one key added. Run terraform plan and confirm it shows exactly one in-place update and one addition, nothing destroyed.
Apply, then remove "reports" from the map. Plan and confirm only item["reports"] is destroyed and its file deleted — key-based identity in action.

Now author the real Azure version: create azure/storage-account.tf with the azurerm_storage_account + azurerm_storage_container (for_each over a map(string) variable containers) from this module's notes, plus variables.tf and environments/dev.tfvars.
Run terraform validate on the Azure configuration (no credentials needed) and terraform fmt -check to confirm formatting.
Write PANEL-WALKTHROUGH.md: narrate the phase-1 to phase-2 change in five sentences, ending with the key-identity sentence, as you would say it to the panel.
handsOnLab.title: for_each Storage Pattern — Local Rehearsal + Azure HCL

choices: Add a count variable per access type and use count.index to pick the type
Change the collection to a map of name to access type, iterate with for_each, use each.key for the name and each.value for the access type
Write three separate resource blocks, one per container
Keep the list and add a second parallel list of access types indexed by count
mockTask.explain: The map refactor is the panel's expected answer: unchanged keys preserve instance identity, so plan shows only in-place access-type updates — no destroys. Count-based or parallel-list approaches reintroduce positional fragility; three hardcoded blocks do not scale.
mockTask.q: Panel: 'The dev team needs a storage account. They hand you three container names. Codify it in Terraform. (You whiteboard the for_each over toset.) Then: requirements changed — each container needs its own access type: private, blob, or container. How do you modify the code?'

notes.body: count creates N copies addressed by index: azurerm_storage_container.team[0], [1], [2]. for_each creates one instance per key: azurerm_storage_container.team["logs"]. The difference that matters is identity under change. Worked example: containers = ["logs", "reports", "uploads"] with count. Remove "reports" from the middle. Terraform now maps [0]=logs, [1]=uploads — the old [1] (reports) is destroyed and the old [2] (uploads) is destroyed and recreated as [1], because identity is positional. Two destroys and a recreate for a one-item removal, and the recreated container loses its blobs. With for_each over toset(["logs", "reports", "uploads"]), removing "reports" destroys only team["reports"]; logs and uploads are untouched because identity is the key. Interview rule: count for truly identical, fungible copies (three identical worker VMs); for_each whenever instances have names or individual settings — which is nearly always in real infrastructure.
notes.title: count vs for_each: index identity vs key identity

notes.body:
for_each accepts a map or a set of strings (use toset() to convert a list). Inside the block, each.key is the map key (or the set element), and each.value is the map value (or the same element for sets). Worked example — the panel scenario, phase 1. The dev team hands you container names; codify them:

resource "azurerm_storage_container" "team" {
  for_each              = toset(["logs", "reports", "uploads"])
  name                  = each.key
  storage_account_name  = azurerm_storage_account.data.name
  container_access_type = "private"
}

This creates team["logs"], team["reports"], team["uploads"], each named by its key. With a set, each.key and each.value are identical ("logs"), so use each.key for the name. The pattern to memorize: for_each = collection, name/address from each.key, per-instance settings from each.value. If you need different settings per instance, the collection must be a map — which is exactly what phase 2 of the scenario demands.
notes.title: for_each over sets and maps: each.key and each.value
Phase 2: requirements change — per-container access types
Modules: packaging the storage pattern for reuse
Variables, validation, and outputs

notes.body:
tfvars files assign values to variables: terraform.tfvars and *.auto.tfvars load automatically; anything else loads via -var-file. Worked example — environments/dev.tfvars:

account_name        = "stteamdatadev01"
environment         = "dev"
containers = {
  logs    = "private"
  reports = "blob"
}

environments/prod.tfvars:

account_name        = "stteamdataprod01"
environment         = "prod"
containers = {
  logs    = "private"
  reports = "private"
  uploads = "container"
}

Run with terraform plan -var-file=environments/prod.tfvars. The same module, two environments, zero code duplication — this is the enterprise pattern M35 builds on. Secrets rule: non-secret values may live in committed tfvars; anything secret goes in gitignored files (secrets.auto.tfvars in .gitignore) or environment variables (TF_VAR_db_password), never in the repo. Precedence to memorize: -var flags beat -var-file, which beats auto.tfvars, which beats defaults. Interview answer: 'tfvars separate what changes per environment from the code that stays identical.'
notes.title: tfvars: per-environment values, never in git for secrets

notes.body: Putting it together as you would in the panel whiteboard exercise. Layout: main.tf (provider + resource group), variables.tf, modules/storage/{main.tf,variables.tf,outputs.tf}, environments/{dev,prod}.tfvars. Step 1: terraform init — downloads the azurerm provider and registers the local module. Step 2: terraform fmt -recursive — canonical formatting; unformatted code fails CI lint gates. Step 3: terraform validate — checks syntax and type consistency without credentials; it catches a map(string) fed to a list(string) variable instantly. Step 4: terraform plan -var-file=environments/dev.tfvars -out=tfplan — review: 1 storage account + 2 containers to add, keys team["logs"] and team["reports"]. Step 5 (the phase-2 change): add uploads = "container" to dev.tfvars, re-plan — output shows exactly one addition, team["uploads"], and nothing else. That single-addition plan is the observable proof of key-based identity, and narrating it is what turns a code sample into a panel-winning answer.
notes.title: Full walkthrough: assembling and verifying the scenario

notes.body: Four traps to memorize. Trap 1: for_each over a list — rejected; for_each needs a map or set of strings, so wrap lists in toset(). Trap 2: unknown keys at plan time — if the map comes from a resource attribute not known until apply (e.g., a computed ID), Terraform errors with 'for_each value depends on resource attributes'; the fix is deriving keys from variables or data known at plan time. Trap 3: mixing count and for_each in one block — forbidden; pick one. Trap 4: referencing instances — with for_each you cannot use splat-index syntax like team[*].name reliably for keyed lookup; use values(azurerm_storage_container.team)[*].name for lists or a for expression { for k, c in azurerm_storage_container.team : k => c.name } for maps. Worked example of the for expression producing a name-to-ID map for outputs: output "container_ids" { value = { for k, c in azurerm_storage_container.team : k => c.id } }. Interview line: 'for_each failures are almost always about keys not being known at plan time.'
notes.title: Common for_each traps and how to dodge them

objectives: Choose correctly between count and for_each and explain the identity consequence of each.
Convert a list of names into a map of name-to-setting to give each instance its own configuration.
Implement the panel's storage-account scenario end to end: containers from a list, then per-container access types.
Author reusable modules with variables, validation, and outputs, wired with tfvars per environment.
Predict plan behavior when items are added, removed, or reordered in for_each and count collections.

Destroys all three and recreates two

quiz.q: for_each = ["logs", "reports"] (a raw list). What happens?

Maps are exempt from replacement rules

quiz.q: In the panel scenario phase 2, why does changing the map to per-container access types cause no recreation?

quiz.explain: Module block arguments map to variable declarations in the child module. Outputs go the other direction (child to caller).
quiz.q: A module block sets account_name = "stx". Inside the module, which declaration receives it?

quiz.explain: Precedence: -var flags > -var-file > auto.tfvars/terraform.tfvars > defaults. CLI flags always win.
quiz.q: You pass -var="environment=prod" and also have environment="dev" in terraform.tfvars. Which wins?

quiz.explain: Secrets never enter the repo. Env vars (TF_VAR_name) or gitignored secret files keep them out of version control; they still land in state, which is why state storage is locked down (M33).
quiz.q: Where should a database password used by Terraform live?

choices: Plan succeeds and defers the instances
Error: for_each value depends on resource attributes that cannot be determined until apply
Instances are created in alphabetical order
quiz.explain: for_each keys must be known at plan time — Terraform needs the full instance set to plan. Derive keys from variables or data sources, not computed attributes.
quiz.q: for_each keys derived from a resource attribute that is only known after apply. Plan result?

notes.body:
The panel question 'walk me through Terraform from testing to prod' wants a promotion story, not a command list. Here is the shape: an engineer branches from main, writes or edits Terraform in a feature branch, and opens a pull request. CI runs terraform fmt -check, terraform validate, and terraform plan -var-file=environments/dev.tfvars, posting the plan as a PR comment. A reviewer approves; merge to main triggers apply to the dev environment automatically. Promotion is a second PR (or a release pipeline) that runs plan against stage with -var-file=environments/stage.tfvars; stage must be green — including QA's sign-off — before the same artifact (the same commit, the same saved plan file) is applied to prod, usually with a manual approval gate. Worked layout:

environments/{dev,stage,qa,prod}.tfvars
modules/...          # shared, versioned

No environment has its own copied code — only its own tfvars. The discipline the panel listens for: the exact plan file applied to prod was reviewed at the PR stage (terraform plan -out=tfplan, then terraform apply tfplan), so prod never applies a surprise.
notes.title: The enterprise lifecycle: testing to prod walkthrough

notes.body:
The panel's 'how was Terraform run at your previous job' answer starts here: secrets arrived as environment variables, never as committed files. Terraform natively reads any variable named TF_VAR_<name> as the value for variable <name>, and providers read their own (ARM_CLIENT_ID / ARM_CLIENT_SECRET / ARM_TENANT_ID / ARM_SUBSCRIPTION_ID for Azure; AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID / AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY for AWS). Worked example — a CI step:

export TF_VAR_db_password="$DB_PASSWORD"
export ARM_CLIENT_SECRET="$AZURE_SECRET"
terraform plan -var-file=environments/prod.tfvars -out=tfplan

The tfvars file holds non-secret per-environment values (names, SKUs, regions); the secrets ride in the process environment, which the CI system populates from its own secret store and masks in logs. Two rules: never echo secrets (even masked values can leak via set -x — use set +x around secret handling), and remember env vars still end up in the state file, so state storage lockdown from M33 remains mandatory. Interview line: 'Code on GitHub, secrets in env vars, tfvars for everything non-secret per environment.'
notes.title: Secrets via environment variables: the panel's answer

notes.body:
The corollary the panel explicitly named: tfvars carrying secrets are never committed. The pattern is a committed template plus an ignored real file. Worked example — commit secrets.tfvars.example:

db_password = "REPLACE_ME"
api_key     = "REPLACE_ME"

And .gitignore contains:

*.tfvars
!environments/*.tfvars
!secrets.tfvars.example

So environments/dev.tfvars (non-secret) is tracked, while any secrets-bearing tfvars is ignored. CI generates the secrets file at runtime from its vault or uses TF_VAR_ env vars instead. Verify locally with git check-ignore -v secrets.auto.tfvars — it should print the matching ignore rule. The failure mode this prevents is real: committed AWS keys get scraped by bots within minutes and the account gets cryptomined before lunch. Interview line: 'If a secret ever touches a committed file, we rotate it — no exceptions, no matter how fast we caught it.'
notes.title: tfvars NOT in git: the secrets file discipline
Jenkins credential injection: withCredentials
HashiCorp Vault: dynamic secrets concept
Consul: service discovery and config concept

notes.body: Two ways to run one codebase against multiple environments. Workspaces: terraform workspace new dev creates a separate state (same backend, key prefixed with env:) while the code and variables stay identical — you switch with terraform workspace select prod and re-apply. Directories: environments/dev/main.tf (or one root with per-env tfvars, as in this module) keeps entirely separate state files and working directories. Worked comparison: workspaces are cheap and built in — terraform workspace list shows dev, stage, prod — but every workspace shares one backend configuration, so a backend outage or a mis-targeted select can hit the wrong environment, and secrets handling is identical across them. Directories (or separate tfvars per env with separate pipeline jobs) give blast-radius isolation: prod's state, credentials scope, and approvals are fully separate artifacts. The enterprise answer: directories (or distinct pipeline stages with their own state keys) for prod separation; workspaces for cheap personal/branch sandboxes. Interview line: 'Workspaces for experiments, directories for environments — prod deserves its own state, its own credentials, and its own gate.'
notes.title: Workspaces vs directories: separating environments
