handsOnLab.title: Ansible Playbooks, Roles, and register — Local Lab

choices: Terraform: delete the resource block and run terraform apply (planned, reviewed destroy). Ansible: write a task with state: absent and run it — no plan, no state, no preview
Both: delete the resource/task and the tool figures out the rest automatically
Terraform: run terraform destroy with no code change. Ansible: delete the playbook file
Terraform: comment out the provider block. Ansible: remove the host from inventory
mockTask.explain: Terraform removal is config-driven against tracked state: block deletion + apply yields a destroy plan you review first (with -target for emergencies and removed blocks for de-adoption). Ansible has no state or plan — removal is a state: absent task you authored and ran, with no safety net. Commenting the provider or dropping inventory entries does not delete anything in either tool.
mockTask.q: Panel: 'A Terraform-managed VM must be deleted. What exactly do you do in the Terraform file — and how does that differ from removing it with Ansible?'

notes.body:
An Ansible playbook is YAML: a list of plays, each play targeting hosts and running a list of tasks. Tasks call modules (apt, copy, service, template) with arguments. Ansible is idempotent by design — running the same playbook twice changes nothing the second time, because modules check state before acting. Worked example — site.yml:

---
- name: Configure web servers
  hosts: webservers
  become: true
  tasks:
    - name: Install nginx
      ansible.builtin.apt:
        name: nginx
        state: present
        update_cache: true

    - name: Ensure nginx is running
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: nginx
        state: started
        enabled: true

Run with ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini site.yml. Run it again: both tasks report ok (no change) instead of changed — that ok-on-rerun is idempotency, and the panel will ask you to demonstrate or explain it. Contrast with a raw shell script, which would reinstall and restart blindly every run. Interview line: 'Tasks describe desired state per resource; modules make reruns safe.'
notes.title: Playbooks, plays, tasks: the anatomy

notes.body:
Handlers are tasks that run only when notified by a changed task, and they run once at the end of the play even if notified multiple times. The classic use is restarting a service after its config changes. Worked example:

  tasks:
    - name: Deploy nginx config
      ansible.builtin.template:
        src: nginx.conf.j2
        dest: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
        mode: "0644"
      notify: Restart nginx

  handlers:
    - name: Restart nginx
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: nginx
        state: restarted

First run: template changes the file (changed) -> handler fires -> nginx restarts. Second run: file already matches (ok) -> no notify -> handler skipped. Predict-the-output drill: if three tasks all notify 'Restart nginx' and all three change, the handler still runs exactly once. Handlers also support listen for grouping (multiple handlers listening on one topic). Interview line: 'notify plus handlers is how Ansible avoids restarting services on every run — restarts happen only when config actually changed.'
notes.title: Handlers: react only when notified

notes.body:
Variables come from playbooks (vars:), inventory, group_vars/, or facts. Templates render Jinja2 (.j2) files with those variables. register — the panel's explicit question — captures a task's result into a variable for later tasks. Worked example:

  tasks:
    - name: Check free disk space
      ansible.builtin.command: df -h /var | tail -1
      register: disk_out
      changed_when: false

    - name: Show disk usage
      ansible.builtin.debug:
        msg: "VAR partition: {{ disk_out.stdout }}"

    - name: Fail if disk is over 90 percent full
      ansible.builtin.fail:
        msg: "Disk critically full: {{ disk_out.stdout }}"
      when: "'90%' in disk_out.stdout or '91%' in disk_out.stdout"

register stores stdout, stderr, rc, changed, and more; changed_when: false marks read-only commands so they report ok instead of changed (keeping reruns clean). when: gates tasks on the captured data. Interview answer to 'how do you capture command output': 'register the task into a variable, then use .stdout / .stdout_lines / .rc in debug, when, or fail — with changed_when: false on read-only commands.'
notes.title: Variables, templates, and register: capturing output

notes.body:
A role is a directory with a conventional layout — tasks/, handlers/, templates/, files/, vars/, defaults/, meta/ — that turns a playbook's logic into a shareable unit. Create one with ansible-galaxy init webserver; the layout appears with main.yml entry points in each directory. Worked example — roles/webserver/tasks/main.yml:

---
- name: Install nginx
  ansible.builtin.apt:
    name: nginx
    state: present
  notify: Restart nginx

and roles/webserver/handlers/main.yml holds the restart handler. Consume it from a playbook:

---
- name: Configure web tier
  hosts: webservers
  become: true
  roles:
    - webserver

Role variables layer cleanly: defaults/ (lowest priority, overridable) vs vars/ (higher). Galaxy (galaxy.ansible.com) hosts community roles, but enterprises usually vendor their own. Interview line: 'Roles are Ansible's modules from M34 — the reuse unit. Playbooks compose roles; roles compose tasks.' The panel's 'most interesting role' question is really asking whether you have built one — after this module's lab, you have.
notes.title: Roles: packaging automation for reuse

notes.body:
Inventory maps hostnames to groups; playbooks target groups, never individual machines by habit. INI and YAML formats both work, and groups nest via :children. Worked example - inventory.ini:

[webservers]
web01.example.com
web02.example.com

[dbservers]
db01.example.com

[prod:children]
webservers
dbservers

Variables attach per host or per group: a host line can carry ansible_user=deployer ansible_host=10.0.0.5, and a [webservers:vars] section sets values for the whole group. Host variables beat group variables beat play variables in the precedence chain - worth memorizing for debugging 'why did my variable not apply' questions. Ad-hoc commands skip playbooks for one-offs: ansible webservers -i inventory.ini -m ping checks connectivity, and ansible webservers -i inventory.ini -m ansible.builtin.apt -a 'name=htop state=present' --become installs a package across the tier in one line. At scale, static files go stale, so dynamic inventory (a plugin or script returning host JSON) queries Azure or AWS at run time - inventory always reflects reality. Interview line: 'Static inventory for the lab, dynamic inventory for the cloud - either way, groups are how one playbook addresses a whole tier.'
notes.title: Inventory: who Ansible talks to

notes.body: Ansible has cloud modules (azure_rm_virtualmachine and friends) that can create VMs, so the panel's challenge is fair — and the answer is about models, not features. Terraform is declarative with state: it records what it created, detects drift on every plan, and converges reality to config — including deleting what should not exist. Ansible is procedural without state: a playbook that creates a VM will happily create a second one on rerun unless you write careful idempotency guards, it cannot show you a plan of what will change, and it cannot detect that someone resized the VM in the portal. Worked contrast: delete the VM in the portal. Terraform: next plan shows '1 to add' — it knows. Ansible: rerunning the playbook recreates it only if your tasks check existence first; nothing ever reports the deletion. The enterprise answer: Terraform provisions the platform (the relatively static, expensive, stateful layer — VNets, VMs, storage), Ansible configures inside it (packages, files, services — the fast-changing layer). Use each for its strength; the panel wants that sentence, not a tool war.
notes.title: Panel deep-dive 1: if Ansible can create VMs, why not just use Ansible?
Panel deep-dive 2: removing resources — Terraform vs Ansible

notes.body: Memorize this matrix; the panel's 'biggest difference' question is answered by the first row. | Dimension | Terraform | Ansible | |---|---|---| | Model | Declarative desired state + state file | Procedural tasks, no state | | Change preview | terraform plan (reviewable diff) | --check mode (best effort, not a true plan) | | Drift detection | Built in — refresh on every plan | None — reruns only converge what tasks cover | | Removal | Config deletion + apply = planned destroy | state: absent task you authored, no preview | | Language | HCL | YAML playbooks | | Agent | Agentless (provider APIs) | Agentless (SSH/WinRM) | | Sweet spot | Provisioning: networks, VMs, storage, DNS | Configuration: packages, files, services, app deploys | | Multi-cloud | One workflow, provider plugins | Cloud modules exist but config mgmt is the strength | | Secrets | Via Vault provider / env (M35) | Ansible Vault (encrypted vars/files) |. The synthesis the panel rewards: they are complements, not competitors — Terraform builds the datacenter, Ansible configures the servers inside it, and Jenkins (M38) orchestrates both. Say: 'I provision with Terraform, configure with Ansible, and I can tell you exactly where each one's job ends.'
notes.title: The comparison matrix: Terraform vs Ansible

objectives: Author playbooks with plays, tasks, handlers, and variable use that run idempotently.
Capture command output with register and branch on it with conditionals and debug.
Structure automation as roles and target hosts with inventory files and groups.
Answer the panel's deep questions: why not use Ansible for everything, and how removal differs between the tools.
State exactly what to change in a Terraform file to remove a resource (config removal + apply vs removed block vs destroy -target).

choices: The task failed silently the second time
Idempotency — the module checked state and made no change on rerun
quiz.explain: Modules check current state before acting. 'ok' on rerun with no changes is the observable definition of idempotent.
quiz.q: A task installs nginx. First run reports 'changed', second run reports 'ok'. What does this demonstrate?

choices: Once, at the end of the play
quiz.explain: Handlers are deduplicated: notified handlers run exactly once at the end of the play, no matter how many tasks notified them.
quiz.q: Three changed tasks all notify 'Restart nginx'. How many times does the handler run?

quiz.explain: register captures the result object (stdout, stderr, rc, changed). The panel asks this verbatim: 'capture command output' = register.
quiz.q: You need the output of df -h for a later conditional task. What do you add to the command task?

quiz.explain: changed_when: false tells Ansible a read-only command never counts as a change, keeping reruns clean and handlers quiet.
quiz.q: A read-only 'check disk' command reports 'changed' every run, spamming handlers. Fix?

choices: defaults/main.yml — lowest, meant to be overridden
quiz.explain: defaults/main.yml holds overridable defaults at the lowest role precedence; vars/main.yml overrides them. The consumer sets values at play/inventory level to beat both.
quiz.q: Where do role default variables live, and what is their precedence?

choices: Both detect and report the deletion
Terraform plan shows '1 to add' (state knows it is missing); Ansible reports nothing unless tasks explicitly check existence
Ansible detects it via facts; Terraform needs refresh
quiz.explain: State is the difference: Terraform compares tracked objects to reality every plan. Ansible has no memory of what it created, so a missing VM is invisible unless your tasks probe for it.
quiz.q: Panel: 'Someone deleted the VM in the portal. Contrast what happens on the next Terraform plan vs the next Ansible playbook run.'

choices: Delete the resource block and apply
Add a removed block with lifecycle { destroy = false } and apply
Run terraform destroy -target on it weekly
quiz.explain: The removed block drops the object from state without destroying it — de-adoption. Plain block deletion would destroy the running VM.
quiz.q: You must decommission a Terraform-managed VM but another team will keep using the actual machine. What do you do?

choices: Delete it in the portal and let the next plan recreate it
terraform destroy -target=azurerm_virtual_machine.old now, then remove the block from config and commit
quiz.explain: destroy -target is the one-off escape hatch, but the config still declares the VM — without removing the block, the next full apply recreates it. Both steps are required.
quiz.q: Emergency: a Terraform-managed VM must be deleted RIGHT NOW, before you can edit code. Safe sequence?

choices: Model: declarative desired state + state file vs procedural tasks with no state
quiz.explain: The model row is the fundamental difference; language and transport are surface. State vs no-state explains plan, drift, and removal differences.
quiz.q: Which row of the comparison matrix answers 'biggest difference between Terraform and Ansible'?

choices: Second run is a clean no-op
Two VMs — the task has no state to know the first exists
CI blocks the second run automatically
quiz.explain: Without state or an explicit idempotency guard, procedural reruns repeat the creation. This is the concrete reason Terraform provisions and Ansible configures.
quiz.q: An Ansible playbook creates a cloud VM with no existence check. It runs twice via CI. Likely outcome?

cards.back: The practice of merging every developer's changes into a shared branch frequently (at least daily) and validating each merge with an automated build and test run.
cards.front: What is continuous integration (CI)?

cards.back: Continuous delivery keeps every change deployable to production but requires a human decision to release. Continuous deployment promotes every green change to production automatically.
cards.front: Continuous delivery vs continuous deployment — the difference?

cards.back: A policy checkpoint in a pipeline — a measurable condition (e.g., coverage >= 80%, zero critical CVEs) that must hold before the pipeline may proceed to the next phase.
cards.front: What is a quality gate?

cards.back: The immutable packaged output of the build phase (container image, zip, chart), tagged with the commit SHA. The same artifact is promoted through every environment — never rebuilt.
cards.front: What is a pipeline artifact?

cards.back: A branching strategy where all developers commit to a single main branch at least daily, using feature flags for incomplete work. Minimizes merge conflicts; needs strong tests.
cards.front: What is trunk-based development?

cards.back: A branching model with long-lived develop and master branches plus feature, release, and hotfix branches. Gives explicit release control; accumulates merge debt.
cards.front: What is GitFlow?

cards.back: Moving one immutable artifact through dev → staging/QA → production, with quality gates between environments. Rollback = redeploying the previous known-good artifact.
cards.front: What is environment promotion?

cards.back: Unit tests exercise one function/class in isolation — fast, cheap, run first. Integration tests exercise components together — slower, need infrastructure, run later.
cards.front: Unit test vs integration test in a pipeline?

cards.back: A minimal post-deployment check that the system is up and its critical paths respond (e.g., homepage loads, login works). Fast signal that a deploy is not fundamentally broken.
cards.front: What is a smoke test?

cards.back: Canary shifts a small percentage of traffic to the new version and watches metrics before full rollout. Blue-green swaps all traffic at once between two identical environments for instant rollback.
cards.front: Canary deployment vs blue-green deployment?

cards.back: The pipeline definition lives in version control alongside the application (Jenkinsfile, workflow YAML), so changes are reviewed, versioned, and reproducible like any other code.
cards.front: What does 'pipeline as code' mean?

cards.back: Fail fast and fail cheap: a unit-test failure in 30 seconds saves the minutes that scanning, packaging, and environment deploys would have wasted on already-broken code.
cards.front: Why run the cheapest tests first in a pipeline?

items.answer: Source (commit triggers the pipeline) → Build (compile, dependencies, lint) → Test (unit, then integration, then end-to-end, cheapest first) → Scan (CVE, secrets, static analysis) → Package (immutable artifact tagged with the commit SHA) → Deploy (promote through dev → staging → production with gates). One artifact built once, promoted everywhere.
items.explain: Panels want the canonical six phases in order plus the build-once-promote-everywhere discipline. Naming the SHA tag shows you understand artifact immutability.
items.prompt: Panel: 'Walk me through the major phases of a CI/CD pipeline from commit to release.'

items.answer: In unit tests, run first in the Test phase. They are fast, cheap, need no infrastructure, and map one-to-one onto the changed code — so most defects die within seconds of the commit, before any scan, packaging, or environment time is spent.
items.explain: This is the expected one-line answer from the panel list. Add the economic reasoning (seconds of compute vs a production incident) to show depth.
items.prompt: Panel: 'Where do pipelines stop bad code most often?'

items.answer: A policy checkpoint: a measurable condition that must hold before the pipeline proceeds. I would enforce 100% unit-test pass as a hard gate and a coverage floor (e.g., 80%) that blocks packaging — plus zero critical CVEs in dependencies as a scan-phase gate.
items.explain: Define gate vs test, then name concrete, measurable gates. Coverage floors and CVE gates are the two most commonly expected examples.
items.prompt: Panel: 'What is a quality gate? Give me two you would enforce.'

items.answer: It depends on release cadence and risk tolerance. For a team shipping frequently with good coverage, trunk-based: daily integration, feature flags, trivial merges, fast pipeline. For audited, scheduled releases with sign-off, GitFlow: explicit release control at the cost of merge debt. I would ask about their cadence before committing.
items.explain: Never pick blindly — panels reward the conditional answer. State the trade (merge pain vs release control) and tie the choice to cadence.
items.prompt: Panel: 'Trunk-based or GitFlow — which would you pick for us and why?'

items.answer: Route a small percentage of production traffic to the new version and watch error rates and latency against the old version. If metrics stay healthy, increase the percentage until full rollout; if they degrade, halt with only a fraction of users affected.
items.explain: Panels check that you know canary is about graded traffic exposure plus metric-gated progression, not just 'deploying carefully'.
items.prompt: Explain a canary deployment to the panel in two sentences.

items.answer: Phase tells the category: the code is fine, so this is environment or configuration drift — wrong secret, missing env var, staging infra issue. I check the first failing deploy step, compare staging config against the last green deploy, and reproduce with the same deployment command locally if possible.
items.explain: Triage by phase: Deploy red with green Build/Test/Scan means the artifact is good and the environment or its configuration is the suspect. Compare against the last known-good state.
items.prompt: Your pipeline is red in the Deploy phase on staging but green everywhere else. What is your triage?

items.answer: Redeploy the previous known-good artifact tag — the immutable image from the last green run, identified by its commit SHA. Because artifacts are never rebuilt between environments, rollback is a fast promotion in reverse, not a new build.
items.explain: The SHA-tagged immutable artifact is what makes rollback safe and instant. Mentioning 'not a new build' shows you understand why build-once matters.
items.prompt: Panel: 'How do you roll back a bad production deploy?'

drills.title: Panel Drill: CI/CD Phases and Quality

handsOnLab.brief: You will build a small Python service with tests, then write a bash pipeline script that enforces the six phases with real quality gates. You will watch the pipeline stop a broken commit at the cheapest phase, then promote a green build through a fake staging and production promotion.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Breaking a test or dropping coverage below 80% makes ./pipeline.sh exit non-zero before the package phase; a green run promotes byte-identical artifacts to staging/ and prod/.
handsOnLab.deliverable: A git repo containing app.py, test_app.py, and pipeline.sh implementing all six phases with two working quality gates, plus a staging/ and prod/ directory holding the identical promoted artifact and a rollback script.
steps: Create a working directory cicd-lab, run git init, and configure a local user name and email.
Write app.py with a single function, e.g. apply_discount(price, percent), handling normal and edge cases.
Write test_app.py with pytest tests covering normal cases plus the zero-quantity edge case; run pytest and confirm green.

Write pipeline.sh with six labeled phases: build (python -m py_compile), test (pytest), scan (a grep-based secret check over the diff), package (tar the source as artifact named with the commit SHA), deploy-staging, deploy-prod.
Add quality gate 1: the test phase must exit non-zero on any failure so later phases never run — verify by breaking one test and running ./pipeline.sh.
Add quality gate 2: a coverage gate using pytest --cov=app --cov-fail-under=80; run the pipeline and confirm it passes.
Deliberately commit a change that drops coverage below 80 (a new untested branch) and watch the pipeline stop at the Test phase before packaging.
Revert the bad change, rerun ./pipeline.sh, and confirm all six phases go green end to end.
Simulate promotion: make deploy-staging copy the artifact to a staging/ directory and deploy-prod copy the identical file to prod/ — assert both files have the same SHA-256 checksum.
Add a rollback step to pipeline.sh that redeploys the previous artifact from an artifacts/ history directory; test it by deploying a bad tag then rolling back.
Write a one-paragraph incident note describing which phase caught which failure during this lab, as you would in a post-incident review.
Clean up: commit the final pipeline.sh and note the total wall-clock time of a green run — that is your feedback-loop budget.
handsOnLab.title: Simulate a Commit-to-Release Pipeline Locally

choices: Commit → build → deploy to production → monitor; most bad code is stopped by production alerts.
Source → build → test (unit first) → scan → package (immutable SHA-tagged artifact) → deploy with gates between environments; most defects are stopped by unit tests early in the test phase.
Commit → scan → merge → release branch → manual QA; most bad code is stopped by the release manager.
Build → test everything in parallel → package → deploy; phase order does not matter as long as tests exist.
mockTask.explain: The canonical order is source, build, test, scan, package, deploy. Unit tests run first because they are the cheapest, fastest feedback — that is where pipelines stop the most defects. The artifact is built once and promoted unchanged; phase order matters because each phase is a progressively more expensive filter.
mockTask.q: Panel: 'Walk me through the major phases of a CI/CD pipeline from commit to release, and tell me where most bad code gets stopped.'

notes.body: Every CI/CD pipeline, regardless of tool, runs the same logical gauntlet. (1) Source: a commit lands on a tracked branch and triggers the pipeline. (2) Build: compile code, resolve dependencies, and run linters — produce binaries or bytecode. (3) Test: execute the automated suite, cheapest tests first. (4) Scan: static analysis, dependency vulnerability scanning, and secret detection. (5) Package: build an immutable artifact (container image, zip, Helm chart) and tag it with the commit SHA. (6) Deploy: promote the artifact through environments toward production, with gates between them. Worked example: a developer pushes commit a1b2c3d fixing a null check. The pipeline compiles the Java service (Build, 40s), runs 240 unit tests (Test, 90s), scans with a CVE database (Scan, 60s), builds image orders-api:a1b2c3d (Package, 45s), and deploys to staging (Deploy, 30s). Total feedback time is about four and a half minutes, and every step is reproducible from the SHA. The key discipline: the artifact built once in Package is the same artifact deployed everywhere — you never rebuild between staging and production, because rebuilding reintroduces untested variance.
notes.title: From Commit to Release: The Six Pipeline Phases

notes.body: Ask a panel where pipelines catch the most defects and the honest answer is unit tests, run early and fast. The reasoning is economic: a bug caught by a unit test costs seconds of compute; the same bug caught in production costs incident response, rollback, and customer trust. Unit tests run in milliseconds each, need no infrastructure, and map one-to-one onto the code that just changed, so they give the tightest feedback loop in the pipeline. Worked example: a pull request changes a discount-calculation function. The pipeline runs 1,800 unit tests in 22 seconds; two fail because the new branch mishandles a zero-quantity edge case. The developer fixes it before any container is built, before any scan runs, before any environment is touched. Had the failure surfaced only in the staging integration tests 20 minutes later, the developer would have context-switched twice. Design rule: order your Test phase by cost — unit first, then integration, then end-to-end — and make the cheap phase a hard gate. If unit tests fail, nothing downstream runs; you do not spend scan and packaging minutes on code already known to be broken.
notes.title: Where Pipelines Stop Code Most: Unit Tests

notes.body: A quality gate is a policy checkpoint inside a pipeline: a measurable condition that must hold before the pipeline may proceed. Gates differ from tests in that they assert properties of the whole change, not behaviors of individual functions. Typical gates: unit-test pass rate of 100 percent, line coverage at or above 80 percent, zero critical-severity CVEs in dependencies, no secrets detected in the diff, and lint with zero errors. Worked example: a team sets a coverage gate of 80 percent. A PR adds 200 new lines but only 120 are covered by tests, dragging total coverage from 84 to 77 percent. The gate fails the build at the Test phase, the artifact is never packaged, and the developer gets a precise message: add tests for the uncovered branches in billing.py. Without the gate, the under-tested code would have shipped silently. Implement gates as first-class pipeline steps that exit non-zero on violation, not as advisory warnings humans must remember to read. A gate that only warns is decoration; a gate that blocks is policy. Keep the gate list short and stable — every gate you add taxes every future build, so each one must earn its minutes.
notes.title: Quality Gates: Fail Fast, Fail Cheap

notes.body: Branching strategy decides how often code integrates, and integration frequency decides how painful merges are. Trunk-based development has every developer commit to a single main branch at least daily, behind feature flags when work is incomplete; releases are cut from trunk whenever it is green. GitFlow maintains long-lived develop and master branches plus feature, release, and hotfix branches, with formal merge ceremonies between them. Trunk-based minimizes merge conflicts and keeps the pipeline fast because there is one branch to keep green; it demands strong test coverage and feature flags, since half-finished work lands on main. GitFlow gives explicit control over what goes into each release, which suits scheduled, audited releases, but merge debt accumulates and the pipeline must validate many branch combinations. Worked example: a five-person team shipping a SaaS product weekly chooses trunk-based with flags; their pipeline stays under five minutes and merges are trivial. A bank shipping a core ledger quarterly with regulatory sign-off chooses GitFlow; the release branch gets a dedicated hardening pipeline. Interview line: pick the strategy that matches release cadence and risk tolerance, and be able to defend the trade.
notes.title: Trunk-Based Development vs GitFlow

notes.body: Environments are isolated copies of the system at different trust levels, and promotion is the controlled movement of one immutable artifact upward through them. Dev is the developer's sandbox: fast, disposable, seeded with fake data. QA or staging mirrors production as closely as affordable — same container images, same database engine, realistic data volumes — because this is where integration, performance, and acceptance tests run. Production is the real system with real data and real users, and nothing enters it except through the pipeline. Worked example: image payments:9f2e1a passes unit tests and scans, then deploys to staging where a load test reveals a connection-pool leak. The image is rejected in staging, fixed in a new commit, and only image payments:44bd07c — built once, tested everywhere — is promoted to production. Environment parity is what makes staging results trustworthy: if staging runs a different database version than production, a green staging run proves nothing. Rollback is promotion in reverse — redeploy the previous known-good artifact tag, which is why every artifact carries its commit SHA and every deployment is recorded.
notes.title: Environments: Dev, Stage/QA, Prod and Promotion

notes.body: When a pipeline goes red, the fastest engineers triage by phase, not by panic. First, read which phase failed — Build, Test, Scan, Package, Deploy — because the phase tells you the category of the problem. Second, read the first failing assertion or command, not the last log line; everything after the first failure is usually cascade noise. Third, reproduce the smallest failing unit locally before touching the pipeline. Worked example: a run fails in the Scan phase with 'CRITICAL CVE-2024-XXXX in libfoo 2.3'. The first failure is the scanner exit code, not the 400 lines of download logs above it. The fix is to bump libfoo to the patched 2.4 in requirements, which you verify locally with the same scanner invocation the pipeline uses, then push. Notice what you did not do: you did not rerun the whole pipeline hoping it passes, and you did not edit the pipeline YAML to skip the scan. Common failure fingerprints to memorize: Build red means dependency or compile error; Test red means behavior regression; Scan red means known vulnerability or leaked secret; Deploy red means environment or configuration drift. State the phase, the first failure, and the smallest reproduction — that is the whole triage method.
notes.title: Anatomy of a Pipeline Failure: Reading the Run

objectives: Name and sequence the six phases of a commit-to-release pipeline and state the purpose of each.
Explain why unit tests stop more defects in pipelines than any other phase, and design a pipeline where they run first and fast.
Define quality gates and place at least three concrete gates (coverage, vulnerability, lint) in a pipeline diagram.
Compare trunk-based development with GitFlow and choose a branching strategy for a given team size and release cadence.
Describe the role of dev, stage/QA, and production environments in promotion and rollback.

quiz.explain: The canonical order is Source → Build → Test → Scan → Package → Deploy. Scanning (vulnerability, secrets, static analysis) runs after tests pass and before the immutable artifact is packaged.
quiz.q: In the canonical commit-to-release pipeline, which phase comes immediately AFTER test and BEFORE packaging?

choices: Unit tests, run early in the pipeline
quiz.explain: Unit tests stop the most defects because they are fast, cheap, need no infrastructure, and map directly onto the changed code — giving the tightest feedback loop. Bugs caught here cost seconds; the same bug in production costs an incident.
quiz.q: A panel asks where pipelines stop bad code most often. The best answer is:

choices: A pytest asserting a discount calculation
An integration test hitting the payments API
Requiring zero critical CVEs in dependencies before packaging
quiz.explain: A quality gate asserts a property of the whole change (dependency CVEs, coverage threshold, no leaked secrets), while tests assert behaviors of code. Gates are policy checkpoints; tests are behavior checks.
quiz.q: Which of these is a quality gate rather than a test?

quiz.explain: Trunk-based development with daily integration and feature flags suits small teams shipping frequently — merges stay trivial and the pipeline stays fast. GitFlow's ceremony pays off for audited, scheduled releases, not weekly SaaS.
quiz.q: A five-person SaaS team shipping weekly with strong test coverage should prefer:

choices: Because rebuilding between environments reintroduces untested variance
It does not matter as long as the commit is the same
quiz.explain: Rebuilding can pull different dependency versions or timestamps, so a rebuilt image is literally untested code. Build once, tag with the commit SHA, promote the identical artifact.
quiz.q: Why must the artifact deployed to production be the same artifact tested in staging?

choices: Exposing only a small percentage of traffic to the new version while metrics are watched
Requiring manual approval for every commit
quiz.explain: Canary rolls the new version out to a small traffic slice first. If error rates or latency spike, only a fraction of users are affected and the rollout halts before full exposure.
quiz.q: A canary deployment primarily reduces risk by:

choices: Rerun the pipeline until it passes
Skip the scan step to unblock the release
Identify the first failing finding, bump the library to the patched version, and verify with the same scan locally
Rebuild the container image with a newer base
quiz.explain: Triage by phase: Scan red means a known vulnerability. Fix the dependency at the source, reproduce the scan locally, then push. Rerunning or skipping the gate hides the finding instead of fixing it.
quiz.q: Your pipeline fails in the Scan phase reporting a critical CVE in a library. The correct first action is:

choices: A green staging run only proves something if staging resembles production
It is required by all cloud providers
quiz.explain: Staging exists to predict production behavior. If staging runs a different database version, OS, or configuration, passing tests there prove nothing about the production deployment.
quiz.q: Environment parity between staging and production matters because:

choices: All types in parallel regardless of cost
Only end-to-end, since they cover everything
quiz.explain: Order by cost: unit tests (milliseconds, no infra) first as a hard gate, then integration, then expensive end-to-end. Cheap failures stop the pipeline before expensive phases burn minutes.
quiz.q: Which ordering of test types in a pipeline follows 'fail fast, fail cheap'?

items.answer: Jenkins, with pipelines written in Groovy via Jenkinsfiles — declarative syntax for standard build-test-scan-deploy flows, dropping into scripted blocks for dynamic logic. I have also worked with YAML-based pipelines in GitHub Actions and Azure DevOps.

items.answer: Yes — a Jenkinsfile is a Groovy script. I use double-quoted strings when I want ${interpolation} evaluated by Groovy, single quotes when the shell should expand the variable, and script blocks for loops or conditionals that declarative steps cannot express.
items.explain: Answer yes, then prove it with the quoting rule — that is the shibboleth. Mentioning script blocks shows you know where raw Groovy lives inside declarative pipelines.
items.prompt: Panel: 'Can you write Groovy directly in a Jenkinsfile?'

items.answer: With a shared library: a versioned Git repo with vars/ steps (each <name>.groovy exposing call()) and src/ classes for logic. Each repo's Jenkinsfile becomes @Library('corp-lib@<version>') _ plus one call like standardPipeline(appName: 'x'). One library fix updates every repo; versioning prevents fleet-wide breakage.
items.explain: This is the canonical panel answer. Hit the four points: vars/src layout, @Library consumption, single-point fix, version pinning.
items.prompt: Panel: 'How would you standardize Jenkinsfiles across all our repos?'

items.answer: Answer honestly. If yes: describe the vars/ steps you wrote, who consumed them, and how you versioned releases. items.prompt: Panel: 'Have you written shared libraries?'

items.answer: Store it in the Jenkins credential store and bind by ID at runtime — environment { TF_TOKEN = credentials('terraform-cloud-token') } or withCredentials for scoped blocks. The value is injected as an env var, masked in console output, and never lives in the repo or the Jenkinsfile. I use single-quoted sh strings so Groovy never interpolates the secret.
items.explain: Connects Jenkins credentials binding to the Terraform-secrets panel question. The three guarantees — not in repo, not in Jenkinsfile, masked in logs — are what the panel is listening for.
items.prompt: Panel: 'How do you get secrets like a Terraform token into a Jenkins build safely?'

items.answer: Keep the pipeline declarative and put a script block inside the deploy stage: fetch the list, then loop over it generating the deploy steps in Groovy. Declarative for structure, scripted only for the dynamic part the grammar cannot express.
items.explain: This tests the declarative-vs-scripted judgment call. The expected pattern is script-inside-declarative, not rewriting the whole pipeline as scripted.

handsOnLab.brief: You will run Jenkins in Docker, create a declarative pipeline for a small app, bind a fake secret with withCredentials, then extract the common logic into a local shared library and watch every repo-style Jenkinsfile shrink to three lines.

notes.body: Jenkins offers two pipeline dialects. Declarative pipeline is the opinionated, structured form: a pipeline block containing agent, stages, and post sections with a fixed grammar that Jenkins validates before running. Scripted pipeline is raw Groovy on top of the Jenkins DSL — a node block with full programmatic freedom: loops, try/catch, dynamic stage generation. Prefer declarative for nearly everything: it is readable, it fails fast on syntax errors, and Blue Ocean renders it cleanly. Reach for scripted (or a script block inside declarative) only when you need genuine programming — generating stages from a matrix in code, or complex retry logic the declarative directives cannot express. Worked example: a declarative pipeline with stages Checkout, Build, Test, and a post block that always publishes JUnit results covers 90 percent of services. The moment you need 'run the deploy stage once per region in a list fetched from an API at runtime,' you drop a script block inside the declarative stage and write the loop in Groovy. Rule of thumb for the panel: declarative by default, scripted by exception, and be able to name the exception.
notes.title: Declarative vs Scripted Pipelines

notes.body: When a panel asks whether you can write Groovy directly in a Jenkinsfile, they are checking that you know a Jenkinsfile IS a Groovy script executed by the Jenkins pipeline engine — not a YAML file with steps. That means Groovy semantics apply: single-quoted strings are plain, double-quoted strings interpolate ${variables}, def declares local variables, and closures like { ... } appear in post conditions and parallel branches. Worked example: in environment { IMAGE = "orders-api:${env.BUILD_NUMBER}" }, the double quotes interpolate the build number at runtime, while sh 'echo $IMAGE' uses single quotes so Groovy leaves the dollar sign alone and the shell expands it. A classic bug is sh "docker build -t $IMAGE ." where Groovy interpolates $IMAGE before the shell sees it — correct here, but the same pattern with a password leaks it into the command string. Trace the evaluation order yourself: Groovy first (double quotes only), then the shell. If you can explain which layer expands which variable, you can answer every Groovy-in-Jenkinsfile question the panel has.
notes.title: Groovy in a Jenkinsfile: What the Panel Means

notes.body: The panel question 'how do you standardize Jenkinsfiles across repos' has one canonical answer: Jenkins shared libraries. Without one, forty repositories each carry a copy-pasted Jenkinsfile that drifts — one team pins an old scanner, another forgets the artifact push. A shared library is a separate Git repository Jenkins trusts, with two layouts: vars/ holds global steps as <name>.groovy files exposing a call() method (so vars/standardBuild.groovy is invoked as standardBuild(...)), and src/ holds plain Groovy classes for logic. Worked example — before: every repo's Jenkinsfile repeats 60 lines of checkout, build, test, scan. After: the library provides vars/standardPipeline.groovy with def call(Map config), and each repo's Jenkinsfile shrinks to @Library('corp-pipeline-lib') _ followed by standardPipeline(appName: 'orders-api', testCmd: 'pytest'). One fix to the scan step in the library updates all forty repos on their next build. Version the library with tags (@Library('corp-pipeline-lib@1.4')) so a library change cannot silently break every build at once.
notes.title: Standardizing Jenkinsfiles with Shared Libraries

notes.body: Jenkins must hand secrets to builds — registry passwords, cloud tokens, Terraform API keys — without ever printing them. Credentials binding does exactly that: secrets live in the Jenkins credential store (or an external vault), and the pipeline references them by ID; Jenkins injects them as environment variables and masks them in console output. Two patterns: the environment directive TF_TOKEN = credentials('terraform-cloud-token') binds a secret-text credential for the whole pipeline, and the withCredentials step scopes username/password or secret files to a block. Worked example: withCredentials([usernamePassword(credentialsId: 'acr-creds', usernameVariable: 'REG', passwordVariable: 'REG_PASS')]) { sh 'echo $REG_PASS | docker login myregistry.azurecr.io -u $REG --password-stdin' }. Note the single quotes around the shell command so Groovy never interpolates the secret, and --password-stdin so the password never appears in a process list. This is the same mechanism teams use for Jenkins credential injection of Terraform secrets: the token is bound at runtime, terraform apply reads it from the environment, and the value never lands in the repo, the Jenkinsfile, or the logs.
notes.title: Credentials Binding: Secrets Without Leaks

notes.body: An agent is where pipeline steps execute; a label routes work to the right machine. agent any runs on any available executor, agent { label 'linux-build' } pins the build to nodes carrying that label, and agent { docker { image 'maven:3.9' } } runs the stage inside a container on a capable node. Labels encode capabilities: operating system, installed toolchains, network access to a private registry, or a GPU. Worked example: a monorepo builds a Java service and a Python worker. The Jenkinsfile uses agent { label 'java-17' } for the service stage and agent { label 'python-311' } for the worker stage, so each runs where its toolchain exists instead of installing everything everywhere. A common failure is a pipeline stuck with 'Waiting for next available executor on linux-build' — the triage is to check the Nodes page for offline agents or a label typo, not to rerun the build. Keep labels coarse (linux-build, windows-test, docker-capable) rather than per-project; fine-grained labels fragment the executor pool and builds queue behind idle capacity.
notes.title: Agents, Labels and Executors

notes.body: The post section of a declarative pipeline defines what happens after stages complete, conditioned on the outcome: always, success, failure, unstable, changed. This is where pipelines earn their operational keep — publishing test reports, archiving artifacts, and notifying humans. Worked example: post { always { junit '**/target/surefire-reports/*.xml' } success { archiveArtifacts artifacts: 'dist/*.whl', fingerprint: true } failure { mail to: 'team@example.com', subject: "Build ${env.JOB_NAME} #${env.BUILD_NUMBER} failed" } }. The junit step turns XML into trend graphs; archiveArtifacts with fingerprinting lets Jenkins trace which build produced which artifact; the mail step fires only on failure so the team is not spammed by green builds. Failure hygiene rules: notify the channel that owns the breakage (not the whole company), include the direct link to the failed build (env.BUILD_URL), and keep the console log free of secrets so the failure link is safe to share. A pipeline that publishes results, archives artifacts, and pages the right people on red is a complete pipeline; one that only runs steps is a script.
notes.title: post Blocks, Notifications and Failure Hygiene

cards.back: A YAML file in .github/workflows/ that maps events (push, pull_request, schedule) to jobs of steps running on runners. The repo's CI/CD defined as code, triggered by GitHub events.
cards.front: What is a GitHub Actions workflow?

cards.back: Event triggers the workflow; jobs are parallel units of work on runners; steps run sequentially inside a job (shell commands or actions); runners are the VMs executing the jobs.
cards.front: Event vs job vs step vs runner in Actions?

cards.back: Declares job dependencies: needs: build makes the job wait for the build job and gives access to its outputs. Without needs, jobs run in parallel.
cards.front: What does needs: do in a workflow?

cards.back: strategy: matrix: runs one job definition once per variable combination (e.g., Python 3.11/3.12 × ubuntu/windows), substituting ${{ matrix.<var> }} — parallel coverage without duplicated YAML.
cards.front: What is a matrix strategy?

cards.back: With artifacts: actions/upload-artifact@v4 in the producing job and actions/download-artifact@v4 in the consuming job (which declares needs:). Runners are ephemeral, so files must be persisted explicitly.
cards.front: How do jobs share files in GitHub Actions?

cards.back: Artifacts pass files between jobs or preserve run outputs (reports, wheels). Caching (actions/cache@v4, keyed by lock-file hash) speeds repeat runs by reusing dependencies.
cards.front: Artifacts vs caching in Actions?

cards.back: A workflow with on: workflow_call that declares typed inputs and secrets, invoked from other workflows via uses: org/repo/.github/workflows/x.yml@ref — DRY for CI across many repos.
cards.front: What is a reusable workflow (workflow_call)?

cards.back: As ${{ secrets.NAME }}, stored in repo/organization/environment settings. Never hardcoded; passed explicitly into reusable workflows' declared secrets.
cards.front: How are secrets referenced in Actions?

cards.back: GitHub-hosted runners are managed VMs (ubuntu/windows/macos-latest) billed per minute. Self-hosted runners run on your infrastructure — needed for private networks, special hardware, or cost control.
cards.front: GitHub-hosted vs self-hosted runners?

cards.back: The pipeline hierarchy: stages (often one per environment, with approvals between) contain jobs, jobs contain steps (tasks or scripts). A deployment job targets an environment.
cards.front: Stages, jobs, steps in Azure DevOps?

cards.back: Reusable YAML fragments included with - template: path.yml plus parameters: — the Azure DevOps equivalent of shared libraries/reusable workflows for standardizing pipelines.
cards.front: What are Azure DevOps templates?

cards.back: When you need self-hosted control: exotic on-prem hardware, air-gapped networks, or custom agent fleets — and you accept owning the controller's upgrades, security, and scaling.
cards.front: When would you pick Jenkins over GitHub Actions?

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: '3.12'
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: pytest
items.explain: The canonical four steps. Note with: is nested under the setup-python step (indentation matters), and run: steps execute shell commands on the runner.
items.prompt: Write a job that checks out code, sets up Python 3.12, installs requirements, and runs pytest.

strategy:
  matrix:
    python-version: ['3.11', '3.12']
    os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest]
runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
# setup-python step:
with:
  python-version: ${{ matrix.python-version }}
items.explain: strategy.matrix defines the axes; runs-on and with: consume ${{ matrix.* }}. This yields 4 parallel runs from one job definition.
items.prompt: Extend that job with a matrix over Python 3.11/3.12 and ubuntu/windows. Show the strategy block and the setup-python line.

items.answer:
# in build:
- uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
  with: { name: wheel, path: dist/app.whl }
# in test:
needs: build
steps:
  - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
    with: { name: wheel, path: dist }
  - run: pip install dist/app.whl
items.explain: Upload names the artifact; download by the same name restores it. needs: build guarantees ordering — without it, test might run before the wheel exists.
items.prompt: Job build produces dist/app.whl; job test must install it. Show the artifact upload, the needs:, and the download.

# callee (.github/workflows/python-ci.yml):
on:
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      python-version: { required: true, type: string }
    secrets:

# caller:
jobs:

items.prompt: Sketch a reusable workflow's on: block that requires a python-version input and a pypi-token secret, and show how a caller invokes it.

    pool: { vmImage: 'ubuntu-latest' }
    steps:
    - script: pytest
- stage: Deploy
  dependsOn: Build
  jobs:
  - job: DeployJob
    steps:
    - script: ./deploy.sh
items.explain: Azure DevOps hierarchy is stages → jobs → steps. dependsOn: orders stages (jobs default to parallel within a stage), and trigger: [main] replaces GitHub's on: push.
items.prompt: Convert this requirement to Azure DevOps YAML: trigger on main, one Build stage (ubuntu-latest) running pytest, then a Deploy stage that depends on Build.

handsOnLab.brief: You will create a GitHub repository with a Python service, author a CI workflow with a build/test matrix and artifact passing, watch it run green on a real pull request, then extract the CI into a reusable workflow called from a second repo.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: The Actions tab shows a green run with 4 matrix jobs, a downloadable artifact on the build job, and a green run triggered through the reusable workflow pinned to @v1.0.
handsOnLab.deliverable: Two GitHub repos: actions-lab with a green matrix CI run, artifact-passing jobs, and a caller workflow pinned to @v1.0; platform-workflows with the reusable workflow; plus a validated azure-pipelines.yml and a platform-choice note.
steps: Create a new public GitHub repo actions-lab with app.py and test_app.py (a small tested function, e.g. a tax calculator).
Add .github/workflows/ci.yml: on push and pull_request to main; one job test on ubuntu-latest with checkout, setup-python 3.12, pip install, pytest.
Commit and push to main; open the Actions tab and confirm the first run goes green.
Add a matrix to the job: python-version ['3.11', '3.12'] and os [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest]; push and confirm 4 parallel runs.

Split into two jobs: build (pip wheel . then upload-artifact the dist/ folder) and test (needs: build, download-artifact, install the wheel, run pytest). Push and verify the artifact appears on the run page.
Add a pip cache step keyed on hashFiles('requirements.txt') before the install; push twice and note the second run's install step is faster.
Open a pull request that breaks one test; confirm the workflow fails on the PR and blocks merge if branch protection is on, then fix it and watch it go green.
Create a second repo platform-workflows with .github/workflows/python-ci.yml using on: workflow_call, declaring a python-version input.

Rewrite actions-lab's ci.yml to a four-line caller: on push/PR, one job with uses: <your-user>/platform-workflows/.github/workflows/python-ci.yml@main and with: python-version '3.12'. Push and confirm green.
Tag platform-workflows v1.0 and pin the caller to @v1.0; push and confirm the pinned run is green.

Draft azure-pipelines.yml in actions-lab mirroring the CI (trigger main, Build stage with pytest, Deploy stage dependsOn Build); validate the YAML parses with python -c 'import yaml,sys; yaml.safe_load(open("azure-pipelines.yml"))'.
Write a short comparison note: which platform you would choose for this repo and why, citing hosting, governance, and ecosystem.
handsOnLab.title: Ship a Real GitHub Actions Pipeline with Matrix, Artifacts, and a Reusable Workflow

choices: Write four separate workflow files, one per combination, and commit the wheel to git.
One workflow with a matrix over python-version and os (4 parallel jobs), a build job that uploads the wheel as an artifact, and a test job with needs: build that downloads it.
One job on ubuntu-latest only; Windows testing is unnecessary.
Run everything in a single step with a shell loop over versions.
mockTask.explain: A matrix expresses the configuration space (2 versions × 2 OSes = 4 runs) without duplicated YAML, and artifacts move the wheel between the ephemeral runners of the build and test jobs, ordered by needs:. Separate files and git-committed binaries are the anti-patterns.
mockTask.q: Panel: 'We need to test our Python service on 3.11 and 3.12, on Linux and Windows, and share the built wheel between the build and test stages. How do you structure this in GitHub Actions?'

notes.body: A GitHub Actions workflow is a YAML file in .github/workflows/ that maps events to automation. The mental model has four layers. Events (on:) decide when the workflow runs: push, pull_request, schedule, workflow_dispatch for manual runs. Jobs are units of work that run in parallel by default on runners — needs: creates ordering between jobs. Steps inside a job run sequentially on the same runner, each step either a shell run: command or a uses: reference to an action. Runners are the machines: GitHub-hosted (ubuntu-latest, windows-latest, macos-latest) or self-hosted on your infrastructure. Worked example: on: pull_request targeting main triggers a job test on ubuntu-latest whose steps check out the PR code (actions/checkout@v4), set up Python (actions/setup-python@v5), install requirements, and run pytest. Push a commit to the PR and the workflow reruns automatically — that is CI without a separate server. Secrets live in the repo or organization settings and are referenced as ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_TOKEN }}, never hardcoded; the ${{ }} expression syntax is evaluated by Actions before the runner sees the step.
notes.title: GitHub Actions: Events, Jobs, Steps, Runners

notes.body: A matrix strategy runs the same job once per combination of variables you declare, turning one workflow definition into N parallel runs. This is how projects test against multiple Python versions, operating systems, or dependency sets without duplicating YAML. Worked example: strategy: { matrix: { python-version: ['3.11', '3.12'], os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest] } } produces four job instances — 3.11/ubuntu, 3.12/ubuntu, 3.11/windows, 3.12/windows — each running the identical steps with ${{ matrix.python-version }} and ${{ matrix.os }} substituted. Add fail-fast: false when you want every combination to report even if one fails, so a Windows-only failure does not hide behind an early abort. Cost awareness matters: a 4-way matrix quadruples runner minutes, so matrix over versions you actually support, not every version ever released. The panel loves matrix questions because they test whether you think in terms of configuration space rather than copy-pasted jobs — if your answer to 'test on three OSes' is three jobs, you have missed the feature.
notes.title: Matrix Builds: One Workflow, Many Configurations

notes.body: Jobs run on fresh runners, so anything a later job needs must be persisted explicitly. Artifacts (actions/upload-artifact@v4 and actions/download-artifact@v4) carry files between jobs or preserve them after the run — test reports, built wheels, coverage HTML. Caching (actions/cache@v4) is different: it stores reusable dependencies keyed by a hash of the lock file, so pip or npm installs skip the network on repeat runs. Worked example: job build installs dependencies and uploads dist/ as artifact api-wheel; job test declares needs: build, downloads api-wheel, and runs pytest against it — the wheel travels through Actions storage, not through git. In the same workflow, actions/cache@v4 keyed on hashFiles('requirements.txt') makes the second run's pip install take seconds instead of minutes. Rules: artifacts expire (set retention-days deliberately), never put secrets in artifacts (anyone with repo read access can download them), and cache keys must include the lock-file hash or you will serve stale dependencies. Artifacts move work forward; caches make repeats cheap.
notes.title: Artifacts and Caching: Passing Work Between Jobs

notes.body: When ten repositories need the same CI, copy-pasting workflow YAML recreates the Jenkinsfile-drift problem from module 38. Reusable workflows solve it: a workflow with on: workflow_call declares typed inputs and secrets, and caller workflows invoke it with uses:. Worked example: the platform team publishes .github/workflows/python-ci.yml in a central repo with on: { workflow_call: { inputs: { python-version: { required: true, type: string } }, secrets: { pypi-token: { required: true } } } }. Each service repo then has a four-line workflow: on: push; jobs: { ci: { uses: org/platform/.github/workflows/python-ci.yml@main, with: { python-version: '3.12' }, secrets: { pypi-token: ${{ secrets.PYPI_TOKEN }} } } }. One fix to the central workflow updates every caller on their next run; pinning @main vs @v1.2 is the same versioning trade as Jenkins library tags. Note the constraints: the called workflow's jobs cannot directly use the caller's secrets unless declared and passed, and reusable workflows must live in the same or a referenced repository — they are composition, not inheritance.
notes.title: Reusable Workflows: DRY for Pipelines

notes.body: Azure DevOps expresses pipelines in azure-pipelines.yml with a four-level hierarchy: stages contain jobs, jobs contain steps, and steps run tasks or scripts. A stage typically maps to an environment (Build, Deploy-Dev, Deploy-Prod) with approvals between them; jobs within a stage can target different pools. Templates are the reuse mechanism: - template: templates/build.yml with parameters: factors out common steps the way shared libraries do in Jenkins. Worked example: trigger: [main] on pool vmImage ubuntu-latest, a Build stage with a job that uses the UsePythonVersion@0 task, runs pip install and pytest as script steps, then publishes results with PublishTestResults@2. A second Deploy stage dependsOn: Build and carries a deployment job targeting an environment with a manual approval check. Variables and variable groups hold configuration; secret variables are masked in logs like Jenkins credentials. For the panel: Azure DevOps shines where the team already lives in Azure — service connections to subscriptions, boards-to-pipelines traceability, and environments with approval gates map naturally onto enterprise release processes.
notes.title: Azure DevOps Pipelines: Stages, Jobs, Templates

notes.body: All three platforms run the same six pipeline phases from module 37; they differ in hosting, expression, and ecosystem fit. Jenkins is self-hosted and Groovy-based: maximum control, any agent you can provision, but you own upgrades, security, and scaling the controller. GitHub Actions is SaaS and YAML-based, colocated with the code: zero infrastructure, a vast marketplace of actions, per-minute billing — ideal when the repo already lives on GitHub. Azure DevOps is SaaS and YAML-based with first-class enterprise constructs: environments with approvals, service connections, variable groups, and tight Azure integration — ideal for Microsoft-centric enterprises. Worked example decision: a startup with all code on GitHub and no ops team picks Actions (no servers, marketplace actions cover everything). A bank standardized on Azure with change-advisory approvals picks Azure DevOps (environments plus approvals match the governance model). A team needing builds on exotic on-prem hardware picks Jenkins with custom agents. Panel line: there is no best platform, only best fit — name the team's constraints (hosting, governance, ecosystem) and match them.
notes.title: Choosing a Platform: Jenkins vs Actions vs Azure DevOps

objectives: Write a GitHub Actions workflow with triggers, jobs, steps, and actions, and explain the event → job → step → runner model.
Use a matrix strategy to run one workflow across multiple language versions or operating systems.
Pass build outputs between jobs with artifacts and speed up runs with caching.
Create a reusable workflow (workflow_call) and call it from another workflow with inputs and secrets.
Describe Azure DevOps pipelines (stages, jobs, templates) and compare the three platforms for a given team.

quiz.explain: pull_request with branches: [main] fires on PRs targeting main; workflow_dispatch: {} adds the manual 'Run workflow' button. push alone would fire on direct pushes, not PRs.
quiz.q: Which trigger runs a workflow on every pull request targeting main, plus manual runs?

quiz.explain: The matrix is the cartesian product: 2 Python versions × 2 operating systems = 4 parallel job instances, each with its own ${{ matrix.python-version }} and ${{ matrix.os }} values.
quiz.q: strategy: { matrix: { python-version: ['3.11', '3.12'], os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest] } } } creates how many job instances?

choices: build uploads with actions/upload-artifact@v4, test declares needs: build and downloads with actions/download-artifact@v4
quiz.explain: Each job gets a fresh runner, so files must move through artifact storage. needs: orders the jobs; upload/download moves the files. Caching is for dependencies, not inter-job outputs.
quiz.q: Job test needs the wheel built by job build. What is required?

choices: jobs: { ci: { uses: org/repo/.github/workflows/ci.yml@main, with: {...}, secrets: {...} } }
quiz.explain: Reusable workflows are called as a job's uses: with a repo path and ref, passing declared inputs via with: and declared secrets via secrets:. The callee must define on: workflow_call.
quiz.q: A reusable workflow is invoked from a caller with:

choices: It makes the matrix run faster
So every combination reports its result instead of cancelling the rest on the first failure
It is required for Windows runners
quiz.explain: Default fail-fast cancels remaining matrix jobs when one fails, which can hide other broken combinations. Setting false gives the full failure picture at the cost of more minutes.
quiz.q: Why is fail-fast: false sometimes set on a matrix?

choices: Templates — reusable YAML included with - template: plus parameters:
quiz.explain: Templates factor common steps into versioned YAML files included by reference, so one fix propagates to every pipeline that includes the template — the same DRY role as shared libraries.
quiz.q: In Azure DevOps, the equivalent of a Jenkins shared library for standardizing pipeline YAML is:

choices: Artifacts are encrypted per-user, so secrets are safe in them
Never put secrets in artifacts — anyone with repo read access can download them
Secrets in artifacts are automatically redacted
Artifacts can only be downloaded by admins
quiz.explain: Artifacts are downloadable by anyone who can read the repo. Secrets belong in the secrets store and are passed as masked environment variables, never persisted to files that leave the runner.
quiz.q: Which is true about secrets in GitHub Actions artifacts?

choices: Azure DevOps pipelines with environments and approvals
quiz.explain: Azure DevOps environments carry approval checks between stages and service connections plug directly into Azure subscriptions — the governance model the bank needs, without custom glue.
quiz.q: A bank needs manual approval gates between staging and production and deep Azure integration. Best fit?

choices: Inserts the stored secret's value at workflow evaluation time, masked in logs
Prints the secret to the log for debugging
Commits the secret to the repo
quiz.explain: The ${{ }} expression is evaluated by Actions before the runner executes the step, substituting the secret value while masking it in logs. The secret itself lives in repo/org settings, never in YAML.
quiz.q: What does ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_TOKEN }} do in a workflow step?

modules.summary: Moves from Jenkins to the YAML-native pipeline platforms: GitHub Actions workflows with events, runners, matrix builds, artifacts, and reusable workflows, plus Azure DevOps multi-stage pipelines and templates. You will write real workflow YAML, trigger real runs, and learn when each platform is the right choice.
modules.title: Modern Pipelines: GitHub Actions & Azure DevOps

drills.title: Panel Drill: Azure Storage, Vault, Monitor, and AKS Triage

handsOnLab.brief: Using the Azure CLI against your own subscription, you will build the Terraform scenario's target by hand: a storage account with per-container access types, a Key Vault holding a secret, diagnostic routing to Log Analytics, and a policy guardrail — then verify everything with read-only commands.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: az storage container show reports off/blob/container respectively; the secret round-trips; the Activity log lists the creation events; the policy assignment appears at the resource-group scope.
handsOnLab.deliverable: A resource group containing a StorageV2 account with three correctly-typed containers, a Key Vault with a retrievable secret and AuditEvent diagnostics flowing, and an Allowed-locations policy assignment — plus a lab-notes file with the resource IDs.
steps: Sign in with az login and set your subscription: az account set --subscription '<your-subscription-id-or-name>'.
Create the resource group: az group create --name rg-il28-lab --location eastus.

Create the storage account: az storage account create --name st<your-initials>il2801 --resource-group rg-il28-lab --location eastus --sku Standard_LRS --kind StorageV2 (keep the name 3–24 chars, lowercase alnum).
Create three containers with different access types: raw-uploads (--public-access off), thumbnails (--public-access blob), public-assets (--public-access container).
Upload a sample file to raw-uploads with az storage blob upload, then verify each container's access type with az storage container show.
Create the Key Vault: az keyvault create --name kv-<your-initials>-il28 --resource-group rg-il28-lab --location eastus.
Store a secret: az keyvault secret set --vault-name <vault> --name db-password --value 'LabOnly-1234!'; retrieve it with az keyvault secret show and confirm the value round-trips.
Create a Log Analytics workspace: az monitor log-analytics workspace create --resource-group rg-il28-lab --workspace-name law-il28-lab.

Enable diagnostics on the vault: az monitor diagnostic-settings create --name kv-diag --resource <vault-resource-id> --workspace <workspace-resource-id> --logs '[{"category":"AuditEvent","enabled":true}]' (get IDs with az keyvault show / az monitor log-analytics workspace show --query id).
Query the control plane: az monitor activity-log list --resource-group rg-il28-lab --max-events 5 -o table; identify your storage account creation event.

Find the built-in policy ID: az policy definition list --query "[?displayName=='Allowed locations'].id" -o tsv; then assign it to the resource group limited to eastus with az policy assignment create --name allowed-locations-il28 --policy <id> --params '{"listOfAllowedLocations":{"value":["eastus"]}}' --scope <rg-id>.

Verify: az policy assignment list --scope <rg-id> -o table shows the assignment; az vm list-usage --location eastus -o table shows current vCPU quota headroom. Document all four resource IDs in a lab-notes file.
handsOnLab.title: Provision Azure Core: Storage, Key Vault, Diagnostics, and Policy

choices: Write three separate azurerm_storage_container resources with hardcoded names and access types.
Use one azurerm_storage_container resource with for_each over a map variable of name → access type, setting container_access_type = each.value.
Create the containers in the Azure portal and import them later.
Use count over a list of names and set every container to private.
mockTask.explain: A map of name → access type with for_each is the panel's expected answer: one resource block, per-container access types, and adding a fourth container later means editing the variable, not the resource. Hardcoded blocks and count-over-list both fail the 'requirements changed' test.
mockTask.q: Panel: 'The dev team needs a storage account. They gave you three container names, and now the requirements changed — each container needs a different access type: private, blob, and container. How do you codify this in Terraform?'

notes.body: An Azure storage account is the container for all Azure Storage data services — blobs, files, queues, tables — and it is exactly what the dev team's Terraform scenario provisions. Three decisions define one: the name, which must be 3–24 characters, lowercase letters and numbers only, globally unique (stdataeast001 is valid; ST_Data-East is not); the performance/redundancy choice — Standard vs Premium tier, and LRS (three copies in one datacenter), ZRS (across zones), GRS (paired region); and the kind, usually StorageV2 (general-purpose v2) which supports all services and tiers. Worked example: the dev team needs durable object storage for nightly exports in East US. You choose name stexportseastus01, Standard tier, GRS for region-pair durability, kind StorageV2. In Terraform that is azurerm_storage_account with account_tier = "Standard", account_replication_type = "GRS". The panel checks two things here: that you know the naming constraints (they break many first attempts) and that you can justify the redundancy choice against cost — GRS doubles the storage bill versus LRS, so you pick it only when regional outage survival is a real requirement.
notes.title: Storage Accounts: The Terraform Scenario's Target

notes.body: Inside a storage account, blob containers hold the objects, and each container carries an access type that is a security decision: private (called off in the CLI) means every request needs authorization; blob means anonymous read access to individual blobs but not listing; container means anonymous read plus anonymous listing of the container's contents. The Terraform scenario's twist — requirements changing to per-container access types — is exactly why the module 34 solution iterates over a map of name → access type instead of a list of names. Worked example: the team asks for three containers: raw-uploads (private — unprocessed customer data), thumbnails (blob — the web app fetches images by direct URL), public-assets (container — a static site lists and serves files). In Terraform: variable "containers" = { raw-uploads = "private", thumbnails = "blob", public-assets = "container" } with for_each over the map and container_access_type = each.value. Interview rule: default everything to private and justify each relaxation. An anonymous-listable container holding anything sensitive is a breach waiting for a scanner to find.
notes.title: Blob Containers and Access Types: private, blob, container

notes.body: Azure Key Vault is the managed store for secrets (passwords, tokens, connection strings), cryptographic keys, and certificates — the place application credentials live instead of app settings or repos. The security model has two layers: the vault's firewall and access control decide who can reach the vault, and access policies (or Azure RBAC) decide which identities may get, list, or set which secrets. Worked example: the payments API needs a database password. You create the vault (az keyvault create --name kv-payments-east --resource-group rg-payments), store the secret (az keyvault secret set --vault-name kv-payments-east --name db-password --value '...'), grant the app's managed identity the 'Key Vault Secrets User' role, and the app fetches the password at startup via the vault URI — the value never appears in configuration files or pipeline logs. Rotation hygiene: enable rotation where the service supports it, version secrets (each set creates a new version), and alert on near-expiry for certificates. The panel's Key Vault questions always circle back to the same principle: no secret in code, no secret in config, no secret in logs — the vault is the single source of truth and managed identity is how workloads prove who they are.
notes.title: Key Vault: Secrets, Keys, Certificates

notes.body: Azure Monitor collects two fundamentally different signal types. Metrics are numeric time series (CPU percent, request count, blob capacity) — cheap, near-real-time, retained briefly, and the basis for alerts. Logs are rich records (who did what, full request details) — verbose, queryable with KQL in a Log Analytics workspace, retained longer, and the basis for investigation. Diagnostic settings are the bridge: you enable them per resource to route its platform logs and metrics to a Log Analytics workspace, a storage account, or an event hub. Worked example: to audit Key Vault access, you create a workspace (az monitor log-analytics workspace create), then az monitor diagnostic-settings create --name kv-diag --resource <vault-id> --workspace <workspace-id> --logs '[{"category":"AuditEvent","enabled":true}]'. Then in the workspace you run KQL: AzureDiagnostics | where ResourceProvider == "MICROSOFT.KEYVAULT" | where OperationName == "SecretGet" | project TimeGenerated, CallerIPAddress, ResultType. Metrics would tell you secret-gets per minute spiked; only the logs tell you which IP did it. Panel line: metrics for alerting, logs for investigating, diagnostic settings to connect the resource to the workspace.
notes.title: Azure Monitor: Metrics, Logs, Diagnostics

notes.body: Azure Policy is governance as code: definitions express rules ('resources must be in East US', 'only approved VM SKUs'), assignments scope them to a management group, subscription, or resource group, and effects decide the behavior — deny blocks the deployment, audit flags it, append/modify remediate it. Worked example: the platform team assigns the built-in 'Allowed locations' policy to the subscription with parameter listOfAllowedLocations = ["eastus"]. A developer's terraform apply targeting West US fails at plan time with a policy denial — the guardrail caught it before any resource existed. Quotas are the other ceiling: each subscription gets limited vCPUs per VM family per region, checked with az vm list-usage --location eastus. Hitting 'quota exceeded' on an AKS scale-up is not a bug; the fix is a support request to raise the quota, not a code change. Two more tools complete the observability picture: Resource Health reports whether Azure itself knows a resource is unhealthy (distinguishing 'my config is broken' from 'the platform is broken'), and Activity logs record every control-plane operation — who created, scaled, or deleted what and when — queryable with az monitor activity-log list.
notes.title: Azure Policy, Quotas and Limits

notes.body: When new AKS nodes fail to appear after scaling, work this checklist in order — it is the panel's expected answer verbatim. (1) Confirm the scale request: az aks nodepool scale --resource-group <rg> --cluster-name <cluster> --name <pool> --node-count <n>, then check the Activity log for the operation's status and error. (2) Cluster autoscaler: if enabled, check its profile and logs — it only scales on unschedulable pods, so no pending pods means no scale. (3) Pending workload: kubectl get events and describe the pending pods; 'Insufficient cpu/memory' tells you the demand side. (4) Quotas: az vm list-usage --location <region> — vCPU quota exhaustion is the most common silent blocker. (5) Region capacity and VM SKU restrictions: the requested SKU may be constrained in that region. (6) Subnet IP space: each node consumes IPs; an exhausted subnet stops scale with no obvious error. (7) Taints, labels, and max pods per node: misconfigured scheduling constraints leave nodes idle. (8) Service principal / managed identity permissions on the VNet and subnet. (9) Azure Policy: a deny assignment (wrong location, disallowed SKU) blocks node creation. (10) Resource Health and Azure Monitor for platform-side issues. Worked example: scale to 5 nodes, only 3 appear. Activity log shows the scale operation succeeded; quotas show 8 of 10 vCPUs used and each node needs 4 — the fourth node cannot fit. The fix is a quota increase, and the evidence trail is quota → Activity log, not guesses.
notes.title: Reference: AKS Node-Troubleshooting Checklist

notes.body: Exposing PaaS services to the internet by default is the opposite of the private-container rule from the storage note. Private Link gives Azure PaaS services — Storage, SQL Database, Key Vault, App Service, Container Registry — a private IP inside your VNet, so traffic never traverses the public internet. The DNS side is where implementations break: you create a Private DNS zone (e.g., privatelink.blob.core.windows.net for storage), link it to the VNet, and the zone carries the A record mapping the service's name to its private IP. Worked example: an AKS cluster must reach a storage account privately. You create the private endpoint in the cluster's VNet, the Private DNS zone privatelink.blob.core.windows.net with a VNet link, and verify from a pod that stdataeast001.blob.core.windows.net resolves to a 10.x address. For on-premises clients, conditional forwarding sends privatelink.* queries to the Azure DNS resolver. Related panel question: Application Gateway vs Load Balancer — the gateway is Layer 7 (HTTP routing, TLS termination, WAF; the classic browser → DNS → App Gateway → AKS backend-pool flow), while Load Balancer is Layer 4 (TCP/UDP distribution). Choose the gateway when you route by URL or host; choose the load balancer for raw throughput.
