quiz.q: A .NET shop on Entra needs a new Python analytics workload. Best approach per the framework?
choices: Force it onto the existing stack regardless of fit
Evaluate it independently: keep .NET on Azure, but allow the analytics workload on the best-fit platform with Terraform managing both
quiz.explain: The framework demands a written reason per workload: identity/skill fit keeps .NET where it is, while analytics gets its own evaluation. Dogma and anarchy both fail.

quiz.q: What does Terraform's portability NOT give you across clouds?
choices: Identical provider schemas and IAM models
quiz.explain: Providers expose entirely different schemas and identity models; only the workflow patterns and abstractions transfer. Assuming schema parity is the classic trap.

quiz.q: A module claims to support AWS and Azure but was only tested on AWS. What is the verdict?
choices: Abstraction without testing is fiction — test against every claimed provider in CI
quiz.explain: Untested provider paths rot silently on provider defaults and schema drift. The professional pattern requires CI-tested parity.

quiz.q: In the hypothetical bank case study, what is 'shadow multicloud'?
choices: Teams adopting clouds without security/governance knowledge
quiz.explain: Untracked adoption bypasses guardrails — the source of breaches and surprise bills. Governance first, provider second.

quiz.q: A proposal moves BI compute to another cloud while the 50 TB dataset stays put. What is the flaw?
choices: BI tools do not work cross-cloud
Metered egress on every refresh plus replica management dwarfs the tool's advantage — compute follows the data
quiz.explain: Data gravity: the transfer and replica costs dominate. Cost the replica plus egress formally before deciding.

quiz.q: Cardholder data must stay in-country and survive a region failure. Which design is correct?
choices: Single region, provider-managed keys, public endpoints
In-country primary + second in-country region, customer-managed keys, private endpoints, verified failover residency
Store it in two different countries for safety
Rely on the provider's compliance badge alone
quiz.explain: Residency plus resilience requires two in-country regions, CMK, no public-internet traversal, and verified — not assumed — failover residency.

quiz.q: Why is 'the cloud is compliant' a dangerous belief?
choices: Compliance is a property of your architecture plus attestations; you inherit the audit burden for everything you configure
Compliance does not apply to finance
quiz.explain: The provider's certifications cover their controls; your configurations, keys, networks, and IAM are your audit burden.

quiz.q: Three teams built their own networking on three clouds; 3 AM incidents are chaos. What is the structural fix?
choices: A central platform team publishing certified landing-zone modules with identical guardrails; new clouds require certification
quiz.explain: The cognitive cost is the problem; the platform team absorbs multicloud complexity behind one interface with enforced guardrails.

quiz.q: Which statement best captures the module's strategy thesis?
choices: Standardize the operating model; make provider exceptions explicit, reviewed, and temporary
quiz.explain: The thesis: governance and operating model are the standardization target; provider choice follows workload reasons with explicit exception handling.

items.prompt: 90 seconds: name the five lenses for choosing a cloud per workload.
items.answer: Service fit, team skill, commercial terms, latency/residency, exit cost.
items.explain: Recite all five, then apply: one written reason per workload, no dogma, no anarchy.

items.prompt: .NET on Entra plus a new Python analytics workload. Your recommendation?
items.answer: Keep .NET on Azure (identity + skill fit); evaluate analytics independently — best-fit platform, Terraform managing both.
items.explain: Per-workload reasoning beats single-cloud dogma and per-team anarchy.

items.prompt: What transfers across clouds in Terraform, and what does not?
items.answer: Transfers: lifecycle, modules, for_each, state, CI applies. Does not: provider schemas, IAM models, pipeline federation.
items.explain: Say both halves — panels probe the boundary, not just the promise.

items.prompt: Sketch the portable network module pattern.
items.answer: Thin provider-specific modules with a common interface (cidr_block in, subnet_ids out); shared locals; CI-tested per provider.
items.explain: Common interface, native implementation, tested parity — the professional pattern.

items.prompt: Define data gravity and its design consequence.
items.answer: Large datasets attract compute; metered egress punishes separation. Consequence: compute follows the data — same cloud/region.
items.explain: One line plus consequence; use the 50 TB BI example if asked to elaborate.

items.prompt: 50 TB dataset, BI compute proposed on another cloud. Your analysis?
items.answer: Egress on every refresh + replica management dwarfs the tool advantage. Formally cost replica + egress, or co-locate.
items.explain: Force the numbers before the decision — qualitative is fine, hand-waving is not.

items.prompt: State the multicloud strategy thesis in one sentence.
items.answer: Standardize the operating model, not necessarily the provider; exceptions explicit, reviewed, temporary.
items.explain: This is the answer to 'should we be multicloud?' — governance first.

drills.title: Timed drill: governance and operating model

items.prompt: What is shadow multicloud and why does it matter?
items.answer: Untracked cloud adoption by teams; bypasses guardrails; causes breaches and surprise bills.
items.explain: Governance first, provider second — say why, not just what.

items.prompt: Name four regulatory controls for a financial workload.
items.answer: In-country regions, customer-managed keys, private endpoints, verified failover residency (+ audit rights).
items.explain: Residency, encryption control, network path, resilience proof.

items.prompt: Why is 'the cloud is compliant' wrong?
items.answer: Compliance = your architecture + provider attestations; you inherit the audit burden for everything you configure.
items.explain: Their certs cover their controls; your configs are your burden.

items.prompt: What is the dominant cost of multicloud?
items.answer: Cognitive: multiplied runbooks, IAM models, networks, playbooks, hiring profiles.
items.explain: Not the meter — the minds. This justifies the platform team.

items.prompt: Structural fix for three teams, three DIY clouds, chaotic incidents?
items.answer: Central platform team; certified landing-zone modules with identical guardrails; certification required for new clouds.
items.explain: Absorb complexity behind one interface; enforce guardrails in code.

items.prompt: Two failure modes of cloud strategy — name both.
items.answer: Single-cloud dogma ('one cloud no matter the fit') and per-team anarchy (every team picks its own).
items.explain: The framework exists to steer between these two ditches.

items.prompt: A regulator asks for audit access to your cloud estate. What did you prepare in advance?
items.answer: Contractual audit rights, centralized logging to the SIEM, CMK key inventory, and architecture docs showing residency and network paths.
items.explain: Audit readiness is designed in — residency, keys, logs, contracts.

handsOnLab.title: Lab: one Terraform root, two clouds, one decision record
handsOnLab.brief: You will write a Terraform root module that provisions a two-tier network on two providers through a common module interface, validate both plans, and write the architecture decision record a panel would expect. Uses only plan (no apply), so there is no cloud spend.
steps: Create the repo layout: root main.tf, modules/network-aws/, modules/network-azure/, each exposing variables cidr_block, az_count and outputs subnet_ids.
Write modules/network-aws: aws_vpc, public/private aws_subnets across az_count AZs, aws_internet_gateway, aws_nat_gateway with EIP, route tables. Keep it to ~60 lines.
Write modules/network-azure: azurerm_virtual_network, subnets, NAT gateway, route tables with equivalent topology. Same interface, native resources.
Write the root module: shared locals for the CIDR plan (10.10.0.0/16 etc.), one module block per cloud, outputs converging to {aws_subnets, azure_subnets}.
Run terraform init and terraform plan with dummy provider credentials (plan-only; use -refresh=false where needed). Confirm both providers plan cleanly.
Break portability deliberately: reference an AWS-only concept in the Azure module, watch plan fail, then fix it — document the failure as the 'abstraction without testing' lesson.
Write the decision record (ADR): workload = internal analytics VPC; evaluate AWS vs Azure vs GCP on the five lenses; record the choice and the rejected options with reasons.
Add the data-gravity section to the ADR: dataset location, query pattern, and why compute stays in the same region/cloud.
Add the governance section: which landing-zone guardrails apply (no public storage, centralized logging, corporate IdP) and who certifies a new cloud.
Run terraform fmt -check and terraform validate; fix all findings.
Peer-review swap: trade ADRs with a study partner (or self-review after 24h) and challenge one lens they underweighted.
Archive the ADR in the repo under docs/adr/0001-cloud-selection.md with status 'accepted'.
handsOnLab.deliverable: A Terraform repo with a common-interface network module implemented for two providers (plan-validated), plus a written architecture decision record covering the five lenses, data gravity, and governance.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: terraform validate passes for both modules; the ADR records a choice with explicit rejected options and reasons; docs/adr/0001-cloud-selection.md exists.

mockTask.q: Leadership proposes moving all analytics compute to Cloud X 'because the BI tool is nicer' while the 50 TB warehouse stays on Cloud Y. As the platform engineer, what is your response?
choices: Require a formal cost model: metered egress per refresh plus replica management, versus co-locating compute with the data; decide on numbers, not preference
mockTask.explain: Data gravity makes this a cost-architecture decision, not a tool-preference one. The formal model (egress + replica + ops) usually favors compute-follows-data; if the numbers still favor the move, it becomes an explicit, reviewed exception.

cards.front: Prometheus pull vs push: what does a failed scrape tell you?
cards.back: The 'up' metric goes to 0 — target death is itself a signal; pull means the monitor knows about outages rather than waiting for pushes that never come

cards.front: Counter vs Gauge vs Histogram (one use each)
cards.back: Counter: requests total (rate it). Gauge: queue depth (read directly). Histogram: latency buckets (histogram_quantile for p99)

cards.front: PromQL: requests per second from http_requests_total
cards.back: rate(http_requests_total[5m]) — or sum by (service) (rate(...)) to aggregate

cards.front: PromQL: p99 latency from a histogram
cards.back: histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))

cards.front: PromQL: 5xx error ratio
cards.back: rate(http_requests_total{code=~'5..'}[5m]) / rate(http_requests_total[5m])

cards.front: Why is rate() on a Gauge wrong?
cards.back: Gauges are not cumulative — rate assumes ever-increasing counters and handles resets; on a gauge it produces nonsense

cards.front: RED vs USE methods
cards.back: RED per service: Rate, Errors, Duration. USE per resource: Utilization, Saturation, Errors

cards.front: EFK pipeline in one sentence
cards.back: Apps log structured JSON to stdout; Fluent Bit DaemonSet tails, enriches, and ships to Elasticsearch; Kibana queries/visualizes

cards.front: Why structured JSON logs are a prerequisite
cards.back: Every field becomes filterable/aggregatable; free-text logs cannot be pivoted by error_code or trace_id during an incident

cards.front: Azure Monitor mapping: Prometheus / Grafana / EFK / Alertmanager
cards.back: Metrics ~ Monitor metrics; dashboards ~ Metrics Explorer (or Grafana w/ Azure source); logs ~ Log Analytics + KQL; alerts ~ alert rules + action groups

cards.front: Cardinality discipline: why not label metrics by user_id?
cards.back: Each distinct label value creates a time series — a million users = a million series = Prometheus OOM. Aggregate at the edge; drop high-cardinality labels

cards.front: Trace sampling strategy at 2M txns/sec
cards.back: Head-based sampling at low rates + tail-based sampling that keeps 100% of error traces — you need the failures, not the successes

items.prompt: Write: per-service requests/sec from http_requests_total.
items.answer: sum by (service) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))
items.explain: rate then aggregate — the most-written query in operations.

items.prompt: Write: 5xx error ratio.
items.answer: rate(http_requests_total{code=~'5..'}[5m]) / rate(http_requests_total[5m])
items.explain: Regex matcher on code; ratio of rates, not rate of ratios.

items.prompt: Write: p99 latency for route /checkout.
items.answer: histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{route='/checkout'}[5m]))
items.explain: Buckets, not raw observations — the _bucket suffix matters.

items.prompt: Why [5m] and not [1m] with a 30s scrape interval?
items.answer: [1m] holds ~2 samples — fragile; [5m] smooths missed scrapes and restarts.
items.explain: rate needs multiple samples; short windows on sparse scrapes lie.

items.prompt: Counter vs Gauge: which gets rate(), which is read directly?
items.answer: Counters get rate(); gauges are read directly (or avg_over_time).
items.explain: Say the rule and the reason: rate assumes cumulative + resets.

items.prompt: Which pod is being OOMKilled most in the last hour? Write it.
items.answer: sum by (pod) (increase(kube_pod_container_status_terminated_reason{reason='OOMKilled'}[1h]))
items.explain: increase over the window, grouped by pod — leads straight to the memory-limit fix.

items.prompt: What does the 'up' metric tell you, and why does pull make it possible?
items.answer: up==0 means the scrape failed (target down). Pull makes target death a first-class signal.
items.explain: Push systems learn about death by absence; pull learns by failed attempt.

items.prompt: Define RED and USE.
items.answer: RED per service: Rate, Errors, Duration. USE per resource: Utilization, Saturation, Errors.
items.explain: RED for services, USE for resources — dashboard design in two acronyms.

items.prompt: EFK pipeline: name the four stages.
items.answer: Structured stdout logs -> Fluent Bit DaemonSet tail/enrich -> Elasticsearch store -> Kibana query.
items.explain: Ephemeral pods make centralization mandatory, not optional.

items.prompt: Checkout errors spike. Your 3-step Kibana triage?
items.answer: Filter level=error+service over window; aggregate by error_code; pivot on trace_id.
items.explain: Filter, aggregate, pivot — say it as the muscle-memory sequence.

items.prompt: Why reject a per-user_id latency metric at 2M txns/sec?
items.answer: Cardinality explosion: a million label values = a million series = Prometheus OOM.
items.explain: Bounded labels + histograms + recording rules instead.

items.prompt: Log strategy at 2M txns/sec: successes vs errors?
items.answer: Sample successes aggressively (e.g. 1%); keep 100% of errors; structured JSON always.
items.explain: You need the failures, not the successes — volume control at the source.

items.prompt: Map to Azure native: Prometheus, Grafana, EFK, Alertmanager.
items.answer: Monitor metrics, Metrics Explorer/dashboards, Log Analytics+KQL, alert rules + action groups.
items.explain: Know both stacks; justify the choice (portability vs zero-ops).

items.prompt: Panel: 'observability at millions of txns/sec' — your one-liner?
items.answer: 'At scale, observability is a sampling and aggregation architecture: bounded cardinality, recording rules, sampled logs, tail-sampled traces.'
items.explain: Then unpack each of the four on demand — the one-liner opens, the details close.

handsOnLab.title: Lab: Prometheus + Grafana + EFK on a local stack
handsOnLab.brief: You will run Prometheus, Grafana, and an EFK pipeline with Docker Compose, instrument a sample Python API with RED metrics and structured logs, build the checkout-style dashboard, and practice the error-spike triage end to end.
steps: Create the lab dir and docker-compose.yml with Prometheus (prom/prometheus), Grafana (grafana/grafana), Elasticsearch (single-node), Fluent Bit, and Kibana. Pin image tags.
Write prometheus.yml scraping your sample API at api:8000/metrics every 15s plus itself; add a recording rule file computing job:5xx_ratio:rate5m.

Write the sample API (Python + prometheus_client): expose http_requests_total (Counter), http_request_duration_seconds (Histogram), queue_depth (Gauge); log structured JSON to stdout with trace_id per request.
Start the stack: docker-compose up -d; verify Prometheus targets at localhost:9090/targets (all UP) and Grafana at localhost:3000.
In Prometheus, run sum by (route) (rate(http_requests_total[5m])) and the p99 histogram_quantile query; confirm numbers move when you curl the API in a loop.
Generate an error spike: hit a /fail endpoint 200 times; watch the 5xx ratio recording rule climb in Prometheus.
Build the Grafana dashboard: one row, four panels — request rate, error ratio (with 1% threshold line), p50/p95/p99 latency, queue depth gauge. Add a $route variable.
Configure Fluent Bit to tail the API container logs, parse JSON, and ship to Elasticsearch; verify documents in Kibana under an index pattern.
In Kibana, filter level=error over the spike window, aggregate by error_code, and pivot on a trace_id — write down the three steps and what each revealed.
Add a Prometheus alert rule: 5xx ratio > 5% for 5m; trigger it with the /fail loop and confirm the alert fires in the Prometheus UI.
Break cardinality deliberately: add a user_id label to a counter, generate traffic, and watch active series explode (Prometheus status page) — then remove the label and note the lesson.
Document the scale plan: for 2M txns/sec, write which labels you would keep/drop, your sampling rates, and your retention tiers. Tear down with docker-compose down -v.
handsOnLab.deliverable: A running-then-removed local observability stack, a RED Grafana dashboard, a written Kibana triage walkthrough, and a one-page 'observability at 2M txns/sec' scale plan.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Dashboard panels answer rate/errors/duration; the alert fires on the induced spike; Kibana triage finds the error_code; the scale plan names kept/dropped labels with reasons.

mockTask.q: Panel: 'How do you do logging and monitoring at millions of transactions per second?' What is the core of a strong answer?
choices: Log every request with full detail and alert on all of it
Sampling and aggregation architecture: bounded label cardinality, recording rules, sampled success logs with 100% of errors, tail-sampled traces keeping failures
Disable monitoring in production for performance
mockTask.explain: Scale breaks naive collection: unbounded labels OOM Prometheus, full logging bankrupts storage. The strong answer names the four controls (cardinality, recording rules, log sampling, trace sampling) and the one-liner: observability at scale is a sampling and aggregation architecture.

notes.title: Prometheus: The Pull Model and Metric Types
notes.body: Prometheus monitors by scraping: it pulls metrics from HTTP endpoints (usually /metrics) on a fixed interval, storing timestamped samples in its time-series database. Pull inverts the usual push assumption and buys you three things: targets can die without losing the monitoring path's knowledge of them (failed scrapes are themselves a signal via the 'up' metric), service discovery (Kubernetes, EC2, DNS) keeps the target list fresh automatically, and exporters are dumb text endpoints — any app can expose metrics with a client library. Four metric types: Counter (monotonically increasing: http_requests_total), Gauge (goes up and down: memory usage, queue depth), Histogram (observations bucketed for latency quantiles), Summary (precomputed quantiles, less flexible). Worked example: your API exposes http_requests_total{method,code} and http_request_duration_seconds_bucket. Which type answers 'requests per second'? Solution: a Counter — rate(http_requests_total[5m]). Which answers 'current queue depth'? A Gauge — read directly. Which answers 'p99 latency'? The Histogram — histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])). The classic mistake is rate() on a Gauge (meaningless — gauges are not cumulative) or averaging a Counter directly (use rate first).

notes.title: PromQL Basics: rate, increase, and histogram_quantile
notes.body: PromQL is Prometheus's query language; a handful of functions covers most operational questions. rate(v range-vector[5m]) gives per-second average increase — the standard way to read counters. increase() gives the total increase over the window. sum by (label) aggregates: sum by (service) (rate(http_requests_total[5m])). avg_over_time, max_over_time smooth gauges. histogram_quantile(0.99, ...) computes the p99 from histogram buckets. Alert expressions combine these with thresholds: rate(http_requests_total{code=~'5..'}[5m]) / rate(http_requests_total[5m]) > 0.05 fires when the 5xx ratio exceeds 5%. Worked example: 'Is checkout slower than yesterday?' Solution: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{route='/checkout'}[5m]))) and compare against the same query with a 24h offset modifier. Second: 'Which pod is OOMKilled most?' — increase(kube_pod_container_status_terminated_reason{reason='OOMKilled'}[1h]) sorted by pod. The trap: rate() needs at least two samples in the window — on a 30s scrape interval, a [1m] window is fragile; use [5m] for stability. And remember counters reset on restart — rate() handles resets, but naive subtraction does not.

notes.title: Grafana: Dashboards That Answer Questions
notes.body: Grafana turns Prometheus (and other sources) into dashboards, but a dashboard is only as good as the questions it answers. Design by the RED method per service — Rate (requests/sec), Errors (error ratio), Duration (latency quantiles) — plus the USE method per resource — Utilization, Saturation, Errors. One row per service with its RED panels; one row per dependency (database, queue) with USE panels. Variables make dashboards reusable: a $namespace or $service dropdown templating every query. Annotations mark deploys so you can correlate a latency spike with the release that caused it. Worked example: build the checkout dashboard. Panels: (1) rate of checkouts: sum(rate(checkout_completed_total[5m])); (2) error ratio: 5xx rate / total rate with a 1% alert threshold line; (3) p50/p95/p99 latency via histogram_quantile; (4) saturation: container CPU throttling rate and memory working set vs limit. Solution review: each panel maps to RED; variables let the same dashboard serve every service; the deploy annotation answers 'what changed?' in one glance. The anti-pattern is the wall of 40 graphs nobody reads — if a panel has never triggered a decision, delete it. Dashboards are operational tools, not art.

notes.title: Centralized Logging: The EFK Pipeline
notes.body: Metrics tell you something is wrong; logs tell you why. The EFK stack — Elasticsearch, Fluent Bit/Fluentd, Kibana (or OpenSearch equivalents) — centralizes logs because containers are ephemeral: when a pod dies, its local logs die with it. The pipeline: application writes structured JSON logs to stdout; the node agent (Fluent Bit as a DaemonSet) tails container logs, parses and enriches them (adds pod, namespace, node labels), and ships to Elasticsearch; Kibana queries and visualizes. Structured logging is the prerequisite — log {timestamp, level, service, trace_id, message, fields} as JSON, never free text, so every field is filterable. Worked example: checkout errors spike; find the cause. Solution: in Kibana, filter level=error AND service=checkout over the spike window, aggregate by fields.error_code — one code dominates; expand a sample document, copy its trace_id, pivot to the trace view to see the failing downstream call. The cost trap is log volume: debug logging in production at millions of transactions per second will bankrupt your Elasticsearch cluster. Set levels per environment (info in prod, debug in dev), sample high-volume access logs, and set index retention (hot 7 days, warm 30, delete after 90) before the disk fills.

notes.title: Azure Monitor: The Native Mapping
notes.body: On Azure, the native observability stack is Azure Monitor: metrics flow into Metrics Explorer, logs into Log Analytics workspaces queried with KQL, and Application Insights provides APM (distributed traces, dependency maps) for applications. Container Insights onboards AKS clusters to collect Prometheus metrics and container logs without running your own stack. The mapping to this module: Prometheus ~ Azure Monitor metrics, Grafana ~ Metrics Explorer/dashboards (or Grafana with the Azure data source), EFK ~ Log Analytics + KQL, Alertmanager ~ Azure Monitor alert rules with action groups. Worked example: replicate the checkout RED dashboard natively. Solution: Container Insights collects the Prometheus endpoints; a Log Analytics query (KQL) aggregates: ContainerLog | where LogEntry contains 'ERROR' | summarize count() by bin(TimeGenerated, 5m); an alert rule fires an action group (email + webhook + PagerDuty) when the 5xx ratio crosses the SLO threshold. The decision framework: run Prometheus/Grafana/EFK yourself for portability and PromQL familiarity across clouds (the multicloud answer from M44), or adopt Azure Monitor for zero-operational-overhead on Azure with KQL as the query skill. Most enterprises end up hybrid: Prometheus for K8s metrics, Azure Monitor for platform/audit logs.

notes.title: Observability at Millions of Transactions per Second
notes.body: The panel asks how you do logging and monitoring at millions of transactions per second — the answer is sampling, aggregation, and cardinality discipline, because naive 'log everything, label everything' collapses. Metrics: keep label cardinality bounded — a label with a million distinct values (like user_id or request_id) creates a million time series and will OOM your Prometheus; aggregate at the edge and drop high-cardinality labels via relabeling. Use recording rules to precompute expensive queries (the 5xx ratio per service computed once, read by every dashboard). Logs: sample aggressively (1% of success logs, 100% of errors), structure everything, and ship to a tiered store. Traces: head-based sampling at low rates plus tail-based sampling that keeps all error traces — you need the failures, not the successes. Worked example: checkout does 2M txns/sec; the team wants per-request logs and per-user latency metrics. Solution: per-user latency as a metric is rejected (cardinality explosion); instead histogram by route with bounded labels, recording rules for the SLO ratios, 1% sampled success logs + 100% error logs, and tail-sampled traces keeping errors. The panel one-liner: 'At scale, observability is a sampling and aggregation architecture, not a collection architecture.'

objectives: Explain the Prometheus pull model and choose Counter, Gauge, and Histogram correctly
Write PromQL for rates, error ratios, and latency quantiles, and design recording rules
Build Grafana dashboards using the RED and USE methods with variables and deploy annotations
Operate the EFK pipeline and triage error spikes via filter-aggregate-pivot
Design observability for millions of txns/sec using cardinality discipline, sampling, and tiered retention

quiz.q: Which PromQL query gives per-service requests per second?
quiz.explain: rate() converts the counter to per-second; sum by (service) aggregates across instances. Bare counters and avg() are meaningless for rates.

quiz.q: You need p99 checkout latency. Which is correct?
quiz.explain: Quantiles come from histogram buckets via histogram_quantile; avg/max of raw observations are not available from aggregated exposition and max is not p99.

quiz.q: A dashboard panel shows rate(queue_depth[5m]). What is wrong?
choices: queue_depth is a Gauge — rate() on a gauge is meaningless; read it directly
quiz.explain: rate() assumes a cumulative counter and corrects for resets; applied to a gauge it fabricates values. Gauges are read as-is or smoothed with avg_over_time.

quiz.q: Checkout errors spike. Fastest EFK triage path?
choices: Kibana: filter level=error AND service=checkout over the window, aggregate by error_code, pivot on trace_id
Increase log verbosity to debug everywhere
quiz.explain: Structured logs make this a three-step pivot: filter, aggregate, trace. SSH-ing into ephemeral pods or enabling debug at scale makes things worse.

quiz.q: At 2M txns/sec, the team wants a per-user-id latency metric. Your response?
choices: Reject: cardinality explosion — a million label values means a million time series; use bounded labels + histograms + recording rules
quiz.explain: High-cardinality labels OOM Prometheus. Latency by route with histograms answers the operational question without per-user series.

quiz.q: Which sampling strategy keeps all error traces at high throughput?
choices: Head-based sampling at low rates plus tail-based sampling that retains error traces
quiz.explain: Tail-based sampling decides after seeing the outcome, so it can keep 100% of failures while dropping the bulk of successes.

quiz.q: In Azure-native terms, what replaces Alertmanager?
choices: Azure Monitor alert rules with action groups
quiz.explain: Alert rules evaluate the signal (metric/log query) and action groups route the notification — the same separation Alertmanager provides.

quiz.q: A recording rule precomputes the per-service 5xx ratio. Why?
choices: Expensive queries run once at scrape time instead of on every dashboard load and alert evaluation
quiz.explain: Recording rules trade a little storage for a lot of query-time savings — critical when many dashboards and alerts share the same ratio.

quiz.q: Debug logging is enabled in production at high throughput and the logging bill explodes. What are the two fixes?
choices: Per-environment log levels (info in prod) plus sampling of high-volume success logs, with tiered retention
quiz.explain: Volume control happens at the source (levels, sampling) and at the store (hot/warm/delete retention tiers). Scaling the store without fixing the source just moves the bill.

modules.title: Alerting, SLOs & Incident Response
modules.summary: Run reliability as an engineering discipline: SLIs, SLOs, and error budgets with real math, burn-rate alerting, on-call routing, incident command, blameless postmortems, and runbooks you prove in a live drill.
objectives: Define SLIs/SLOs and compute error budgets, applying freeze policies to ship-vs-stabilize decisions
Configure fast-burn and slow-burn alerts and explain why burn rate beats absolute thresholds
Design alert routing chains and on-call escalation with alert-quality rules
Run incidents with roles and the mitigate-first protocol, then write blameless postmortems with Five Whys
Write, execute, and maintain runbooks proven in live drills

notes.title: SLIs, SLOs, and Error Budgets
notes.body: A Service Level Indicator (SLI) is what you measure — e.g. the fraction of checkout requests that succeed within 500ms. A Service Level Objective (SLO) is the target — 99.9% of checkouts succeed within 500ms over a 30-day window. The error budget is the allowed failure: 100% minus the SLO, so 99.9% leaves a 0.1% budget. Error budgets turn reliability into a currency: while budget remains, the team may ship features and take risks; when the budget burns out, all engineering effort shifts to reliability until it recovers. Worked example: checkout serves 10 million requests in 30 days with a 99.9% SLO. Error budget = 0.1% x 10M = 10,000 failed requests. After a bad deploy causes 8,000 failures in one day, the remaining budget is 2,000 — the release freeze policy triggers (say, below 25% remaining), so the next two feature releases are held and the team works on the flaky payment dependency instead. Solution logic: budgets make the ship-vs-stabilize tradeoff explicit and pre-agreed, so it is policy, not politics. The trap: SLOs without consequences are vanity metrics — an SLO nobody acts on teaches the organization to ignore all SLOs.

notes.title: Burn Rate: How Fast Are You Spending Reliability?
notes.body: Burn rate measures how fast the error budget is being consumed relative to the SLO window. A burn rate of 1 spends budget exactly on target; 10 burns ten times too fast. Alerting on burn rate (rather than raw error counts) is the Google SRE practice because it is self-normalizing: it works for 10 requests/sec and 10,000 alike. The standard setup uses two alert speeds: a fast-burn alert (e.g. burn rate 14 over 1 hour — pages immediately, you will exhaust budget in days) and a slow-burn alert (burn rate 3 over 6 hours — tickets, you are leaking budget steadily). Worked example: SLO 99.9% over 30 days; in the last hour, errors ran at 2% against a 0.1% budget. Burn rate = 2% / 0.1% = 20. At this pace the 30-day budget dies in 1.5 days — page now. Contrast: errors at 0.3% sustained for 6 hours gives burn rate 3 — a ticket, investigated today, not a 3 AM page. Solution: configure both alerts; the fast one protects the budget, the slow one catches the bleed. The anti-pattern is alerting on absolute thresholds ('more than 100 errors') — it pages the low-traffic service for noise and sleeps through the high-traffic service's real outage. Burn rate alerts scale with the service.

notes.title: Alert Routing and On-Call Design
notes.body: Alerts must reach the right human with the right context in minutes. The routing chain: detection (Prometheus alert rule or Azure Monitor alert) -> notification grouping (Alertmanager groups by service/severity to prevent 200 separate pages for one outage) -> on-call schedule (who is primary this week) -> escalation policy (no ack in 10 min -> secondary; 20 min -> manager). Alert quality rules: every page must be actionable (the runbook link tells you what to do), every page must be urgent (if it can wait until morning, it is a ticket, not a page), and alerts need severity tiers — critical (page), warning (ticket), info (dashboard). Worked example: design routing for the checkout service. Solution: Prometheus rule 'CheckoutHighErrorBudgetBurn' (fast-burn) -> Alertmanager route matching service=checkout, severity=critical -> PagerDuty/on-call primary with a runbook link to the checkout triage doc; slow-burn -> ticketing queue with a 4-hour SLA; deploy annotations feed the dashboard so the responder sees what shipped. The on-call health metric: pages per shift. More than 2-3 pages per on-call week means the alerts are miscalibrated or the service is genuinely unhealthy — either way, the fix is engineering, not heroics. Alert fatigue kills response quality faster than any outage.

notes.title: Incident Roles and the First 30 Minutes
notes.body: Incidents need roles, not heroes. The three core roles: Incident Commander (coordinates, makes decisions, keeps the timeline — does NOT debug), Communications Lead (status page and stakeholder updates every 15-30 minutes), and Responders (diagnose and mitigate). The first-30-minutes protocol: (1) declare the incident and page the roles (2 min); (2) assess blast radius from dashboards — which services, which users, since when (5 min); (3) mitigate first, root-cause later — roll back the deploy, fail over, shed load, or flip the feature flag (10 min); (4) communicate the current status and next update time (ongoing). Worked example: checkout p99 triples at 14:02, deploy went out at 13:55. The Responder wants to read code; the Commander orders the rollback first. Solution: rollback at 14:08, p99 recovers by 14:12, incident downgraded — root-causing the bad query happens after, in the postmortem, with no users still bleeding. The principle: mitigation before diagnosis. Every minute of 'let me just check one thing' while users fail is a choice to keep the outage running. Declare early — a false alarm costs a page; a late declaration costs an outage.

notes.title: Blameless Postmortems and the Five Whys
notes.body: A blameless postmortem asks what allowed the failure, never who caused it — because blame suppresses the reporting that prevention depends on. The document has a fixed shape: summary, impact (duration, affected users/requests), timeline (detection, mitigation, resolution with timestamps), root causes (usually 2-3 contributing factors, never one), and action items (each with an owner and a due date — an action item without an owner is a wish). The Five Whys drill past the proximate cause: 'Checkout failed' -> why? 'Payment service timed out' -> why? 'Its connection pool was exhausted' -> why? 'A retry storm from the bad deploy multiplied load 8x' -> why? 'No retry budget or circuit breaker on that client' -> why? 'Resilience patterns were never added to the integration checklist.' The fix lands at the fifth why, not the first. Worked example: write the action items for the retry-storm outage. Solution: (1) add circuit breaker + retry budgets to the payment client — owner: payments team, due in 2 weeks; (2) add a deploy-canary error-budget gate — owner: platform team, due in 1 month; (3) load-test retry behavior in staging — owner: QA, due in 3 weeks. Each is verifiable; each prevents recurrence rather than punishing the deployer.

notes.title: Runbooks: The Lab You Write Before the Fire
notes.body: A runbook is the written procedure for a known failure mode — diagnosis steps, mitigation commands, escalation criteria, and rollback instructions — kept where the on-call can reach it at 3 AM. A good runbook has: symptoms (what the alert looks like), blast radius check (the two dashboard links), diagnosis (the exact kubectl/PromQL/KQL commands), mitigation (the exact commands, copy-pasteable), escalation (when to wake the secondary, when to declare a major incident), and rollback. Runbooks decay: every postmortem must update the runbook it used, and runbooks get a quarterly review owner. Worked example: the checkout error-budget runbook. Symptoms: fast-burn alert fires. Diagnosis: (1) kubectl get pods -n checkout (CrashLoopBackOff?); (2) Prometheus: 5xx ratio by pod (one pod or all?); (3) check deploy annotations (did something just ship?). Mitigation: if one bad pod — kubectl delete pod to reschedule; if post-deploy — kubectl rollout undo deployment/checkout; if downstream — flip the payment feature flag off. Escalation: no improvement in 15 min -> page secondary + declare major. Solution review: every step is a command, not prose; the responder never has to invent triage while stressed. The lab below has you write and then execute one — because a runbook you have never run is a rumor, not a procedure.

cards.front: SLI vs SLO vs error budget (with numbers)
cards.back: SLI: measured (fraction of checkouts succeeding <500ms). SLO: target (99.9% over 30d). Budget: 100% - SLO = 0.1% allowed failures

cards.front: Error budget math: 10M requests, 99.9% SLO
cards.back: Budget = 0.1% x 10M = 10,000 failed requests per 30 days; policy (e.g. freeze below 25% remaining) makes ship-vs-stabilize pre-agreed

cards.front: What is burn rate?
cards.back: Error-budget consumption speed relative to the SLO window; 1 = on target, 10 = ten times too fast

cards.front: Fast-burn vs slow-burn alerts
cards.back: Fast-burn (e.g. rate 14 over 1h): page now, budget dies in days. Slow-burn (e.g. rate 3 over 6h): ticket, steady leak

cards.front: Why alert on burn rate instead of absolute error counts?
cards.back: Self-normalizing across traffic levels: absolute thresholds page low-traffic services for noise and miss real outages on high-traffic ones

cards.front: Alert routing chain (4 stages)
cards.back: Detection -> grouping (Alertmanager) -> on-call schedule -> escalation policy (no-ack timers)

cards.front: Three rules of alert quality
cards.back: Every page actionable (runbook link), every page urgent (else it is a ticket), severity tiers (critical/warning/info)

cards.front: Incident roles (3) and the Commander's job
cards.back: Incident Commander (coordinates/decides, does NOT debug), Communications Lead (updates every 15-30 min), Responders (diagnose/mitigate)

cards.front: First-30-minutes protocol
cards.back: Declare + page (2 min) -> assess blast radius (5 min) -> mitigate first: rollback/failover/shed load (10 min) -> communicate on a cadence

cards.front: Mitigation before diagnosis — why?
cards.back: Every minute of investigating while users fail extends the outage; roll back first, root-cause in the postmortem

cards.front: Blameless postmortem: fixed shape
cards.back: Summary, impact, timeline, root causes (contributing factors), action items — each with owner + due date

cards.front: What does the Fifth Why usually reveal?
cards.back: The systemic gap (missing checklist, absent pattern, untested behavior) — the fix lands at the fifth why, not the first

cards.front: Runbook required sections
cards.back: Symptoms, blast-radius check, diagnosis commands, mitigation commands, escalation criteria, rollback — all copy-pasteable

cards.front: On-call health metric
cards.back: Pages per shift: >2-3/week means miscalibrated alerts or a genuinely unhealthy service — fix with engineering, not heroics

quiz.q: Checkout: 10M requests/30d, SLO 99.9%. A bad deploy causes 8,000 failures in a day. What happens under a 25%-remaining freeze policy?
choices: Remaining budget is 2,000 of 10,000 (20%) — below 25%, so feature releases freeze and effort shifts to reliability
quiz.explain: Budget = 10,000; 8,000 spent leaves 20%, under the 25% threshold. The policy converts the tradeoff into a pre-agreed action, not a debate.

quiz.q: SLO 99.9%/30d. Last hour errors ran at 2% vs 0.1% budget. What is the burn rate and response?
choices: Burn rate 20 — page immediately; budget dies in ~1.5 days at this pace
quiz.explain: Burn rate = observed error ratio / budget ratio = 2%/0.1% = 20. Fast-burn threshold crossed: page now.

quiz.q: Errors at 0.3% sustained for 6 hours against a 0.1% budget. Response?
choices: Slow-burn: ticket it for investigation today — a steady leak, not an imminent exhaustion
quiz.explain: Burn rate 3 over hours is the slow-burn pattern: real, worth a ticket with an SLA, but not a 3 AM page.

quiz.q: Which alert deserves to be a page?
choices: Disk at 70% with weeks of headroom
Fast-burn error-budget alert with a runbook link and a mitigation command
quiz.explain: Pages must be actionable and urgent. Disk at 70% is a ticket; the burn alert names the failure and the fix.

quiz.q: During an incident, the Responder wants to keep debugging while users fail. The Commander should:
choices: Order mitigation first (rollback/failover) — diagnosis happens after users stop bleeding
quiz.explain: Mitigation before diagnosis is the core protocol; root-causing belongs in the postmortem, not in the outage window.

quiz.q: Who writes the status updates during an incident?
quiz.explain: Dedicated comms role on a cadence keeps stakeholders informed and keeps responders free to mitigate.

quiz.q: A postmortem action item reads 'be more careful next time'. What is wrong?
choices: No owner, no due date, not verifiable — it is blame in disguise, not prevention
quiz.explain: Action items need owner + due date + verifiability, and must fix the system (the fifth why), not scold the human.

quiz.q: Five Whys on a retry-storm outage ends at 'resilience patterns were never in the integration checklist'. What does this tell you?
choices: The systemic fix: add circuit breakers/retry budgets to the checklist — the first why (timeout) was only the proximate cause
quiz.explain: The fifth why reveals the process gap; fixing it prevents the whole class of outage. Stopping at the first why just restarts the timer.

quiz.q: On-call gets 8 pages a week, all actionable but exhausting. What is the correct response?
choices: Treat it as an engineering problem: recalibrate thresholds, fix flaky alerts, and address the underlying reliability debt
quiz.explain: Pages-per-shift is a health metric; sustained high paging means miscalibrated alerts or real unreliability — both fixed with engineering, not endurance.

drills.title: Timed drill: SLO math under pressure

items.prompt: Define SLI, SLO, error budget in one breath.
items.answer: SLI: what you measure. SLO: the target over a window. Budget: 100% minus SLO — the allowed failures.
items.explain: One breath, three terms — the panel's warm-up.

items.prompt: 10M requests, 99.9% SLO. Budget?
items.answer: 10,000 failed requests per 30 days.
items.explain: 0.1% of 10M — show the arithmetic, not just the number.

items.prompt: 8,000 failures spent, freeze policy at 25% remaining. Decision?
items.answer: 20% remains — below threshold: freeze features, shift to reliability.
items.explain: Policy makes it automatic — say 'pre-agreed, not political'.

items.prompt: Errors at 2%/hour vs 0.1% budget. Burn rate and action?
items.answer: Burn rate 20 — page now; budget dies in ~1.5 days.
items.explain: Observed/budget = 20. Fast-burn = page.

items.prompt: Errors at 0.3% for 6 hours. Burn rate and action?
items.answer: Burn rate 3 — ticket for today; slow-burn leak.
items.explain: Contrast with the previous item — the panel wants both speeds.

items.prompt: Why burn-rate alerts instead of 'more than 100 errors'?
items.answer: Self-normalizing: absolute counts page quiet services for noise and miss loud-service outages.
items.explain: Scales with the service — the SRE-correct answer.

items.prompt: SLO with no consequences is what?
items.answer: A vanity metric — teaches the org to ignore all SLOs.
items.explain: Consequences (freeze policy) are what make SLOs real.

items.prompt: Name the three incident roles and the Commander's one rule.
items.answer: Commander (coordinates, never debugs), Comms Lead (updates every 15-30 min), Responders (mitigate).
items.explain: The Commander's rule — does not debug — is what the panel listens for.

items.prompt: First 30 minutes: the four beats.
items.answer: Declare+page, assess blast radius, mitigate first, communicate on cadence.
items.explain: Say the timeboxes: 2 / 5 / 10 minutes, then ongoing comms.

items.prompt: p99 triples 7 minutes after a deploy. First action?
items.answer: Rollback the deploy — mitigation before diagnosis.
items.explain: Users are bleeding; root-cause later in the postmortem.

items.prompt: Postmortem fixed shape — the five sections.
items.answer: Summary, impact, timeline, root causes, action items (owner + due date).
items.explain: Recite all five; stress owner+date on actions.

items.prompt: Run the Five Whys on: 'checkout failed because payment timed out.'
items.answer: Timeout -> pool exhausted -> retry storm 8x load -> no retry budget/circuit breaker -> never in the integration checklist.
items.explain: End at the systemic gap — that is where the fix lives.

items.prompt: Write one good action item for the retry storm.
items.answer: 'Add circuit breaker + retry budgets to payment client — owner: payments team, due in 2 weeks.'
items.explain: Verifiable, owned, dated, systemic — the four tests.

items.prompt: A runbook section list — name all six.
items.answer: Symptoms, blast-radius check, diagnosis commands, mitigation commands, escalation criteria, rollback.
items.explain: Copy-pasteable commands, not prose — runnable at 3 AM.

handsOnLab.title: Lab: burn-rate alerts, on-call routing, and a live incident drill
handsOnLab.brief: You will define SLIs/SLOs for a sample service, build fast-burn and slow-burn alerts, design the on-call routing chain, write a runbook, and then run a simulated incident against it — including the postmortem.
steps: Pick the sample API from M45 (or any service) and define two SLIs: success ratio and p99 latency under 500ms; set SLOs (99.9% and 99%) over 30 days; compute the error budgets in requests.
Write the Prometheus alert rules: fast-burn (burn rate 14, 1h window, severity critical) and slow-burn (burn rate 3, 6h window, severity warning) for the success-ratio SLI.
Configure Alertmanager: group by service and severity; route critical to a simulated pager (webhook to a local endpoint or a log file); route warning to a ticket file. Test with amtool if available.
Induce a fast burn: run the /fail loop from M45 at high rate; confirm the critical alert fires and the 'page' is logged with the runbook link.
Induce a slow burn: trickle failures at ~0.3% for a sustained period (or simulate with a recording); confirm only the warning route triggers.

Write the runbook: symptoms, the two dashboard links, diagnosis commands (kubectl get pods, the 5xx-by-pod query, deploy annotation check), mitigation commands (delete bad pod, rollout undo, feature-flag flip), escalation criteria (15 min no improvement -> secondary + major).
Run the live drill: have a partner (or a script) break the service without telling you how; execute the runbook start to finish, timing each phase; record where the runbook was unclear.
Hold the postmortem: write summary, impact, timeline with timestamps, root causes via Five Whys, and 3 action items with owners and due dates.
Update the runbook with everything the drill exposed; set a quarterly review reminder and owner.
Compute your drill metrics: time-to-detect, time-to-mitigate, pages received; compare against your SLO policy targets.
Write the on-call improvement note: given your drill paging volume, are the thresholds right? What would you retune?
Archive the postmortem and runbook in the repo; present the 5-minute incident story as if to a panel.
handsOnLab.deliverable: SLI/SLO definitions with budgets, working fast/slow-burn alerts with routing, an executed runbook, and a complete blameless postmortem with owned action items.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Fast-burn pages and slow-burn tickets on induced failures; the drill postmortem has timeline, Five Whys, and dated owned actions; the runbook was updated from drill findings.

mockTask.q: Your service has a 99.9% SLO. Errors run at 2% for the last hour. The on-call asks whether to page. What do you decide, and why?
choices: Do not page — wait for more data
Page now: burn rate is 20x, the 30-day budget exhausts in about 1.5 days at this pace — this is the fast-burn case
Page only if it lasts 24 hours
mockTask.explain: Burn rate = 2%/0.1% = 20. The fast-burn alert exists precisely for this: budget death in days, not weeks. Waiting converts a mitigable incident into an exhausted budget.

modules.title: Shift-Left Security: SAST/DAST & Dependency Scanning
modules.summary: Push security into the developer workflow: SAST/DAST/IAST lenses, dependency scanning, pipeline gates with real teeth, Trivy image scanning in CI, governed triage, and the OWASP coverage map panels expect.
objectives: Distinguish SAST, DAST, and IAST and place each correctly in the pipeline
Scan dependencies with npm audit, pip-audit, and related SCA tooling
Design pipeline security gates with thresholds and speed-appropriate placement
Scan container images with Trivy in CI and remediate via the base-first ladder
Run governed triage with allowlists, metrics, and an OWASP coverage map

notes.title: SAST, DAST, and IAST: Three Different Lenses
notes.body: Shift-left means finding vulnerabilities where they are cheapest to fix — in the developer's workflow, not in production. Three techniques cover three lenses. SAST (Static Application Security Testing) reads source code without running it: it finds SQL injection patterns, hardcoded secrets, and insecure crypto before the code ever executes. Tools: Semgrep (semgrep scan --config auto), Bandit for Python (bandit -r src/), CodeQL. DAST (Dynamic AST) attacks the running application: OWASP ZAP spiders the site and fires payloads at it, finding what static analysis cannot — authentication flaws, server misconfigurations, runtime injection. IAST (Interactive AST) instruments the running app (an agent inside the JVM/CLR) and watches real execution, combining code context with runtime proof. Worked example: where does each catch a SQL injection? SAST flags the string-concatenated query at commit time; DAST proves it by injecting ' OR '1'='1 into the live login form in staging; IAST watches the test suite execute the vulnerable path and reports the exact tainted-data flow. The panel point: SAST is fast and early but noisy; DAST is proof but late and needs a running environment; IAST is precise but requires instrumentation. Mature pipelines run SAST on every PR, DAST nightly against staging, IAST in integration tests.

notes.title: Dependency (SCA) Scanning: Your Code Is 10% Yours
notes.body: Modern applications are overwhelmingly third-party code — frameworks, transitive dependencies, native packages — and vulnerabilities arrive through them (the supply-chain reality behind every 'critical CVE in a library you never chose'). SCA (Software Composition Analysis) scans your dependency manifests and lockfiles against vulnerability databases. The commands are built into your toolchain: npm audit (and npm audit fix, carefully), pip-audit -r requirements.txt for Python, dotnet list package --vulnerable, cargo audit, go list with govulncheck. The pipeline step fails the build on critical/high CVEs, with an allowlist for accepted risks that carries an expiry date and an owner — never a permanent ignore. Worked example: pip-audit reports CVE-2024-XXXX critical in requests 2.28.0 via requirements.txt. Solution: (1) confirm exploitability — is the vulnerable code path reachable? (2) upgrade to the patched 2.32.x and run the test suite; (3) if the upgrade breaks, evaluate the backported patch or isolate the call path, and only then add a time-boxed exception with owner and review date. The trap: npm audit fix blindly upgrading majors and breaking the build the night before release — pin versions (the M50 requirements.txt lesson), review the diff, and let CI prove the upgrade.

notes.title: Pipeline Security Gates: Fail the Build, Not the Audit
notes.body: A security gate is a pipeline stage that blocks promotion when risk exceeds policy: SAST findings above threshold, critical CVEs in dependencies, container image vulnerabilities, or leaked secrets. Gate design matters more than gate existence. Thresholds: fail on critical always; fail on high unless allowlisted with expiry; warn on medium. Placement: fast checks (SAST, SCA, secret scan) on every pull request where the developer can fix in minutes; slow checks (full DAST, image scan of the final artifact) on merge to main before staging deploy. Worked example: a Jenkins/GitHub Actions stage after unit tests: run trivy on the built image, semgrep on the diff, pip-audit on requirements. If any critical appears, the stage fails, the PR is blocked, and the finding links to the exact line and the fix guidance. Solution review: the developer fixes it in the PR in ten minutes; the alternative — found in a quarterly audit — costs a ticket, a meeting, and a hotfix. The anti-pattern is the advisory-only gate that everyone ignores: a gate that never blocks is a dashboard, not a control. Start strict on new code (block), advisory on legacy (ratchet), and tighten the ratchet quarterly.

notes.title: Container Image Scanning in CI with Trivy
notes.body: Container images bundle an OS userland plus your app, so they inherit every CVE in both. Scanning the final image in CI — after build, before push — is the choke point: trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1 myapp:pr-123 fails the pipeline on high/critical findings. Scan the base image separately and regularly, because base CVEs arrive without any code change on your part. The remediation ladder: (1) rebuild on a patched base (use minimal bases — distroless or alpine — to shrink the CVE surface); (2) update the application dependencies; (3) only then, allowlist a specific CVE with expiry when it is provably unreachable. Worked example: trivy flags CRITICAL CVE-2024-YYYY in openssl inside your python:3.11 base. Solution: check for python:3.11-slim patched tag or the distroless variant, rebuild, rescan — the finding should clear; if the patch is not yet released, document the exposure window, add a 14-day allowlist with owner, and set a calendar reminder, not a permanent ignore. The M-series callback: this is the Dockerfile lesson made operational — multi-stage builds and minimal bases from the Docker module are what make these scans passable in the first place.

notes.title: Triaging Findings: Signal, Noise, and the Allowlist
notes.body: Scanners produce findings; engineers produce judgments. Triage sorts every finding into: true positive and exploitable (fix now), true positive but unreachable (allowlist with expiry and justification), false positive (suppress with reason, revisit on tool upgrade), and duplicate (dedupe to the root cause). The allowlist is a governed document, not a junk drawer: each entry has the CVE/finding ID, why it is accepted (unreachable path, compensating control), an owner, and an expiry date — expired entries re-alert automatically. Metrics keep the program honest: mean time to remediate criticals, percentage of findings allowlisted (a rising share means the gate is being bypassed culturally), and scanner coverage (what percentage of repos run the gates). Worked example: SAST flags 'hardcoded password' on test fixtures using 'password123' against a local test database. Solution: true positive pattern, unreachable in production — but the right fix is not an allowlist, it is moving the fixture to a secrets-free test helper; allowlist only when the code cannot be made clean. The panel point: 'How do you handle false positives?' is a culture question — the answer is a governed triage process with expiry, not 'we ignore the scanner.'

notes.title: Mapping to OWASP: What the Scanners Are Hunting
notes.body: The OWASP Top 10 is the shared vocabulary for what all this tooling hunts: injection (SAST + DAST), broken access control (DAST + manual review), cryptographic failures (SAST flags weak algorithms), vulnerable components (SCA), security misconfiguration (DAST + image scan), and the rest. Each pipeline gate maps to categories: SAST covers injection and crypto; SCA covers vulnerable components; DAST covers access control, misconfiguration, and auth failures; image scanning covers the platform layer beneath the app. Worked example: map a pipeline to the Top 10 for a panel. Solution: 'PR gates — Semgrep (injection, crypto), pip-audit/npm audit (vulnerable components), gitleaks (secrets, feeding M48); merge gates — Trivy image scan (misconfiguration, known OS CVEs); nightly — ZAP baseline against staging (access control, auth, misconfiguration). Every Top 10 category has at least one automated check, and the allowlist governs the exceptions.' The interview move: never recite the Top 10 as trivia — narrate it as your pipeline's coverage map. That turns a memorization question into an architecture answer, which is exactly what senior panels reward.

cards.front: SAST vs DAST vs IAST (one line each)
cards.back: SAST: reads code without running it (early, noisy). DAST: attacks the running app (proof, needs staging). IAST: instruments runtime during tests (precise data-flow)

cards.front: Real SAST commands (Python + general)
cards.back: bandit -r src/ (Python); semgrep scan --config auto (multi-language)

cards.front: Real SCA commands (npm + Python)
cards.back: npm audit / npm audit fix; pip-audit -r requirements.txt; dotnet list package --vulnerable

cards.front: Real DAST baseline command
cards.back: zap-baseline.py -t https://staging.example.com (OWASP ZAP baseline scan)

cards.front: Real container image scan that fails CI on HIGH/CRITICAL
cards.back: trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1 myapp:tag

cards.front: Pipeline gate placement: fast vs slow checks
cards.back: Fast (SAST, SCA, secret scan) on every PR; slow (full DAST, final image scan) on merge before staging

cards.front: Gate thresholds that actually work
cards.back: Fail on critical always; fail on high unless allowlisted with expiry; warn on medium; advisory-only gates are dashboards, not controls

cards.front: Remediation ladder for a base-image CVE
cards.back: Rebuild on patched/minimal base -> update app deps -> time-boxed allowlist with owner (never permanent)

cards.front: Allowlist entry required fields
cards.back: Finding/CVE ID, justification (unreachable/compensating control), owner, expiry date — expired entries re-alert

cards.front: Triage categories for scanner findings
cards.back: True+exploitable (fix), true+unreachable (allowlist w/ expiry), false positive (suppress w/ reason), duplicate (dedupe)

cards.front: Program health metrics (3)
cards.back: Mean time to remediate criticals; % findings allowlisted (rising = cultural bypass); scanner coverage across repos

cards.front: Map gates to OWASP: which gate covers 'vulnerable components'?
cards.back: SCA (npm audit / pip-audit) on every PR — the dependency gate

quiz.q: Where does SAST catch a SQL injection, and where does DAST prove it?
choices: SAST at commit time flags the concatenated query; DAST proves it by injecting into the live staging login form
quiz.explain: SAST sees the code pattern early; DAST demonstrates exploitability against the running app. IAST would trace the tainted flow during tests.

quiz.q: pip-audit reports a critical CVE in requests 2.28.0. What is the correct sequence?
choices: Confirm exploitability -> upgrade to patched version and run tests -> time-boxed exception only if upgrade is impossible
quiz.explain: Verify reachability, upgrade and prove with CI, and only then allowlist with owner and expiry. Blind auto-fix can break the build.

quiz.q: Which gate placement is correct?
choices: Fast checks (SAST/SCA/secret scan) per PR; slow checks (full DAST, final image scan) on merge
All security testing once a year
quiz.explain: Speed-appropriate placement: PR gates give ten-minute fixes; merge gates protect staging; nightly DAST covers depth.

quiz.q: trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1 myapp:pr-123 exits 1. What happened?
choices: The image contains HIGH or CRITICAL findings, so the pipeline stage fails and the PR is blocked
quiz.explain: --exit-code 1 turns findings into a gate failure — the choke point between build and push.

quiz.q: Trivy flags a critical OpenSSL CVE in your python:3.11 base. First remediation step?
choices: Rebuild on a patched/minimal base (slim or distroless) and rescan
quiz.explain: The remediation ladder starts with the base: patched minimal bases clear whole CVE classes. Allowlisting is the last resort, time-boxed.

quiz.q: SAST flags 'hardcoded password' in test fixtures using password123 against a local test DB. Best handling?
choices: Fix the code: move fixtures to a secrets-free helper; allowlist only what cannot be made clean
quiz.explain: Triage prefers fixing over allowlisting; the allowlist is for provably unreachable findings, not for cleanable code.

quiz.q: A gate that reports findings but never blocks is:
choices: A dashboard, not a control — start strict on new code, advisory on legacy with a quarterly ratchet
quiz.explain: Controls must control. The ratchet pattern (block new, advisory legacy, tighten quarterly) makes strictness adoptable.

quiz.q: Which Top 10 category does the SCA gate cover?
quiz.explain: SCA exists for the components category — npm audit/pip-audit on every PR is its operational form.

quiz.q: Mean time to remediate criticals is rising and allowlist share is climbing. What does this indicate?
choices: Cultural bypass: findings are being deferred rather than fixed — tighten ownership and review the allowlist
quiz.explain: Rising allowlist share with slowing remediation means the gate is being routed around. Metrics exist to catch exactly this.

items.prompt: Python SAST scan of src/ — command?
items.answer: bandit -r src/
items.explain: Bandit is the Python SAST staple — recursive scan, know the flag.

items.prompt: Multi-language SAST with auto ruleset — command?
items.answer: semgrep scan --config auto
items.explain: Semgrep auto config is the PR-gate default.

items.prompt: Python dependency CVE scan — command?
items.answer: pip-audit -r requirements.txt
items.explain: Reads the pinned requirements — the M50 pinning lesson in action.

items.prompt: npm dependency audit and careful fix — commands?
items.answer: npm audit; npm audit fix (review the diff, let CI prove it).
items.explain: Audit first, fix deliberately — blind fix breaks builds.

items.prompt: Fail CI on HIGH/CRITICAL image CVEs — command?
items.answer: trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1 myapp:tag
items.explain: The image gate: after build, before push.

items.prompt: DAST baseline against staging — command?
items.answer: zap-baseline.py -t https://staging.example.com
items.explain: ZAP baseline: spiders and fires payloads at the running app.

items.prompt: SAST vs DAST vs IAST in one breath?
items.answer: SAST reads code early/noisy; DAST attacks runtime/proof; IAST instruments tests/precise.
items.explain: Then map: SAST per PR, DAST nightly, IAST in integration tests.

items.prompt: Gate thresholds: critical / high / medium?
items.answer: Fail critical always; fail high unless allowlisted w/ expiry; warn medium.
items.explain: Say the three tiers — panels test whether your gates have teeth.

items.prompt: Fast vs slow gate placement?
items.answer: Fast (SAST/SCA/secrets) per PR; slow (full DAST, final image) on merge.
items.explain: Speed-appropriate: ten-minute fixes vs staging protection.

items.prompt: Base-image critical CVE: the remediation ladder?
items.answer: Patched/minimal base rebuild -> app dep updates -> time-boxed allowlist w/ owner.
items.explain: Ladder order matters — allowlist is last, never first.

items.prompt: Allowlist entry: four required fields?
items.answer: Finding ID, justification, owner, expiry.
items.explain: Expired entries re-alert — the anti-junk-drawer rule.

items.prompt: Triage categories — name all four.
items.answer: True+exploitable (fix), true+unreachable (allowlist), false positive (suppress), duplicate (dedupe).
items.explain: Every finding lands in exactly one bucket.

items.prompt: Program health: three metrics?
items.answer: MTTR for criticals; % allowlisted; scanner coverage.
items.explain: Rising allowlist share = cultural bypass — metrics catch it.

items.prompt: Narrate your pipeline as an OWASP coverage map (30 seconds).
items.answer: PR: Semgrep (injection/crypto), SCA (components), secret scan; merge: Trivy (platform CVEs); nightly: ZAP (access control/auth/misconfig).
items.explain: Turns trivia into architecture — the senior-panel move.

handsOnLab.title: Lab: shift-left gates on a real pipeline
handsOnLab.brief: You will wire SAST, SCA, secret scanning, and Trivy image gates into a CI pipeline for a sample app, watch them catch planted vulnerabilities, triage the findings, and prove the allowlist discipline.
steps: Clone the sample app (Python Flask + Dockerfile) and plant three issues: a bandit-flaggable subprocess call, an outdated requests version in requirements.txt, and a fake AWS key in a comment.
Add the PR-gate job: bandit -r src/ with exit-code fail, semgrep scan --config auto, pip-audit -r requirements.txt, and gitleaks detect --no-git (or equivalent secret scan).
Run the pipeline and record all three findings; verify the build fails (non-zero exit).
Triage each: fix the subprocess call properly, upgrade requests and let tests prove it, remove the fake key and rotate the pattern.
Rebuild the Docker image with a minimal base (python:3.11-slim) and multi-stage build; run trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1 on it.
Record the Trivy findings; remediate by base/dependency updates; for one provably-unreachable finding, create an allowlist entry with ID, justification, owner, and 14-day expiry.
Add the merge gate: full Trivy scan of the final image before push; confirm a critical blocks the push.
Run zap-baseline.py -t against a local staging deploy of the app; record the DAST findings and map each to an OWASP Top 10 category.
Write the coverage map: which gate covers which Top 10 categories, in a one-page table.
Measure: time from finding to fix for each planted issue; note which gate caught it fastest.
Expire-test: backdate the allowlist expiry and confirm the pipeline re-alerts.
Document the ratchet plan: which gates block today, which are advisory on legacy repos, and the quarterly tightening schedule.
handsOnLab.deliverable: A CI pipeline with four working gates, triaged findings with a governed allowlist, a ZAP baseline report, and an OWASP coverage map.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: All planted issues are caught and fixed; the pipeline fails on a new critical; the allowlist entry re-alerts after expiry; the coverage map covers every Top 10 category.

mockTask.q: Your new SAST gate flags 200 findings on a legacy repo on day one, and developers demand it be turned off. What do you do?
choices: Make it advisory on legacy code with a quarterly ratchet, but keep it blocking on new code — and triage the 200 into fix/allowlist-with-expiry buckets with owners
mockTask.explain: Day-one blocking on legacy debt kills adoption; advisory-with-ratchet preserves the control while the backlog is triaged. New code stays strict so debt stops growing, and every legacy finding gets an owner and an expiry — not a permanent pass.

modules.title: Secrets, Supply Chain & Identity
modules.summary: Lock down the last mile: Vault/Key Vault secret management with practiced rotation, the secrets-in-git ritual, SBOMs and cosign signing, least-privilege RBAC across five layers, and the Security+ domain crosswalk.
objectives: Manage secrets in Vault/Key Vault with dynamic credentials and rehearsed rotation
Prevent, detect, and remediate secrets committed to git with gitleaks gates
Generate SBOMs and sign container images, enforcing verification at deploy time
Apply least-privilege RBAC across Kubernetes, cloud, application, database, and pipeline layers
Map secrets and supply-chain work to CompTIA Security+ domains for panel conversations

notes.title: Secret Management: Vault and Key Vault
notes.body: Secrets — API keys, database passwords, TLS private keys — must live in a purpose-built secret store, never in code, config files, or chat. HashiCorp Vault and Azure Key Vault provide the same core contract: encrypted storage, fine-grained access policies, audit logging of every read, dynamic secrets (credentials generated on demand with a TTL, e.g. a database password that lives 1 hour), and rotation. The access pattern: the application authenticates to Vault (via Kubernetes auth, Azure auth, or AppRole — never a hardcoded token in production) and reads the secret at startup or via a sidecar injector; CI pipelines fetch secrets at runtime from the store instead of storing them as pipeline variables. Worked example: a Flask app needs the Postgres password. Anti-pattern: DATABASE_URL with the password in the deployment YAML committed to git. Solution: store it with vault kv put secret/checkout db_password=<value>; the pod uses the Vault agent injector annotation to render the secret into a file at startup; rotation is vault kv put with the new value plus a database password change — no redeploy, no git history. On Azure the equivalent is az keyvault secret set --vault-name kv-prod --name db-password, referenced from AKS via the Secrets Store CSI driver. The audit property is the point: the store logs who read what, when — something env vars and files can never do.

notes.title: Rotation and the Blast Radius of a Leak
notes.body: Every secret has a lifetime, and rotation is how you bound the blast radius when (not if) one leaks. Static secrets should rotate on a schedule (90 days is the common policy; 30 for high-value) and immediately on any suspected exposure, personnel departure, or the 'it was in a Slack thread' incident. Dynamic secrets are better: Vault generates a database credential per application instance with a 1-hour TTL — there is nothing long-lived to leak, and revocation is automatic. The rotation procedure must be rehearsed: (1) generate the new secret in the store; (2) update consumers (rolling restart or sidecar re-render); (3) verify the new credential works; (4) revoke the old one; (5) confirm nothing still uses it via the audit log. Worked example: an AWS access key was pasted into a public Slack channel. Solution sequence: immediately deactivate (not delete — preserve for forensics) the key in IAM, generate a replacement, update the one consumer via the secret store, verify, then delete the old key; search git history and logs for the key string; write the postmortem on how a long-lived key ended up copy-pasteable. The lesson the panel wants: the incident is survivable because rotation was a practiced procedure, not an improvisation — and the long-term fix is replacing the key with an OIDC-assumed role so there is no key to leak next time.

notes.title: Secrets in Git: The Antipattern and Its Detection
notes.body: Committing a secret to git publishes it to every clone, fork, and backup forever — deleting it later does not unpublish it, because history retains it. Prevention is a pipeline gate: gitleaks detect --no-git (or the pre-commit hook gitleaks protect) scans diffs for key patterns and fails the PR before the secret lands. Detection on existing repos: gitleaks detect --source . --verbose across history finds what is already burned. Remediation of a burned secret is a fixed ritual: (1) revoke/rotate the secret immediately — it is compromised, full stop; (2) purge it from history only if the repo can tolerate a force-push (git filter-repo), understanding clones still have it; (3) audit where the secret was valid during exposure (cloud audit logs); (4) add the gitleaks gate so it cannot recur. Worked example: gitleaks flags AKIA... in a commit from 6 months ago. Solution: the key is burned — rotate it now, check CloudTrail for usage of that key ID during the window, purge history if the team accepts the force-push, and enable the pre-commit hook today. The interview answer: 'A secret in git is a compromised secret; rotation first, history surgery second, prevention gate third.' Never 'we deleted the file so it is fine.'

notes.title: Supply Chain: SBOMs and Signing
notes.body: You cannot secure what you cannot inventory: an SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) lists every component in your artifact — OS packages, language dependencies, base image layers. Generate it in CI: syft packages myapp:tag -o spdx-json > sbom.json produces a machine-readable inventory you attach to the release. Signing proves the artifact you deploy is the artifact you built: cosign sign --key cosign.key myapp:tag (or keyless with OIDC via cosign sign --oidc-issuer) creates a signature; admission controllers verify it before pods start — unsigned images do not run. The chain: SBOM generation -> vulnerability scan of the SBOM -> sign the artifact -> verify at deploy time. Worked example: a critical CVE is announced in a base-image library at 9 AM. With SBOMs: query which of your 40 services' SBOMs contain the library version — 3 do; rebuild and resign those 3 by noon. Without SBOMs: manually audit 40 Dockerfiles and guess. Solution review: the SBOM turns a fire drill into a database query, and signing guarantees the rebuilt images are the ones that deploy. The panel framing: SBOM answers 'what is in it?', signing answers 'did we build it?', and together they are the supply-chain answer to 'how do you know what is running in prod?'

notes.title: RBAC and Least Privilege Across the Full Stack
notes.body: The panel asks about RBAC across a full-stack app — the answer spans every layer with one principle: least privilege, each identity getting only what its job requires. Kubernetes RBAC: Roles/ClusterRoles bound to ServiceAccounts via RoleBindings — the checkout ServiceAccount gets get/list on its own ConfigMaps, not cluster-admin. Cloud IAM: the patterns from M42/M43 (IRSA, Workload Identity) scoped to single buckets/queues. Application layer: role checks in the API (admin vs analyst vs viewer), row-level filtering on queries, and the database user granted SELECT on exactly the tables it needs. Pipeline: the deploy identity can apply to the staging namespace but needs an approval gate for prod. Worked example: design access for a data analyst who needs read-only dashboards. Solution: cloud IAM read-only role on the warehouse; Kubernetes read-only ClusterRole on the analytics namespace; application role 'viewer' with no export permission; database GRANT SELECT on the marts schema only; no CI deploy rights; no secret-store read. Every layer says the minimum. The failure mode is role explosion (400 custom roles nobody understands) — counter it with a small set of standard roles per layer, reviewed quarterly, with every exception carrying an owner and expiry, exactly like the M47 allowlist discipline.

notes.title: CompTIA Security+ Domain Crosswalk
notes.body: This module maps cleanly onto the CompTIA Security+ domains, which is useful interview framing: the domains are the industry's shared checklist, and narrating your work against them shows structured thinking. Domain 1 (General Security Concepts): least privilege, zero trust, and the control types your gates implement. Domain 2 (Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Mitigations): CVE triage, supply-chain attacks, and secret exposure as threat vectors. Domain 3 (Security Architecture): secret stores, signing infrastructure, and network segmentation for secret access. Domain 4 (Security Operations): rotation procedures, incident handling for leaks, log auditing of secret access, and vulnerability scanning operations. Domain 5 (Security Program Management): the allowlist governance, rotation policies, and compliance evidence (who accessed what secret when) that auditors ask for. Worked example: a panel asks 'how does your secrets program map to Security+?' Solution: 'Architecture gives us Vault/Key Vault with dynamic secrets; Operations gives us rotation runbooks and leak incident procedures with audit logs; Program Management gives us the 90-day rotation policy and the governed exception process — and the scanners from M47 feed the vulnerability management in Domain 4.' The point is not the certification — this course confers none — it is speaking the domain language that security-minded panels expect.
