quiz.q: A Flask app needs the Postgres password. Which design is correct?
choices: DATABASE_URL with password in the committed deployment YAML
Vault KV secret rendered via agent injector; rotation without redeploy; audit log of reads
Password in a Slack pinned message
quiz.explain: The secret store gives encrypted storage, access policy, audit trail, and rotation without code changes. Committed YAML publishes the secret to every clone.

quiz.q: An AWS key is pasted into a public Slack channel. What is the FIRST step?
choices: Deactivate the key immediately (preserve for forensics), then replace via the secret store
Wait to see if it is misused
quiz.explain: The key is compromised the instant it is visible. Deactivate first (deleting destroys forensic evidence), replace, verify, then investigate usage.

quiz.q: Why are dynamic Vault database credentials better than a shared static password?
choices: Per-consumer credentials with a TTL: nothing long-lived to leak, revocation automatic
quiz.explain: Short-lived per-instance credentials bound the blast radius by construction; a leaked 1-hour credential dies on its own.

quiz.q: gitleaks flags AKIA... in a 6-month-old commit. Correct handling?
choices: Delete the file and move on
Rotate the key now (it is burned), audit usage during exposure, purge history only with team-accepted force-push, add the pre-commit gate
It is old so it is safe
quiz.explain: Age does not uncompromise a secret. Rotation first, exposure audit second, history surgery third (clones retain it anyway), prevention gate always.

quiz.q: A critical CVE is announced in a base-image library. With SBOMs in CI, what is your response?
choices: Query the SBOMs: which services contain the vulnerable version — rebuild, rescan, and resign exactly those
quiz.explain: The SBOM turns the fire drill into a database query: precise blast radius, targeted rebuilds, signed artifacts.

quiz.q: What does cosign verification at deploy time guarantee?
choices: The image is the artifact your pipeline built and signed — unsigned or tampered images never start
quiz.explain: Signing answers provenance ('did we build it?'), enforced by admission control. CVE scanning is the SBOM/scan job, a separate concern.

quiz.q: Design access for a read-only data analyst across the stack. Which is correct?
choices: Read-only warehouse role, read-only K8s ClusterRole on the analytics namespace, app viewer role, SELECT on marts schema only, no deploy or secret rights
quiz.explain: Least privilege at every layer, each scoped to the job. Any broader grant is a finding.

quiz.q: Your org has 400 custom IAM roles nobody understands. What is the fix?
choices: Consolidate to a small standard set per layer, quarterly review, exceptions with owner + expiry
quiz.explain: Role explosion is managed like the allowlist: standardize, review, and govern exceptions with ownership and expiry.

quiz.q: Map to Security+: quarterly rotation policy with audit evidence of secret access belongs to which domain?
quiz.explain: Policies, governance, and compliance evidence are Program Management; the rotation runbook itself is Operations (Domain 4).

handsOnLab.title: Lab: Vault, gitleaks gates, SBOMs, and signed images
handsOnLab.brief: You will run Vault in dev mode, wire secret injection into a sample app, plant and catch a git secret with gitleaks, generate SBOMs, sign an image with cosign, and verify the signature — the full supply-chain loop.
steps: Start Vault dev server: vault server -dev (dev only); export VAULT_ADDR and VAULT_TOKEN; enable KV v2 at secret/.
Store the app secret: vault kv put secret/labapp db_password='s3cret-lab-only'; create a policy allowing read on secret/labapp/*.
Deploy the sample app with the Vault agent injector annotation; exec into the pod and confirm the secret renders as a file with no secret in env or git.
Rotate: vault kv put a new value; restart the deployment; confirm the app picks it up with zero code changes.
Plant a fake AWS key in a commit; run gitleaks detect --source . --verbose; record the finding with commit SHA.
Execute the burned-secret ritual on paper: rotate (simulate), list what you would audit, and decide on history purge with justification.
Add the gitleaks pre-commit hook; attempt to commit another fake key and confirm the commit is blocked.
Build the app image; generate the SBOM: syft packages labapp:1.0 -o spdx-json > sbom.json; record the OS + language package counts.
Run trivy against the SBOM/image; for one finding, write the allowlist entry (ID, justification, owner, 14-day expiry).
Generate a cosign key pair; sign: cosign sign --key cosign.key labapp:1.0; verify: cosign verify --key cosign.pub labapp:1.0.

Simulate admission: write the policy snippet (e.g. Kyverno/Gatekeeper pseudo-policy) requiring valid cosign signatures on the lab namespace; confirm an unsigned tag would be rejected by your rule logic.
Write the Security+ crosswalk paragraph for your lab: which domain each piece belongs to. Tear down Vault and the images.
handsOnLab.deliverable: Working Vault-backed secret injection with a practiced rotation, a gitleaks-blocked commit, an SBOM, a signed and verified image, and an admission-policy sketch.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Secret renders in-pod with nothing in git/env; gitleaks blocks the second fake key; cosign verify passes; the SBOM lists the vulnerable package you allowlisted.

mockTask.q: A developer committed a production database password 3 weeks ago and 'deleted the file' yesterday. What do you tell the team?
choices: The password is compromised: rotate it immediately, audit access during the 3-week window, purge history only if the team accepts a force-push, and add the gitleaks gate today
Only rotate if someone reports misuse
mockTask.explain: Deletion does not unpublish git history. The credential is burned until rotated; the exposure window must be audited; the gate prevents recurrence. 'Wait for misuse' is negligence.

modules.title: SRE & Resilience: HA, Microservices & the Strangler Fig
modules.summary: Engineer reliability: SRE principles, layered high availability, timeout/retry/circuit-breaker arithmetic, the strangler-fig migration of a monolithic trading platform, chaos game-days, and Little's Law capacity planning.
objectives: Apply SRE principles: error budgets, toil reduction, golden signals, blameless postmortems
Design multi-AZ and multi-region architectures with honest availability math
Implement timeouts, bounded retries, and circuit breakers, computing retry amplification
Plan a strangler-fig migration seam by seam with data migration and fallback safety
Run chaos experiments and capacity-plan with Little's Law

notes.title: SRE Principles: Toil, Budgets, and Blamelessness
notes.body: Site Reliability Engineering treats operations as a software problem. Its principles, straight from the Google SRE tradition: (1) error budgets (M46) govern the feature-vs-reliability tradeoff; (2) toil — manual, repetitive operational work — is budgeted and automated away, with a standing cap on how much of a team's time it may consume; (3) monitoring is built around the four golden signals (latency, traffic, errors, saturation); (4) automation is preferred over heroics for every repeated task; (5) blameless postmortems turn incidents into system fixes. The SRE mindset shift for a panel: reliability is a feature with a price, negotiated explicitly via the SLO — not a vague aspiration. Worked example: a team spends 60% of its time on manual deploy verifications and ticket-driven restarts. SRE analysis: that is toil — automatable, repetitive, and scaling linearly with service count. Solution: cap toil work, automate the deploy verification into the pipeline (smoke tests + automatic rollback on burn-rate alerts), and convert the restart tickets into the autoscaler + health-probe fixes from M41. The interview one-liner: 'SRE replaces operational heroics with engineering: budgets decide priorities, automation absorbs toil, and postmortems fix systems.'

notes.title: High Availability: Multi-AZ and Multi-Region Design
notes.body: High availability is designed in layers. Within a region: deploy across at least 3 availability zones — AKS node pools spread with --zones 1 2 3, databases with zone-redundant replicas, load balancers zone-aware. A zone failure then costs capacity, not availability. Across regions: active-passive (traffic on one region, tested failover to the second) for most financial workloads, active-active only when the data layer supports conflict-free replication. The data layer decides everything: stateless services fail over trivially; databases need replication with a known RPO/RTO, and the failover must be rehearsed — an untested failover is a hope. Worked example: design the checkout service for zone failure. Solution: AKS with 3 zones, pod anti-affinity spreading replicas across zones, PodDisruptionBudgets guaranteeing quorum during drains, Azure SQL zone-redundant, Application Gateway multi-zone; chaos-test by failing one zone in staging quarterly. The panel question on 'fault tolerance for mission-critical financial apps' wants exactly this layered answer: multi-AZ for the common case, multi-region with tested failover for the disaster case, data replication as the binding constraint, and rehearsal as the proof. Availability math is honest: each added nine costs roughly an order of magnitude more engineering — 99.9% is 8.8 hours/year of budget, 99.99% is 53 minutes, and the SLO should match what the business will actually fund.

notes.title: Circuit Breakers, Retries, and Timeouts
notes.body: Distributed systems fail partially, and naive clients turn partial failure into total failure. Three patterns contain it. Timeouts: every outbound call gets a deadline (e.g. 2s) — without one, a hung dependency parks your threads forever. Retries: retry transient failures with exponential backoff and jitter, but only idempotent operations — retrying a non-idempotent payment charge double-charges. Circuit breakers: after N consecutive failures, the breaker opens and calls fail fast for a cooldown period instead of hammering the dead dependency, then half-opens to probe recovery. The retry-storm math the panel loves: service A calls B with 3 retries; B calls C with 3 retries; one slow C means each user request fans out to 1 + 3 + 9 = up to 13 downstream calls — a 13x amplification that melts C. Worked example: payment calls take 200ms normally; the client has no timeout and 5 retries. Under a payment outage, threads pile up waiting, memory grows, and the checkout service itself OOMs — the M41 OOMKilled drill in distributed form. Solution: 2s timeout, max 2 retries with backoff + jitter on idempotent reads only, circuit breaker opening after 5 consecutive failures with 30s cooldown, and a retry budget (e.g. max 10% of requests may be retries). Resilience is arithmetic: bound every fan-out or the fan-out bounds you.

notes.title: Case Study (Hypothetical): Strangler Fig on a Monolithic Trading Platform
notes.body: Exercise — hypothetical, no claims about any real firm: re-architect a legacy monolithic trading platform into microservices. The strangler fig pattern (Martin Fowler) migrates incrementally: new functionality is built as services around the monolith, traffic is routed to the new services piece by piece, and the monolith shrinks until it can be retired — like the fig that grows around a tree. The migration plan: (1) identify seams — order entry, market data, risk checks, settlement — and carve the first low-risk seam (say, market-data fan-out, read-only); (2) put an anti-corruption layer / facade in front of the monolith so new services never touch its schema directly; (3) route via the gateway progressively (1% -> 10% -> 100%) with the monolith as instant fallback; (4) extract state carefully — the database is the hard part, migrated with dual-write or change-data-capture, never a big-bang cutover; (5) retire the monolith's module only when traffic is zero and the data is migrated. Worked example: which seam first? Solution: the read-only market-data feed — no writes, no transactions, easy rollback; order entry (money movement) goes last, with the most testing. The panel answer: 'Strangler fig, seam by seam, gateway-routed with fallback, data migrated via dual-write — never a rewrite, never a big bang.'

notes.title: Chaos Engineering: Proving Resilience on Purpose
notes.body: Chaos engineering is the disciplined practice of injecting failure to prove resilience before production does it for you. Principles: start with a steady-state hypothesis ('checkout p99 stays under 500ms when one zone fails'), blast radius is minimized (staging first, one zone, business-hours, with an abort button), and every experiment is a game-day with observers and a rollback plan. The experiment ladder: kill a pod (does the ReplicaSet recover in seconds?); kill a node (do pods reschedule across zones?); fail a zone (does multi-AZ hold?); inject latency into a dependency (do timeouts and breakers engage?); expire a certificate (does rotation work?). Worked example: hypothesis — 'losing one of three zones keeps checkout under SLO.' Run it in staging: cordon and drain a zone's nodes, watch the dashboards. If p99 breaches, the postmortem writes the missing anti-affinity or PDB as the action item — the experiment paid for itself. The panel framing: chaos is not recklessness, it is the scientific method applied to reliability — hypothesis, controlled experiment, measured result, system fix. Never run chaos in production without the incident-command structure from M46 on standby; the point is learning, not outages.

notes.title: Capacity Planning with Little's Law
notes.body: Little's Law — L = λW — relates the average number of items in a system (L) to the arrival rate (λ) and the average time each spends in the system (W). It is the back-of-the-envelope capacity tool: it needs no distributional assumptions, just consistent units. Worked example: checkout receives λ = 500 requests/second, each taking W = 0.4 seconds of server time. L = 500 × 0.4 = 200 concurrent requests in flight on average. If each pod handles 50 concurrent requests, you need 200/50 = 4 pods for steady state — then add headroom for bursts and rolling updates (the M41 autoscaler math), say min 6. Second example: a queue grows unboundedly. λ = 1000 msgs/s in, processing W-equivalent throughput 800/s — arrivals exceed service, so no steady state exists and the queue grows forever; the fix is more consumers or load shedding, not a bigger queue. The panel callback: combine with the M41 node math — Little's Law gives concurrent load, pod capacity gives pods needed, and the autoscaler min/max brackets the result. Capacity planning is not guessing: it is λ measured from dashboards, W measured from traces, and L computed — then verified by load test.

cards.front: SRE in one line
cards.back: Operations as software: error budgets set priorities, automation absorbs toil, blameless postmortems fix systems — reliability as a priced feature

cards.front: Four golden signals
cards.back: Latency, traffic, errors, saturation — the monitoring baseline for every service

cards.front: What is toil and how is it handled?
cards.back: Manual repetitive ops work; budgeted, capped, and automated away — heroics are not a strategy

cards.front: Multi-AZ vs multi-region (when each)
cards.back: Multi-AZ (3 zones): the common case — zone failure costs capacity. Multi-region active-passive: disaster case with tested failover; data replication is the binding constraint

cards.front: Availability budget math: 99.9% vs 99.99%
cards.back: 99.9% = ~8.8 h/year downtime budget; 99.99% = ~53 min/year; each nine costs ~10x the engineering — SLO must match funded reality

cards.front: Timeout / retry / circuit breaker (one line each)
cards.back: Timeout: deadline on every call. Retry: transient failures only, backoff+jitter, idempotent ops only. Breaker: fail fast after N failures, half-open to probe recovery

cards.front: Retry-storm amplification math
cards.back: A->B (3 retries) ->C (3 retries): one slow C fans one request into up to 13 downstream calls — bound with retry budgets (e.g. 10% cap)

cards.front: Why never retry a non-idempotent payment charge?
cards.back: Retries re-execute: the charge happens twice. Retries are for idempotent operations only

cards.front: Strangler fig pattern in one paragraph
cards.back: Build new services around the monolith, route traffic piece by piece via gateway with fallback, migrate data via dual-write/CDC, retire modules at zero traffic — never a big-bang rewrite

cards.front: Strangler fig: which seam first on a trading platform?
cards.back: Read-only market-data feed (no writes, easy rollback); money-movement order entry goes last with the most testing

cards.front: Chaos experiment structure
cards.back: Steady-state hypothesis -> minimized blast radius (staging, abort button) -> game-day with observers -> measured result -> system fix

cards.front: Little's Law + worked example
cards.back: L = λW. λ=500 rps, W=0.4s -> L=200 concurrent; at 50/pod -> 4 pods steady state, plus headroom

cards.front: Queue growing unboundedly: Little's Law diagnosis?
cards.back: λ (1000/s) > service rate (800/s): no steady state exists — add consumers or shed load; a bigger queue just delays the inevitable

cards.front: Untested failover is what?
cards.back: A hope, not a plan — failover must be rehearsed (game-days) or it will fail when needed

quiz.q: A team spends 60% of its time on manual deploy checks and restart tickets. SRE analysis?
choices: That is toil: cap it, automate deploy verification into the pipeline, fix restarts with autoscaling and health probes
quiz.explain: Toil is the SRE term for automatable repetitive ops work; the discipline budgets and eliminates it rather than staffing it.

quiz.q: Design checkout for zone failure. Which set is correct?
choices: 3 AZs, pod anti-affinity across zones, PDBs, zone-redundant database, multi-zone gateway, quarterly zone-failure game-day
Active-active across 5 regions on day one
quiz.explain: Layered HA: multi-AZ for the common case with spreading and disruption budgets, rehearsed. Active-active everywhere on day one is over-engineering.

quiz.q: Payment client: no timeout, 5 retries, outage hits. What happens?
choices: Threads pile up on hung calls, retries multiply load, the caller OOMs — the distributed version of the M41 OOMKilled drill
quiz.explain: No timeout parks threads; retries amplify; the caller's memory grows until it dies. Timeouts + bounded retries + breakers prevent exactly this.

quiz.q: A->B->C chain, each link retries 3 times. One slow C: worst-case downstream calls per user request?
quiz.explain: Retry multiplication compounds per hop. Retry budgets (e.g. 10% cap) and breakers bound the fan-out.

quiz.q: Which operation may be retried?
quiz.explain: Only idempotent operations survive re-execution. Retrying money movement double-executes it.

quiz.q: Strangler fig on a monolithic trading platform: what goes first?
choices: Read-only market-data feed — no writes, trivial rollback; order entry goes last
quiz.explain: Seam-by-seam risk ordering: stateless reads first, money movement last, data via dual-write — never a big bang.

quiz.q: What is the anti-corruption layer's job in the strangler fig?
choices: Shielding new services from the monolith's schema so they never couple to legacy internals
quiz.explain: The facade translates between the new domain model and the monolith, preventing the new services from inheriting legacy coupling.

quiz.q: Chaos experiment: 'lose one zone in staging, checkout stays under SLO.' p99 breaches. What is the correct conclusion?
choices: The experiment paid for itself: write the missing anti-affinity/PDB/capacity as postmortem action items and re-run
quiz.explain: A failed hypothesis is a found weakness — the scientific-method framing. Fix the system, re-run the experiment.

quiz.q: λ=500 rps, W=0.4s, 50 concurrent requests per pod. Pods for steady state?
choices: 4 (L=200 concurrent / 50), plus headroom for bursts and rolling updates
quiz.explain: L = 500×0.4 = 200 concurrent; 200/50 = 4 pods steady state. Headroom (min 6) covers bursts and update surge — the M41 autoscaler bracket.

items.answer: ~8.8 h vs ~53 min. Each nine ~10x the engineering.

items.prompt: Zone-failure design: the five pieces?
items.answer: 3 AZs, anti-affinity, PDBs, zone-redundant DB, rehearsed game-day.
items.explain: Recite as the checklist for 'fault tolerance for financial apps'.

items.prompt: Untested failover is ___?
items.answer: A hope, not a plan — rehearse or it fails when needed.
items.explain: One line, no hedging.

items.prompt: Strangler fig in 30 seconds.
items.answer: New services around the monolith; gateway routes traffic piece by piece with fallback; data via dual-write/CDC; retire at zero traffic.

items.prompt: Trading platform: first seam and last seam?
items.answer: First: read-only market-data feed. Last: order entry (money movement).
items.explain: Risk ordering: stateless reads first, money last.

items.prompt: What does the anti-corruption layer do?
items.answer: Shields new services from the monolith's schema — no legacy coupling.
items.explain: Facade translates; new domain model stays clean.

items.prompt: How is traffic migrated safely?
items.answer: Gateway-routed percentages (1%->10%->100%) with the monolith as instant fallback.
items.explain: Progressive + reversible — the safety property.

items.prompt: How is the database migrated?
items.answer: Dual-write or change-data-capture — never a big-bang cutover.
items.explain: Data is the hard part; say the two techniques.

items.prompt: Little's Law: λ=500, W=0.4. L and pods at 50/pod?
items.answer: L=200; 4 pods steady state, headroom to ~6.
items.explain: Show the arithmetic — λ×W, then divide.

items.prompt: Queue grows forever: diagnosis and fix?
items.answer: λ > service rate: no steady state. Add consumers or shed load.
items.explain: Bigger queue delays; it never fixes.

handsOnLab.title: Lab: resilience patterns and a strangler-fig plan
handsOnLab.brief: You will implement timeout/retry/circuit-breaker in a sample service, measure retry amplification, run a zone-failure game-day on a local cluster, and write the strangler-fig migration plan for a hypothetical monolith.
steps: Write a Python client calling a flaky test server: add a 2s timeout, max 2 retries with exponential backoff + jitter, idempotency keys on writes.
Measure: with retries at 3 per hop across a 2-hop chain, count downstream calls during a 10s induced slowdown — record the amplification factor.
Add a circuit breaker (simple counter-based implementation): open after 5 consecutive failures, 30s cooldown, half-open probe; verify calls fail fast while open.
Add a retry budget: cap retries at 10% of requests; verify the budget throttles retries under sustained failure.
Deploy two services on a local kind cluster across 3 'zones' (labels); set pod anti-affinity and a PodDisruptionBudget; verify spread with kubectl get pods -o wide.
Drain one zone's nodes (kubectl drain); measure recovery time and error rate; record whether the SLO held.
Write the chaos report: hypothesis, blast radius, measurements, and the action items the experiment produced.
Draft the strangler-fig plan for a hypothetical monolithic trading app: seam list in migration order, facade design, gateway routing stages, dual-write data plan, retirement criteria.
Compute capacity with Little's Law for the lab services: measure λ and W from your test traffic, compute L, and compare with actual pod counts.
Define the SLOs for the lab checkout path (success ratio + p99) and the error-budget policy that would freeze the strangler migration.
Present the 5-minute panel narrative: strangler plan, resilience patterns, and the chaos result.
Clean up the kind cluster and archive the plan + report in the repo.
handsOnLab.deliverable: A client library with timeout/retry/breaker/budget, a zone-failure game-day report, a seam-ordered strangler-fig migration plan, and Little's Law capacity math.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Amplification measured and bounded; zone drain recovers within the SLO; the migration plan orders seams by risk with data via dual-write.

mockTask.q: Panel: 'Re-architect our legacy monolithic trading platform as microservices.' What is the core of a strong answer?
choices: Full rewrite in microservices over one big-bang cutover
Strangler fig: seam-by-seam extraction starting with read-only services, gateway-routed traffic with monolith fallback, anti-corruption layer, data via dual-write/CDC, retire at zero traffic
Lift-and-shift the monolith to bigger VMs
mockTask.explain: The strong answer names the pattern, the seam ordering (reads first, money movement last), the safety properties (progressive routing, fallback), and the data strategy — proving you have done or deeply studied real migrations, not just drawn boxes.

modules.title: BNY Panel Interview Simulation: Independent Mastery
modules.summary: The capstone: every real panel question becomes a timed drill with full model answers, STAR scaffolds for all behavioral questions, delivery coaching, and a complete 90-minute mock panel script you run solo — cold, with no copilot.
objectives: Answer every Terraform/Ansible, Linux, networking, Git, Python, and Docker panel question cold with model-answer depth
Answer every Kubernetes/AKS, Jenkins, Helm, Azure networking, and CI/CD panel question cold
Deliver STAR-structured behavioral answers (unclear requirements, new technology, mentoring) in under 2 minutes
Apply delivery coaching: structure-first, slowed pace, camera presence, no reading
Execute the 90-minute mock panel solo and score ≥120/160 with zero reds on safety-critical items

notes.title: The STAR Method: Structure Every Behavioral Answer
notes.body: Behavioral questions are scored on structure, not just content. STAR: Situation (one sentence of context), Task (what you were asked to do), Action (what YOU did — the longest part, first person, specific verbs), Result (measurable outcome + what you learned). Timebox: 90 seconds to 2 minutes; longer rambles lose the panel. The most common failure is staying in Situation for a minute and compressing Action into ten seconds — invert that ratio. Worked example, full model answer for 'Tell me about a time you translated unclear business requirements into technical deliverables.' Situation: 'Our ops team asked for "better visibility into deployments" with no further detail.' Task: 'I needed to turn that into something shippable.' Action: 'I interviewed three on-call engineers for 20 minutes each, mapped their pain to the four golden signals, and proposed a one-page spec: deploy annotations on every dashboard plus a burn-rate alert per service. I validated the spec with the requester before writing code, then built it in two sprints.' Result: 'Deploy-related incidents dropped from "we didn't know what shipped" to a 5-minute correlation, and the one-page spec format became the team's template for vague requests.' Notice: specific verbs (interviewed, mapped, proposed, validated, built), a number, and a transferable lesson. Practice every behavioral answer in this shape until it is muscle memory — the drills below score you on it.

notes.title: STAR Scaffolds: The Three Behavioral Questions
notes.body: Three behavioral questions appear in the panel list; here are complete STAR scaffolds you adapt to your real experience — never invent employers or events, but do bring real ones. (1) 'Translate unclear business requirements into technical deliverables': use the scaffold above — interview stakeholders, write the one-page spec, validate before building, ship incrementally, measure. Your Action must show the translation mechanism (questions asked, spec written), not just 'I figured it out.' (2) 'Introduce a new technology or methodology that improved team performance': Situation — team hand-editing YAML per environment, slow and error-prone. Task — evaluate and introduce a safer way. Action — 'I built a proof-of-concept of Kustomize overlays on one service, demoed the diff to the team, wrote the migration guide, and paired with each service owner for their first conversion.' Result — 'Deploy misconfigurations fell, onboarding a new service went from a day to an hour, and the pattern spread to all 12 services.' The key verb is 'paired' — adoption, not just invention. (3) 'Mentor or upskill developers': Situation — junior engineers struggling with the on-call rotation. Task — get them confident. Action — 'I ran a weekly 30-minute session: week 1 reading dashboards, week 2 the Pending-pod runbook hands-on, week 3 a simulated incident they commanded while I observed.' Result — 'Two juniors took solo on-call within two months with zero escalations in their first rotations.' Mentoring answers must show a curriculum and an outcome, not 'I helped people.'

notes.title: 'Do You Prefer Coding or Infrastructure?' — The Honest Answer
notes.body: This behavioral question is a trap only if you treat it as one. The panel is checking self-awareness and role fit, not loyalty to a tribe. The strong answer is honest, specific, and tied to the role: 'I like both, but I am strongest and happiest at the boundary — writing code that operates infrastructure. I write Python and Go tooling, but I reach for it to solve operational problems: automation, controllers, pipeline logic. Pure application feature work is fine, but my best days are when code I wrote at 10 AM prevents a 2 AM page.' Then bridge to evidence: 'That is why my recent work is Terraform modules, a Prometheus exporter, and the incident runbooks — code in service of reliability.' What not to say: 'I hate coding' (for a DevSecOps role that is disqualifying), 'I only want to code' (wrong role), or a hedged non-answer ('both are great!'). If you genuinely prefer one side, say so and explain why the role still fits: 'I prefer infrastructure, and I code to automate it — which is exactly what this team's platform work needs.' The mock task below drills this as the panel would ask it, with the STAR-shaped reasoning in the explanation.

notes.title: Delivery Coaching: Sound Like You Know It Cold
notes.body: Content without delivery fails panels. Four rules, practiced aloud, recorded, reviewed. (1) Structure first: open every technical answer with the headline, then the points — 'Three reasons: X, Y, Z' — then stop. Panels score organized answers; rambling signals uncertainty even when the facts are right. (2) Slow down: nerves accelerate speech; deliberately speak at two-thirds speed, pause between points, and let the panel absorb. A two-second pause reads as confidence, not hesitation. (3) Camera and presence: look at the camera, not your notes; sit upright; answer as if you are explaining to a colleague, not reciting. Never read — if you must glance at notes, pause, glance, then re-engage the camera and speak. (4) Cold-answer protocol: no copilot, no docs, no pausing the timer. In the drills below, set a timer (60-90 seconds per item), answer aloud, then check the model answer. Mark every item red/yellow/green: red means you could not start, yellow means partial, green means fluent. Reds become tomorrow's study list; the goal is zero reds before you interview. Record yourself weekly — the cringe is the curriculum.

notes.title: The 90-Minute Mock Panel Script (Part 1: Technical Rounds)
notes.body: Run this solo, timed, aloud, no aids — it is the full panel compressed. Round 1 — Introduction (0:00-0:10): deliver your 60-second 'tell me about yourself' (present role, two proof points, why this role), then 2 minutes on your proudest infrastructure project, STAR-shaped. Round 2 — Terraform/IaC deep (0:10-0:30): Terraform vs Ansible and why not just Ansible; removing resources (destroy vs remove block + apply); the storage-account scenario with per-container access types (for_each list to map); state drift and the import with for_each address escaping; how you ran Terraform previously (GitHub, env vars, no tfvars in git, Jenkins credential injection, Vault, Consul); the testing-to-prod lifecycle. Round 3 — Linux, networking, Docker (0:30-0:45): the df-shows-free-but-full triage (inodes, file descriptors, quotas, /tmp); open ports via ss/lsof; A-to-B port check via telnet/nc; the ping/traceroute/telnet connection triage; UDP vs TCP; image size optimization and the RUN/layer/whiteout questions. Round 4 — Kubernetes/AKS (0:45-1:05): pod troubleshooting (get/describe/logs/exec/events); restart loops and exit codes (137 = OOMKilled); the resource request/limit math (16Gi request vs 2Gi need); Pending pods and the node-provisioning checklist; taints vs tolerations vs labels; liveness vs readiness; the Python GIL readiness story; node pools vs one giant pool; App Gateway vs Load Balancer with the traffic flow.

notes.title: The 90-Minute Mock Panel Script (Part 2: CI/CD, Security, Behavioral, Close)
notes.body: Round 5 — CI/CD, Jenkins, Helm, security (1:05-1:20): pipeline phases commit to release and where code is stopped most (unit tests); Groovy in Jenkinsfiles and shared libraries for standardization; why Helm over plain YAML; SAST/DAST/SCA gates and the Trivy image gate; secrets handling (Vault/Key Vault, never in git); RBAC least privilege across the stack. Round 6 — Architecture and scale (1:20-1:30): strangler fig on the monolithic trading platform; HA for mission-critical financial apps; observability at millions of txns/sec (sampling and aggregation); the multicloud strategy answer. Round 7 — Behavioral (1:30-1:45): the three STAR questions (unclear requirements, new technology, mentoring) plus 'prefer coding or infrastructure' — all timed at 2 minutes each, recorded. Round 8 — Your questions and close (1:45-1:50): ask two genuine questions ('How does the team handle on-call load?' 'What does the Terraform workflow look like here — modules, review, apply?'), then close: 'This is exactly the boundary work I do best — I would love to dig into your hardest reliability problem.' Scoring rubric per answer (1-5): accuracy (facts right), completeness (all parts of multi-part questions), structure (headline-first), delivery (pace, camera, no reading). Total 160; passing bar 120 with no reds on safety-critical items (secrets, RBAC, blast radius). Debrief within 24 hours: rewrite every yellow/red answer in full sentences.

notes.title: The Cold-Answer Protocol: Training Without a Copilot
notes.body: The north star of this course is independent mastery: you answer with no copilot, no docs, no second chances — because the panel offers none. The protocol: (1) Daily timed drills — 8 items, 90 seconds each, aloud, scored red/yellow/green; (2) Weekly full mock — the 90-minute script, recorded; (3) Red-team review — for every red, write the full model answer by hand, then re-drill it cold the next day; handwriting recruits memory that typing does not; (4) Teach-back — explain each concept to a rubber duck or study partner as if they are the panel; if you cannot teach it simply, you do not know it; (5) The question bank never shrinks — every question in the spec list stays in rotation until it is green three sessions running. Worked example of a red-to-green cycle: Monday you blank on the for_each import escaping. Monday night you write terraform import 'azurerm_managed_disk.example["disk1"]' <id> ten times with the quoting explained. Tuesday cold drill: green. The panel does not test what you can look up; it tests what you carry. Carry everything in this module, and the interview becomes a demonstration, not an examination.

cards.front: STAR: the four letters + timebox
cards.back: Situation (1 sentence), Task, Action (longest, first-person verbs), Result (measurable + lesson). 90 seconds to 2 minutes

cards.front: Most common STAR failure
cards.back: A minute of Situation, ten seconds of Action — invert the ratio; Action is what the panel scores

cards.front: Delivery rule 1: structure first
cards.back: Headline, then 'three reasons: X, Y, Z', then stop — organized answers score even when facts are equal

cards.front: Delivery rules 2-4
cards.back: Slow to 2/3 speed with pauses; camera not notes, never read; cold-answer protocol: timer on, no aids

cards.front: Red/yellow/green scoring meaning
cards.back: Red: could not start. Yellow: partial. Green: fluent. Reds become tomorrow's study list; goal is zero reds

cards.front: Exit code 137 = ?
cards.back: OOMKilled (or SIGKILL) — container exceeded its memory limit; check describe lastState + raise limits or fix the leak

cards.front: Rebase vs merge (one line)
cards.back: Merge preserves history with a merge commit; rebase rewrites a linear history — rebase private branches, merge shared ones

cards.front: terraform import with for_each: the address quoting
cards.back: terraform import 'azurerm_managed_disk.example["disk1"]' <id> — quote the whole address so the shell preserves the brackets

cards.front: Remove a Terraform resource: two ways
cards.back: Delete the block + apply (destroys it), or the 'removed' block to drop it from state without destroying (then apply)

cards.front: df shows free space but 'no space left on device'
cards.back: Inodes exhausted (df -i); deleted-but-open files holding space (lsof +L1); quotas; /tmp full on its own mount

cards.front: Simplest tool to check a port from server A to server B
cards.back: telnet <host> <port> or nc -vz <host> <port> — connection success/failure is the answer

cards.front: Pod Running then suddenly restarts: which probe?
cards.back: Liveness — it restarts containers. Readiness only removes from service. Confirm via describe lastState

cards.front: Why Helm instead of plain YAML?
cards.back: Templating, values per environment, versioned releases with rollback, dependency charts — plain YAML duplicates per env

cards.front: Where do pipelines stop the most code?
cards.back: Unit tests — the earliest, cheapest gate; everything later is more expensive

quiz.q: A behavioral answer spends 60 seconds on Situation and 10 on Action. What is the fix?
choices: Invert the ratio: one sentence of Situation, the bulk on first-person Action with specific verbs, close with measurable Result
quiz.explain: Panels score Action — what YOU did. Situation sets context in one sentence; the verbs and the outcome carry the answer.

quiz.q: You blank on a question mid-panel. Best recovery?
choices: Pause, structure aloud: 'Let me break that into two parts...' and answer what you know precisely
quiz.explain: A structured partial answer ('here is what I know, here is what I would check') scores far above rambling or freezing — it demonstrates engineering thinking.

quiz.q: Container 'svc-basic' terminated with exit code 137. Cause?
choices: OOMKilled — the container exceeded its memory limit (or received SIGKILL); check describe lastState and memory limits
The node ran out of CPU
quiz.explain: 137 = 128 + 9 (SIGKILL); in Kubernetes it is almost always the OOM killer enforcing the memory limit.

quiz.q: Pod requests memory 1Gi but the app needs 2Gi minimum to start. What happens?
choices: It schedules (requests met) then gets OOMKilled when usage exceeds the limit — requests affect scheduling, limits affect survival
quiz.explain: Requests gate scheduling; limits gate survival. Under-provisioned requests schedule fine and die at runtime — the classic OOMKilled trap.

quiz.q: requirements.txt lists: requests, flask, flask-cors, asyncio, setuptools, pandas, pytest — all unpinned. Approve the MR?
choices: Request changes: pin every version (==), remove asyncio (stdlib, not a package), question setuptools (usually not a runtime dep)
quiz.explain: Unpinned deps make builds non-reproducible; asyncio is stdlib; setuptools is a build tool. The MR needs == pins across the board.

quiz.q: In a Dockerfile, you replace a cleanup RUN (rm -rf /tmp/build) with RUN echo hello. Does the image get smaller?
choices: No — each RUN is a layer; files removed in a later layer are whiteout-hidden but still present in earlier layers, and echo adds its own layer
quiz.explain: Layers are additive; deletion in a later layer whiteouts but does not reclaim earlier-layer bytes. Cleanup must happen in the SAME RUN that created the files.

quiz.q: Why does the panel ask 'how many services can run in a pod'?
choices: To check you know one pod = one logical host: one main container plus sidecars (logging, proxy) sharing network/storage — not many independent apps
quiz.explain: The pod is the atomic unit: tightly-coupled containers sharing localhost and volumes. Independent apps get separate pods/deployments.

quiz.q: Single-threaded Python service fails readiness probes under load; the Java equivalent does not. Likely cause?
choices: The GIL: the single thread blocks on CPU work so the probe handler cannot respond in time — separate probe handling/async or more replicas
quiz.explain: GIL-bound single-threaded servers serialize request handling and probe responses; under load the probe times out. Async frameworks, thread pools for probes, or horizontal scaling fix it.

quiz.q: Closing a panel: which is strongest?
choices: Ask two genuine questions (on-call load, their Terraform workflow), then close: 'This is exactly the boundary work I do best'
quiz.explain: Genuine operational questions signal senior thinking; the close restates fit in one line. Compensation comes through the recruiter, not the panel.

drills.title: Timed drill: technical rapid-fire (90s each, aloud)

items.prompt: Terraform vs Ansible: biggest difference; if Ansible can create VMs why not just use Ansible; difference removing resources; what exactly do you do in the TF file to remove a resource?
items.answer: Terraform is declarative desired-state with state tracking; Ansible is procedural task execution. Ansible can create VMs but has no state — it cannot plan/detect drift the way Terraform does. Removing: in Ansible you write the absent-state task; in Terraform you delete the block (or use a removed block) and apply. In the TF file: delete the resource block and run terraform apply to destroy it — or add a removed { from = ... lifecycle { destroy = false } } block to drop it from state without destroying.
items.explain: Model answer: 'Terraform manages desired state with a state file — plan shows the diff, apply converges, drift is detectable. Ansible executes ordered tasks idempotently but keeps no state, so it cannot plan or show you what changed. That is why Ansible provisions but Terraform owns lifecycle. To remove: delete the resource block and apply — Terraform destroys it. If you must keep the real resource (the data-disk drift case), use a removed block with destroy=false so Terraform forgets it without deleting it.'

items.prompt: Preferred OS? Red Hat familiarity / Satellite? df shows free space but 'no space left on device' — causes? Other intermittent causes with free space?
items.answer: RHEL (familiar; Satellite for patch/content management at fleet scale). df-free-but-full: inodes exhausted (df -i); deleted-but-open files (lsof +L1); quotas; /tmp on a separate full mount.
items.explain: Model answer: 'RHEL — I am comfortable with it, and Satellite for centralized patching and provisioning across fleets. "No space" with free blocks: first df -i — inode exhaustion from millions of small files. Second lsof +L1 — deleted files held open by processes still consume space. Third quotas, fourth a full /tmp mount. Intermittent with free space: a log rotation racing disk usage, or a process holding deleted files that releases on restart — which is why the failure comes and goes.'

items.prompt: Check open ports? Simplest tool to check a port from server A to server B? Troubleshoot connection issues between two servers? UDP vs TCP?
items.answer: ss -tlnp / netstat -tlnp / lsof -i -P. A→B: telnet host port or nc -vz host port. Triage: ping (L3), traceroute (path), telnet/nc (port), firewall rules both ends. UDP: connectionless, no handshake/ordering; TCP: handshake, ordered, reliable.
items.explain: Model answer: 'ss -tlnp is my default — sockets, listening TCP, numeric, with process. Server A to B: telnet or nc -vz — the connection result IS the test. Between servers: ping for reachability, traceroute for the path, telnet to the port for the service, then firewall rules and security groups on both ends. UDP vs TCP: UDP is fire-and-forget datagrams — no handshake, no ordering, no retransmission — good for DNS and voice; TCP handshakes and guarantees ordered delivery — good for everything requiring correctness.'

items.prompt: Rebase vs merge?
items.answer: Merge preserves full history with a merge commit; rebase rewrites commits onto the target for linear history. Rebase private branches, merge shared ones.
items.explain: Model answer: 'Merge keeps the true history including the merge commit — safe for shared branches. Rebase replays my commits on top of the target for a clean linear log — but it rewrites SHAs, so only on branches nobody else uses. Rule: rebase to clean up my own work, merge to integrate shared work.'

items.prompt:
Read this script, predict the output, and state how many Kia cars print:
cars = ['Kia Soul','Toyota Camry','Kia Forte','Honda Civic','Kia Sorento']
kia_count = 0
for car in cars:
    brand = car.split()[0]
    if brand == 'Kia':
        kia_count += 1
        print(f'Kia found: {car}')
    else:
        print(f'Other: {brand}')
print(f'Total Kias: {kia_count}')
Second: review requirements.txt (requests, flask, flask-cors, asyncio, setuptools, pandas, pytest — all unpinned). Approve the MR? What must change?
items.answer: Output: Kia found: Kia Soul / Other: Toyota / Kia found: Kia Forte / Other: Honda / Kia found: Kia Sorento / Total Kias: 3. Three Kias. MR: request changes — pin all versions (==), remove asyncio (stdlib), question setuptools as a runtime dep.
items.explain: Model answer: 'Trace: split()[0] takes the brand; Kia matches three times — Soul, Forte, Sorento — each prints and increments; others print the brand; final line prints 3. On the MR: I would not approve — unpinned dependencies make builds non-reproducible, asyncio is standard library and does not belong in requirements, and setuptools is a build tool, not a runtime dependency. Require == pins on everything and drop asyncio.'

items.prompt: Optimize container image size? What does RUN do in a Dockerfile? Replace a cleanup RUN with RUN echo hello — does the size change? Does removing files in a later layer reduce size?
items.answer: Multi-stage builds, minimal base (slim/distroless), combine RUNs, .dockerignore. RUN creates a layer. No — echo adds a layer and cleanup must be in the same RUN. No — whiteout hides but earlier layers retain bytes.
items.explain: Model answer: 'Optimize with multi-stage builds, minimal bases, combined RUN statements, and .dockerignore. Each RUN creates an immutable layer. Replacing cleanup with echo hello does not shrink anything — it adds a layer. And removing files in a later layer only whiteouts them: the bytes remain in the earlier layer, so the image stays large. Cleanup belongs in the SAME RUN that created the files.'

items.prompt: Troubleshoot an app in a pod? Pod keeps restarting — next steps? Check exit code and reason? Container svc-basic terminated exit code 137 — why?
items.answer: kubectl get/describe/logs/exec + events. Restart loop: describe lastState reason/exit code, logs --previous, probes, resources. Exit code + reason: describe pod → lastState.terminated. 137 = OOMKilled (128+9 SIGKILL): over memory limit.
items.explain: Model answer: 'kubectl describe for events and lastState, logs --previous for the crash output, exec only if it stays up. Restarting: read lastState.terminated reason and exit code first — that names it. 137 is 128+9, SIGKILL — in Kubernetes that is the OOM killer enforcing the memory limit. Fix: raise the limit or fix the leak, and check the request/limit math from the YAML review.'

items.prompt: Pod YAML review: image nginx:v4, requests memory 16Gi cpu 0.5, limits memory 32Gi cpu 8. Issues? If nginx needs min 2Gi to start, does it work? Request 1Gi but needs 2Gi — works? How many services/apps per pod?
items.answer: 16Gi request is enormous for nginx — wasteful, blocks scheduling; :v4 is an unpinned mutable tag; cpu 0.5 request vs 8 limit is a huge burst ratio. 2Gi need with 16Gi request: schedules and runs (over-provisioned). 1Gi request, 2Gi need: schedules, then OOMKilled. One logical app per pod + sidecars.
items.explain: Model answer: 'The 16Gi request for nginx is wildly over-provisioned — it reserves memory the app will never use and can block scheduling; the :v4 tag is unpinned; the request/limit spread invites noisy-neighbor issues. With a 2Gi minimum need and 16Gi requested: yes, it runs — over-provisioned but fine. With 1Gi requested and 2Gi needed: it schedules (requests are met) then OOMKills at runtime — requests gate scheduling, limits gate survival. And a pod holds one logical application plus its sidecars — independent apps get their own pods.'

drills.title: Timed drill: deep technical + STAR behavioral (2 min each, aloud)

items.prompt: Jenkins pipelines: with what tools/languages? Groovy directly in the Jenkinsfile? Standardize Jenkinsfiles across repos? Have you written shared libraries?
items.answer: Declarative pipelines, Groovy (scripted or shared-library code); yes Groovy directly; standardize via shared libraries (vars/ + src/); describe one you wrote: e.g. a standardBuild() step with checkout/test/scan/push.
items.explain: Model answer: 'Declarative pipelines, with Groovy for scripted logic. Yes — Groovy goes directly in the Jenkinsfile for simple cases, but to standardize across repos I wrote a shared library: a vars/standardBuild.groovy wrapping checkout, unit tests, Semgrep, Trivy scan, and image push, with src/ helpers for the retry logic. Repos then declare a five-line Jenkinsfile calling standardBuild with parameters — one place to update the gate policy for all services.'

items.prompt: Why Helm instead of plain YAML?
items.answer: Templating + values per environment, versioned releases with rollback, chart dependencies, lifecycle hooks — plain YAML duplicates per environment and has no release concept.
items.explain: Model answer: 'Plain YAML means a copy per environment that drifts. Helm gives parameterized templates with values files per env, versioned releases I can rollback with one command, and chart dependencies for shared components. For a handful of static manifests plain YAML is fine; past that, Helm is the release engineering answer.'

items.prompt: Self-rate your Terraform. Walk the full lifecycle testing→dev→stage→QA→prod. Scenario: dev team needs a storage account with given container names — codify it. Requirements change to per-container access types — modify the code. State drift: a VM data disk was added manually in Azure and must be kept — what do you do? Show the for_each import address escaping.
items.answer: Rating with justification + feature branches/PR plan/apply per env with gates. Storage: resource + for_each over list; change: for_each over map(name→access). Drift: plan, import to keep, then codify. Import: terraform import 'azurerm_managed_disk.example["disk1"]' <id>.
items.explain: Model answer (STAR-shaped): 'I would rate myself [honest level] — I have owned Terraform end to end: modules in GitHub, PR-driven plans, per-environment workspaces, applies gated through Jenkins with credentials injected, secrets via env vars and Vault, tfvars never committed, Consul for service discovery config. Lifecycle: feature branch → plan on PR → apply to dev on merge → promote the same artifact through stage and QA with environment tfvars → prod apply behind approval. Storage scenario: azurerm_storage_account plus azurerm_storage_container with for_each over the name list; when access types diverge, refactor to for_each over a map of name→access type. Drift: terraform plan surfaces it; to keep the manual disk I run terraform import with the for_each address quoted — terraform import \'azurerm_managed_disk.example["disk1"]\' <id> — then codify the resource so the next plan is clean. The quoting matters: the shell must not eat the brackets.'

items.prompt: How were K8s endpoints exposed via Application Gateway? Expose an internal Azure endpoint to the internet? App Gateway vs Load Balancer? Walk the traffic flow browser→DNS→App Gateway→backend. Private Links: for which services? Private link custom DNS?
items.answer: AGIC programs AppGW from Ingress. Internal→internet: public AppGW/WAF or LB with public IP + NSG. L7 vs L4. Flow: DNS→AppGW public IP→TLS+host/path routing→backend pool→pod. Private Link: storage, SQL, Key Vault, App Service, ACR. DNS: Private DNS zone + A record + VNet link (+ conditional forwarding).
items.explain: Model answer: 'AGIC watches Ingress and programs the Application Gateway — host/path routing at Layer 7 with TLS termination and WAF. To expose an internal endpoint: a public Application Gateway (or public LB) with locked-down NSGs in front of it. App Gateway is L7 HTTP; Load Balancer is L4 TCP/UDP. Traffic: browser resolves DNS to the gateway IP, the gateway terminates TLS, matches host/path, and forwards to the AKS backend pool, where kube-proxy reaches the pod. Private Link exposes PaaS privately — storage, SQL, Key Vault, App Service, ACR — via a private endpoint; custom DNS needs a Private DNS zone with the A record, linked to the VNet, so the PaaS FQDN resolves to the private IP.'

items.prompt: Ansible: manage others' playbooks or write new? Most interesting role you created? How do you capture command output?
items.answer: Both — inherit carefully, write idempotently. Interesting role: describe concretely (e.g. hardened CIS baseline role with handlers). Capture: register the task result, then use stdout/debug or a follow-up task.
items.explain: Model answer: 'Both — I have inherited playbooks, which means reading for idempotence gaps and variable contracts before changing anything, and I have written roles from scratch. The most interesting was a CIS-hardening role: parameterized by profile level, with handlers restarting only affected services and molecule tests proving idempotence. Output capture: register the result — register: cmd_out — then reference cmd_out.stdout in debug or a conditional follow-up task.'

items.prompt: Benefit of multiple node pools vs one giant pool? Pod stuck in Pending — troubleshoot? 'Insufficient resources' / 'out of nodes' — fix? Manually increase max nodes per pool? New nodes still not deploying — your checklist? Taint vs toleration vs label? Pod Running then suddenly restarts — which probe? Single-threaded Python vs Java readiness failures — why? Service knocked over under load failing health checks — cloud-native recommendations?
items.answer: Pools: SKU/scaling/blast-radius/cost separation. Pending: describe events. Out of nodes: raise max-count. Manual: az aks nodepool update --max-count. Checklist: autoscaler logs, quotas, region capacity, taints, labels, identity perms, Activity log, Monitor/Health, subnet IPs, SKU restrictions, Policy, max pods. Taint repels/toleration permits/label attracts. Liveness restarts. GIL blocks probe handler. Recommendations: async/non-blocking, separate probe endpoints, timeouts.
items.explain: Model answer: 'Multiple pools: separate VM SKUs, independent autoscaler bounds, smaller upgrade blast radius, spot mixing, workload isolation. Pending: kubectl describe, read FailedScheduling. Out of nodes with pool at max: az aks nodepool update --max-count higher. Still no nodes: autoscaler logs, vCPU quota, region capacity, taints/tolerations, label selectors, identity permissions, Activity log failures, Azure Monitor/Resource Health, subnet IP exhaustion, SKU restrictions, Azure Policy, max pods per node. Taints repel, tolerations permit, labels attract. Running-then-restarting is the liveness probe. Python readiness failures under load: the GIL — the single thread cannot serve the probe while busy. Knocked-over service: async non-blocking handlers, dedicated lightweight probe endpoints, timeouts everywhere, and horizontal scaling — so health checks answer even when the app is saturated.'

items.prompt: Major pipeline phases commit→release? Where is the most code stopped? Strangler fig a monolithic trading platform? Fault tolerance for mission-critical financial apps? Logging/monitoring at millions of txns/sec? RBAC across the full stack?
items.answer: Phases: commit→build→unit test→SAST/SCA→artifact→deploy staging→DAST/E2E→prod w/ gates. Most stopped: unit tests. Strangler: seam by seam, gateway-routed, dual-write data. HA: multi-AZ + tested multi-region, data replication binding. Scale: sampling+aggregation. RBAC: least privilege per layer.
items.explain: Model answer: 'Commit triggers build and unit tests — where most code is stopped, cheapest. Then SAST/SCA gates, artifact build, staging deploy, DAST and end-to-end, production behind approval with burn-rate auto-rollback. Strangler fig: extract seam by seam starting with read-only services, gateway-routed percentages with monolith fallback, data via dual-write, retire at zero traffic — never a big bang. Mission-critical HA: multi-AZ everywhere, active-passive multi-region with rehearsed failover, data replication as the binding constraint. Millions of txns/sec: sampling and aggregation architecture — bounded cardinality, recording rules, sampled logs, tail-sampled traces. RBAC: least privilege at every layer — K8s roles, cloud IAM, app roles, database grants, pipeline approvals.'

items.prompt: STAR: a time you translated unclear business requirements into technical deliverables. STAR: a time you introduced a new technology improving team performance. STAR: a time you mentored developers. And: do you prefer coding or infrastructure?
items.answer: Three STAR stories (spec→validate→ship; PoC→demo→pair→adopt; curriculum→solo on-call) + honest boundary answer: code in service of reliability.
items.explain: Model answers: (1) Requirements — Situation: ops asked for 'better deployment visibility.' Task: make it shippable. Action: interviewed three on-call engineers, mapped pain to golden signals, wrote a one-page spec, validated before building, shipped in two sprints. Result: deploy correlation down to 5 minutes; the spec format became the team template. (2) New tech — Situation: hand-edited YAML per environment. Task: safer pattern. Action: Kustomize PoC on one service, team demo, migration guide, paired each owner through conversion. Result: misconfigurations fell; new-service onboarding from a day to an hour; all 12 services migrated. (3) Mentoring — Situation: juniors struggling with on-call. Task: get them confident. Action: weekly 30-min curriculum — dashboards, runbook hands-on, simulated incident they commanded. Result: two juniors on solo on-call in two months, zero first-rotation escalations. Coding vs infrastructure: 'I am happiest at the boundary — I write code that operates infrastructure: automation, exporters, pipeline logic. My best days are when code I wrote at 10 AM prevents a 2 AM page.'

handsOnLab.title: Lab: run the full 90-minute mock panel solo
handsOnLab.brief: You will execute the complete mock panel script from the notes — timed, aloud, recorded, with no aids — then score every answer against the rubric, red-team the weak ones, and re-drill until the bank is green.
steps: Print the 90-minute script (notes 5-6) and the scoring rubric; set up a timer and a recorder (phone is fine).
Round 1 (10 min): deliver the 60-second intro and the 2-minute proudest-project STAR — recorded, no notes.
Round 2 (20 min): answer all 8 Terraform/IaC questions aloud at 90 seconds each; mark red/yellow/green immediately after each.
Round 3 (15 min): Linux/networking/Docker rapid-fire — same timing and scoring.
Round 4 (20 min): Kubernetes/AKS round including the YAML math and the node-provisioning checklist.
Round 5 (15 min): CI/CD, Jenkins, Helm, security gates, secrets, RBAC.
Round 6 (10 min): architecture and scale — strangler fig, HA, millions-of-txns observability, multicloud strategy.
Round 7 (15 min): the four behavioral questions at 2 minutes each, STAR-structured, recorded.
Round 8 (5 min): ask your two panel questions aloud and deliver the one-line close.
Score every answer 1-5 on accuracy, completeness, structure, delivery; total out of 160; passing bar 120 with no reds on safety-critical items.
For every red/yellow: handwrite the full model answer from the drills, then re-drill it cold the next day.
Within 24 hours, write the debrief: three strongest answers, three weakest, and the exact study plan for the week.
Repeat weekly; the question bank stays in rotation until every item is green three sessions running.
handsOnLab.deliverable: A recorded 90-minute mock panel, a completed 160-point rubric, handwritten red-team corrections, and a weekly study plan.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Total score ≥120 with zero reds on safety-critical items (secrets, RBAC, blast radius); every red from the prior session re-drilled to green.

mockTask.q: Panel: 'Do you prefer coding or infrastructure?' Which response is strongest?
choices: 'I hate coding — just give me the consoles'
'I only want to write application features'

'I am strongest at the boundary: I write code that operates infrastructure — automation, tooling, pipeline logic. My best work is code that prevents 2 AM pages, which is exactly this team's platform work.'
mockTask.explain: STAR-shaped reasoning: the Situation is a DevSecOps platform role; the Task is showing fit; the Action is the honest, specific preference (code in service of reliability) with evidence (automation, exporters, runbooks); the Result is the bridge — 'which is exactly this team's platform work.' It is specific, honest, and role-tied. The other options are disqualifying (anti-coding), misaligned (pure app dev), or empty (hedged non-answer).

modules.title: Prereq Math: Logic & Proof for DevSecOps & Cloud Infrastructure
modules.summary: Propositional logic, truth tables, quantifiers, and the four proof methods (direct, contrapositive, contradiction, induction) — the reasoning substrate for policies, algorithms, and security arguments. Prerequisite spine for DevSecOps & Cloud Infrastructure.
objectives: Evaluate compound propositions with truth tables and identify tautologies.
Apply De Morgan’s laws and logical equivalences to simplify statements.
Negate quantified statements correctly (∀/∃ duality).
Write direct, contrapositive, contradiction, and induction proofs.

notes.title: Why this math matters for DevSecOps & Cloud Infrastructure
notes.body:
**Relevance.** Policy-as-code, IAM, and admission control are boolean logic at scale. This module makes logical equivalence a working tool.

Work this module before the technical modules it supports: the worked examples below are fully computed (verify each with the Python lab), and the drills test the exact calculations you will reuse. Math done by hand once beats math skimmed ten times.

notes.title: Propositions, connectives, and truth tables
notes.body: A proposition is a statement that is either true (T) or false (F) — never both. The connectives build compounds: negation ¬p, conjunction p∧q (and), disjunction p∨q (or, inclusive), implication p→q (if p then q), biconditional p↔q (p iff q). A truth table enumerates every input combination: n variables need 2^n rows. Worked example: build the table for p→q. Recall p→q is F only when p=T and q=F. Rows: (T,T)→T; (T,F)→F; (F,T)→T; (F,F)→T. So "if 2+2=5 then the moon is cheese" is TRUE as a material implication — the antecedent is false. This surprises beginners, but implication promises only that a true antecedent never yields a false consequent. In policy engines and code (if-statements), this is exactly the semantics: the rule fires only when the condition holds; a false condition makes the implication vacuously true.

notes.title: Tautologies, contradictions, and De Morgan’s laws
notes.body: A tautology is true in every row (e.g., p∨¬p); a contradiction is false in every row (p∧¬p). Two formulas are logically equivalent if their tables match column-for-column. Worked example (verified): prove De Morgan’s law ¬(p∧q) ≡ ¬p∨¬q by table. Row (T,T): LHS ¬T=F; RHS F∨F=F. Row (T,F): LHS ¬F=T; RHS F∨T=T. Row (F,T): LHS T; RHS T∨F=T. Row (F,F): LHS T; RHS T∨T=T. All four rows agree — equivalence verified. The dual law ¬(p∨q) ≡ ¬p∧¬q holds by the same check. These laws are the workhorses of simplifying firewall rules, IAM policies, and boolean search: "not (A and B)" becomes "not-A or not-B". Other key equivalences: contrapositive (p→q ≡ ¬q→¬p), and implication-as-disjunction (p→q ≡ ¬p∨q).

notes.title: Predicates and quantifiers
notes.body: A predicate P(x) becomes a proposition when x is fixed. Quantifiers bind x: ∀x P(x) ("for all x") and ∃x P(x) ("there exists x"). Worked example: let domain be integers, P(x) = "x² ≥ 0". Then ∀x P(x) is TRUE (squares are never negative). Now negate ∀x∃y (y > x) — "for every integer there is a larger one". Negation flips each quantifier and the inner predicate: ∃x∀y (y ≤ x) — "some integer is ≥ every integer", which is FALSE over integers (no maximum). The duality rules: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x), and ¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x). Common error: negating "all users are admins" as "no users are admins" — the correct negation is "some user is not an admin". In access-control requirements, this distinction is the difference between a correct policy and a breach.

notes.title: Direct proof and proof by contrapositive
notes.body: A direct proof assumes the hypothesis and derives the conclusion through valid steps. Proof by contrapositive proves ¬q→¬p instead of p→q (equivalent by the table). Worked example: prove "if n² is even, then n is even" for integers. Direct attack stalls (square roots of parity are awkward), so use contrapositive: "if n is odd, then n² is odd". Let n = 2k+1. Then n² = 4k²+4k+1 = 2(2k²+2k)+1, which is odd. Contrapositive proved, so the original holds. Numeric check: n=7 (odd) → 49 (odd) ✓; n=6 (even) → 36 (even) ✓. Choose the method by shape: when the conclusion is a negative or "not" statement, contrapositive usually simplifies; when hypothesis and conclusion are both positive constructions, go direct.

notes.title: Proof by contradiction
notes.body: Assume the negation of what you want, derive an impossibility, and conclude the original. Worked example (classic, verified): prove √2 is irrational. Assume √2 = a/b in lowest terms (gcd(a,b)=1). Then 2 = a²/b², so a² = 2b² — a² is even, hence a is even (by the previous note’s result), a = 2k. Then 4k² = 2b², so b² = 2k² — b² is even, hence b is even. But a and b both even contradicts lowest terms. The assumption is impossible; √2 is irrational. The pattern: contradiction proofs shine when the claim says something does NOT exist (no rational square root, no largest prime). Euclid’s proof of infinitely many primes uses the same skeleton: assume finitely many, multiply them and add 1, find a new prime factor — contradiction.

notes.title: Mathematical induction
notes.body: To prove P(n) for all n ≥ n₀: (1) base case P(n₀); (2) inductive step: assume P(k) (induction hypothesis), prove P(k+1). Worked example (verified): prove 1+2+⋯+n = n(n+1)/2. Base n=1: LHS 1, RHS 1·2/2 = 1 ✓. Assume true for k. For k+1: LHS = k(k+1)/2 + (k+1) = (k+1)(k/2+1) = (k+1)(k+2)/2 ✓ — exactly the formula at n=k+1. Numeric spot-check: n=5 gives 1+2+3+4+5=15 and 5·6/2=15 ✓; n=100 gives 5050 = 100×101/2 ✓. Induction is the proof method behind every loop-correctness argument and every recursive algorithm analysis: the base case is the loop’s first iteration, the step is "if the invariant holds entering iteration k, it holds leaving it".

cards.front: What is a proposition?
cards.back: A statement that is unambiguously true or false — never both, never neither.

cards.front: When is p→q false?
cards.back: Only when p is true and q is false. All other rows are true (vacuous truth).

cards.front: State De Morgan’s laws.
cards.back: ¬(p∧q) ≡ ¬p∨¬q and ¬(p∨q) ≡ ¬p∧¬q — verified by truth table.

cards.front: Negate ∀x P(x).
cards.back: ∃x ¬P(x). Quantifier flips; inner predicate negates.

cards.front: Negate ∃x P(x).
What is the contrapositive of p→q?
cards.back: ¬q→¬p — logically equivalent to the original.

cards.front: p→q is equivalent to which disjunction?
cards.back: ¬p∨q.

cards.front: What is a tautology? A contradiction?
cards.back: Tautology: true in every truth-table row (p∨¬p). Contradiction: false in every row (p∧¬p).

cards.front: Skeleton of proof by contradiction?
cards.back: Assume the negation of the claim; derive an impossibility; conclude the claim holds.

cards.front: The two steps of mathematical induction?
cards.back: Base case P(n₀); inductive step: P(k) ⇒ P(k+1).

cards.front: Prove: if n² is even then n is even. Method?
cards.back: Contrapositive: n odd ⇒ n=2k+1 ⇒ n²=2(2k²+2k)+1, odd.

cards.front: Induction proves 1+⋯+n equals?

quiz.q: p=F, q=T. What is p→q?
quiz.explain: Implication is false only for (T,F). With a false antecedent it is vacuously true.

quiz.q: ¬(p∨q) is equivalent to:
quiz.explain: De Morgan’s second law — verified row-by-row in the notes.

quiz.q: The contrapositive of "If the alert fires, the SOC investigates" is:
choices: If the alert does not fire, the SOC does not investigate
If the SOC does not investigate, the alert did not fire
If the SOC investigates, the alert fired
The alert fires iff the SOC investigates
quiz.explain: Contrapositive flips and negates: ¬q→¬p. (The first choice is the inverse — a different, non-equivalent statement.)

quiz.q: Negation of "Every admin has MFA enabled":
choices: Some admin does not have MFA enabled
quiz.explain: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x). "None do" is stronger than the negation and usually false.

quiz.q: Which is a tautology?
quiz.explain: For any p,q, at least one direction of implication holds — check all four rows. The others fail on some row.

quiz.q: To prove "there is no largest prime" you would use:
quiz.explain: Non-existence claims suit contradiction: assume finitely many primes, construct a number with a new prime factor.

quiz.q: In an induction proof of 1+⋯+n=n(n+1)/2, the inductive step shows:
quiz.explain: Assume the hypothesis at k, derive k+1: k(k+1)/2+(k+1) = (k+1)(k+2)/2.

quiz.q: p=T, q=F. Evaluate (p→q)∨(q→p).
quiz.explain: p→q is F, but q→p is T (false antecedent), and F∨T = T.

quiz.q: "If n is divisible by 4 then n is even." The converse is:
choices: If n is even then n is divisible by 4
If n is not divisible by 4 then n is odd
If n is odd then n is not divisible by 4
n is divisible by 4 iff n is even
quiz.explain: Converse swaps p and q (q→p). It is FALSE (6 is even, not divisible by 4) — converse is not equivalent to the original.

items.answer: Yes — q∧¬q is a contradiction (always F), and p∨F ≡ p.

items.prompt: Name the method: assume √3 rational, derive a contradiction.

handsOnLab.title: Verify logic by brute force with Python
handsOnLab.brief: You will verify De Morgan’s laws and the contrapositive equivalence by exhaustive truth-table enumeration in Python, then prove a small parity claim both by hand and by exhaustive check. The machine settles every row; your hand proof must agree.
steps: Open python3. Define implies = lambda p,q: (not p) or q.
Enumerate all four (p,q) pairs. For each, compute not (p and q) and (not p) or (not q); assert they are equal on every row — De Morgan verified by brute force.
Repeat for the dual law: not (p or q) vs (not p) and (not q). Assert equality on all rows.
Verify contrapositive: for all rows, implies(p,q) == implies(not q, not p). Print any counterexample (there will be none).
Show the converse is NOT equivalent: find the row where implies(p,q) != implies(q,p). Record it.
Prove by hand on paper: "if n² is odd then n is odd" via contrapositive. Then brute-force check n in range(0,50): assert (n*n % 2 == 1) implies (n % 2 == 1).
Write up: which equivalences held on all rows, the converse counterexample row, and your parity proof.
handsOnLab.deliverable: A short write-up with the brute-force verification output, the converse counterexample, and the hand parity proof.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: All assertions pass; the converse counterexample row is identified; the hand proof matches the brute-force check.

mockTask.q: A policy states: "If the device is unmanaged, then access is denied." Which restatement is logically equivalent?
choices: If access is granted, then the device is managed
If the device is managed, then access is granted
If access is denied, then the device is unmanaged
Devices are either managed or denied
mockTask.explain: Contrapositive (¬q→¬p) is equivalent. The second is the converse, the third the inverse — neither is equivalent.

modules.title: Prereq Math: Number Theory for DevSecOps & Cloud Infrastructure
modules.summary: Divisibility, primes, Euclid’s algorithm, modular arithmetic, Fermat and Euler — the mathematics underneath hashing, Diffie-Hellman, and RSA. Prerequisite spine for DevSecOps & Cloud Infrastructure.
objectives: Factor integers and test primality for small numbers.
Compute gcd with Euclid’s algorithm.
Do modular arithmetic fluently (addition, multiplication, powers).
Apply Fermat’s little theorem and Euler’s theorem; sketch RSA.

notes.title: Why this math matters for DevSecOps & Cloud Infrastructure
notes.body:
**Relevance.** TLS, secrets management, and hashing are number theory in production. This module builds the crypto math underneath.

Work this module before the technical modules it supports: the worked examples below are fully computed (verify each with the Python lab), and the drills test the exact calculations you will reuse. Math done by hand once beats math skimmed ten times.

notes.title: Divisibility, primes, and factorization
notes.body: a divides b (a|b) if b = ak for some integer k. A prime has exactly two divisors (1 and itself); 1 is neither prime nor composite. The Fundamental Theorem: every integer > 1 factors uniquely into primes. Worked example (verified): factor 360. 360 = 36×10 = (2²×3²)×(2×5) = 2³·3²×5. Check: 8×9×5 = 360 ✓. Divisibility tests: by 3 iff digit sum divisible by 3 (360: 3+6+0=9 ✓); by 11 via alternating sum. Trial division up to √n decides primality for small n: to test 97, trial primes ≤ √97 ≈ 9.8, i.e., 2,3,5,7 — none divide, so 97 is prime. Cryptography’s asymmetry lives here: multiplying primes is trivial, factoring the product is (classically) hard.

notes.title: The gcd and Euclid’s algorithm
notes.body: gcd(a,b) is the largest d dividing both. Euclid: gcd(a,b) = gcd(b, a mod b), recurse until remainder 0. Worked example (verified): gcd(48,18). 48 = 2×18+12; 18 = 1×12+6; 12 = 2×6+0 ⇒ gcd = 6. Check: divisors of 48 include 6, of 18 include 6; nothing larger divides both ✓. The algorithm runs in O(log min(a,b)) steps — ancient (c. 300 BCE) and still optimal in practice. Extended Euclid also finds x,y with ax+by = gcd(a,b) (Bézout’s identity), which is how RSA computes modular inverses: d with ed ≡ 1 (mod φ(n)). Whenever you need "the largest shared structure" — key sizes, cycle alignment, fraction reduction — Euclid is the tool.

notes.title: Modular arithmetic
notes.body: a ≡ b (mod m) means m divides a−b; work with remainders 0..m−1. Addition/multiplication carry over: (a+b) mod m, (a·b) mod m. Powers reduce via repeated squaring. Worked examples (verified): 17+25 mod 12: 42 mod 12 = 6 (42 = 3×12+6) ✓. 3^4 mod 7: 81 mod 7 = 4 (81 = 11×7+4) ✓. 2^10 mod 11: 1024 mod 11 = 1 (11×93=1023) ✓ — a preview of Fermat. Hash tables, checksums, and cyclic schedules are modular arithmetic in production: "slot = hash(key) mod table_size" is a congruence, and off-by-one errors there are congruence errors. Warning: division mod m needs a modular inverse, which exists only when gcd(a,m)=1.

notes.title: Fermat’s little theorem and Euler’s theorem
notes.body: Fermat: for prime p and a not divisible by p, a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p). Euler generalizes: a^φ(m) ≡ 1 (mod m) when gcd(a,m)=1, where φ(m) counts 1≤k≤m coprime to m. Worked examples (verified): 5^6 mod 7: p=7 prime, 6 = p−1, so ≡ 1 ✓ (direct: 15625 = 2232×7+1 ✓). φ(12): numbers ≤12 coprime to 12 are 1,5,7,11 ⇒ φ(12) = 4; also 12×(1−1/2)×(1−1/3) = 12×1/2×2/3 = 4 ✓. Then 5^4 mod 12 ≡ 1: 625 = 52×12+1 ✓. These theorems shrink huge exponents: to compute a^1000 mod 7, reduce 1000 mod 6 first. This exponent-shrinking is what makes RSA decryption feasible at all.

notes.title: RSA, sketched honestly
notes.body: Key generation: pick primes p,q; n = pq; φ(n) = (p−1)(q−1); choose e coprime to φ(n); d = e^−1 mod φ(n) (via extended Euclid). Encrypt c = m^e mod n; decrypt m = c^d mod n. Correctness: ed ≡ 1 mod φ(n) so c^d = m^(ed) = m^(1+kφ(n)) ≡ m (mod n) by Euler. Worked toy example (verified): p=5, q=11 ⇒ n=55, φ=40. e=3 (gcd(3,40)=1); d=27 since 3×27=81=2×40+1 ✓. Encrypt m=7: c = 7³ mod 55 = 343 mod 55 = 13 (55×6=330) ✓. Decrypt: 13^27 mod 55 = 7 ✓ (Euler guarantees it; Python confirms). Real RSA uses 2048-bit primes — the toy shows the mechanism, not the security. The hardness assumption: factoring n is infeasible; everything else is arithmetic.

notes.title: Hashing, randomness, and where number theory bites
notes.body: Non-cryptographic hashing leans on modular arithmetic: Python’s tuple hash, Java’s 31×h+c string hash, and FNV all mix via multiply-and-mod. Worked example (verified): FNV-1a-ish toy on "ab" with mod 2^8: h=0; h = (h⊕2)×33+97 mod 256: start 0⊕2=2? (use offset basis 0 for the toy) — concretely: h=((0×33)+97) mod 256 = 97; h=((97×33)+98) mod 256 = (3201+98) mod 256 = 3299 mod 256 = 227 (256×12=3072; 3299−3072=227) ✓. Different strings can collide (pigeonhole); good hashes spread uniformly. Diffie-Hellman key exchange is Fermat/Euler in action: both sides compute g^(ab) mod p from exchanged g^a, g^b — eavesdroppers face the discrete-log problem. Takeaway: whenever data meets "mod", number theory governs correctness and security margins.

handsOnLab.title: Verify number theory with Python
handsOnLab.brief: You will verify Euclid’s algorithm, Fermat’s little theorem, Euler’s theorem, and the toy RSA round-trip with Python’s built-in pow(a,e,m). Every hand computation in the notes must reproduce exactly.
steps: Open python3. Implement euclid(a,b) with the mod loop; assert euclid(48,18)==6 and euclid(1071,462)==21.
Fermat check: for prime p=7 and a in 1..6, assert pow(a,6,7)==1.
Euler check: assert pow(5,4,12)==1 (phi(12)=4) and pow(2,6,9)==1 (phi(9)=6).
Toy RSA round-trip: n=55, e=3, d=27; for m in [2,7,13,42]: c=pow(m,e,n); assert pow(c,d,n)==m. Confirm encrypt(7)==13.
Factor check: write trial_factor(360) returning [2,2,2,3,3,5]; assert product equals 360.
Break-it moment: try RSA with p=5,q=11 but e=2 (not coprime to 40) — show decryption fails for some m, and explain why.
Write up: which verifications passed and why pow(a,e,m) (modular exponentiation) is efficient while pow(a,e)%m would explode.
handsOnLab.deliverable: Write-up with all verification outputs plus the e=2 failure analysis.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: All asserts pass; the e=2 failure is explained via gcd(e,φ(n))≠1.

mockTask.q: A developer implements "encryption" as c = (m * 7) mod 55 and calls it RSA-like. What’s the fundamental problem?

It needs a bigger modulus only
mockTask.explain: Linear congruences invert instantly via extended Euclid (gcd(7,55)=1). RSA’s security comes from exponentiation + the factoring hardness, not from modular arithmetic alone.

drills.prompt: df -h shows 40% free but writes fail with 'No space left on device'. Diagnosis?

drills.title: L4 vs L7
